name: WyoFile
title: Weiser Knoll Fire explodes on South Pass, quickly becoming Wyoming’s largest wildfire of 2026
description:
The fast-moving blaze prompted evacuations and chewed through dozens of square miles of sagebrush-steppe and pinyon juniper in its first 24 hours.
The post Weiser Knoll Fire explodes on South Pass, quickly becoming Wyoming’s largest wildfire of 2026 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A wind-driven blaze tore downslope across the Wind River Range foothills Sunday and Monday, quickly chewing up enough acreage to become Wyoming’s largest wildfire of the year.
The Weiser Knoll Fire ignited on Sunday afternoon due to a mechanical fire on a trailer being towed, Fremont County Fire Protection Chief Ron Wempen told County 10 News. Within hours, the blaze was throwing up a smoke column and quickly burning through sagebrush and grasslands on South Pass — and it didn’t let up once darkness fell. 
“It burned fairly active all night,” said Jerod DeLay, Wyoming’s fire management officer. “There was some pretty extreme fire behavior yesterday, with the dry fuels and the wind and low humidity.” 
The Weiser Knoll Fire started Aug. 9, 2026, southeast of Lander and by Monday afternoon had grown to more than 13,000 acres. (InciWeb)
Trying to keep the fire west of Twin Creek Road, wildland fire crews conducted controlled fire operations and “for the most part were successful,” DeLay said. 
As of midafternoon Monday, the fire perimeter also remained confined to an area east of Wyoming Highway 28 and south of U.S. Highway 287, according to Fremont County Emergency Management Coordinator Milan Vinich.
Nevertheless, the Weiser Knoll Fire’s estimated acreage grew dramatically over its first 24 hours and reached 13,350 acres with no official containment by 3 p.m. on Monday. Winds gusted to 41 mph in nearby Lander that afternoon, and a Red Flag warning — which means there are “critical fire conditions” — remains in effect until 9 p.m. Tuesday, increasing the likelihood for growth. 
A Fremont County evacuation order remains in place for the Twin Creek drainage and portions of South Pass.

A helicopter drops water on the Weiser Knoll Fire.  (Sequeil Lozier/U.S. Wildland Fire Service)

The new U.S. Wildland Fire Service is taking the lead on the fast-growing wildfire, trying to extinguish it with a “type 3” incident management team. An estimated 85 personnel committed to the 21-square-mile blaze and a handful of aircraft have also assisted, including multiple helicopters and large and small fixed-wing air tankers. 
Wyoming State Forestry also dispatched its new Lander-based wildland firefighting team to help combat the Weiser Knoll Fire. The team was diverted from the 443-acre Bare Fire in the Wyoming Range, DeLay said. 
In the hours after the conflagration began, engines from all over Fremont County swarmed on South Pass to try to tamp down the fast-moving front of flames. 
“You had Jeffrey City, Lander, Hudson and Fremont County battalions 1, 4, 5, 12, 3, 9, and 10 on it,” Vinich told WyoFile. “BLM, U.S. Forest Service and BIA engines were also involved.” 
Wyoming so far in 2026 has mostly dodged the massive wildfires that have plagued other parts of the intermountain West. Neighboring Utah has already broken its state record for wooded and forested acres burned, the gargantuan 550,0000-acre Big Grass Fire is burning along the Oregon-Idaho state line and year-to-date acreage burned across the country is more than 50% above average and the most in at least a decade, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.
Wyoming has had an active year, too. But the Weiser Knoll Fire is the largest incident of the year, surpassing Sheridan County’s Lumin Fire, which was extinguished in late July.
“We’ve been pretty successful this year,” DeLay said. “Most of the fires have been one, two or three day events, so we’ve been pretty fortunate that way.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Court records reveal self-notarizations among non-Nebraska petitioners arrested for suspected fraud
description: At least four of the five out-of-state individuals arrested in connection with gathering allegedly fraudulent signatures on Lincoln petitions self-notarized the petition pages they circulated that have led to 10 felony charges so far.
text:
The backroom of the Lancaster County Election Commission office on April 24, 2026. Backers of three petitions seeking to restructure city elections in Lincoln submitted signatures this week to send their ideas to voters in the capital city this November.  (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — At least four of the five out-of-state individuals arrested in connection with gathering allegedly fraudulent signatures on Lincoln petitions self-notarized the petition pages they circulated that have led to 10 felony charges so far.
The five defendants each face two Class IV felony counts involving falsifying their circulator’s oath, accepting money or other things of value for signing, or offering money or other things of value in exchange for a signature on two separate petitions, according to the charges signed by Deputy Lancaster County Attorney John Schmidt. 
The five individuals facing charges and being extradited to Nebraska are:

Jessica Davis, 23, of Boynton Beach, Florida.
David Alijandro Johnson, 24, of Irvington, New Jersey.
Nathan Kirschbaum, 32, of Las Vegas, Nevada.
Jason Luciano, 32, of Las Vegas, Nevada.
Ryan C. McKinney, 41, of St. Louis, Missouri.

On 10 reviewed petition pages, Johnson is the only one of the five circulators who did not notarize his own affidavits. Each page had 20 signatures, except for one with 19, which Davis circulated.
The 199 signatures reviewed account for a fraction of the more than 4,450 signatures that local election officials flagged as suspected to be fraudulent on a petition seeking to enact term limits on Lincoln City Council members by amending the Lincoln city charter.
An additional 8,870 signatures were flagged as potentially fraudulent across two related petitions from the same petition campaign. Those efforts would amend the city charter to move the dates of city elections to align with statewide elections and allow certain residents within 3 miles of city limits to vote in municipal elections.


Local election officials rejected 65% of the signatures the Good Government Lincoln group submitted for verification. Sponsors fell short of the 4,981 valid signatures they needed on each measure.
It’s not clear if the five defendants circulated or notarized more petition pages. Circulators sign the circulator’s affidavit on each petition page they turn in, which could lead to duplicate charges.
Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie denied the Nebraska Examiner’s public records request to review the petition pages Monday. Christie wrote the records “are actively being used to investigate claims of fraud,” which is an exception under state law.
Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office investigator Brian Gruber wrote in separate probable-cause affidavits for the arrests that investigators had called “several” listed signers who confirmed they didn’t sign. Investigators also reviewed each defendant’s known cellphone number and location data, which Gruber said placed them in Nebraska on the date of notarization.
State law requires the following to be printed on all petition pages: “WARNING TO PETITION SIGNERS — VIOLATION OF ANY OF THE FOLLOWING PROVISIONS OF LAW MAY RESULT IN THE FILING OF CRIMINAL CHARGES: Any person who signs any name other than his or her own to any petition or who is not qualified to sign the petition shall be guilty of a Class I misdemeanor. Any person who falsely swears to a circulator’s affidavit on a petition, who accepts money or other things of value for signing a petition, or who offers money or other things of value in exchange for a signature upon any petition shall be guilty of a Class IV felony.”
A Class IV felony carries a maximum sentence of two years’ imprisonment and 12 months’ post-release supervision or a $10,000 fine, or both.
The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office, which oversees elections, also oversees notaries. The office and state law are clear that notaries cannot notarize their own documents.


Under state law, licensed notaries must be Nebraska residents or those living in a bordering state “if such person is employed in or has a regular place of work or business in this state and the Secretary of State has obtained evidence of an address of the physical location of such employment or place of work or business prior to such appointment and commission.”
None of the five arrested individuals have an active or expired notarial commission for Nebraska, according to a database from the Secretary of State’s Office.
Prosecutors said Friday that the investigation was still in its early stages but said they did not have evidence that ballot sponsors or specific notaries committed wrongdoing. A notary could be charged with “official misconduct” for an improper notarization.
The Good Government Lincoln campaign did not respond to questions from the Examiner on Monday regarding what oversight and training ballot sponsors provided to circulators and notaries during signature collection, and whether any changes have been made since. The Examiner also asked how the campaign hired paid circulators and notaries and whether the arrested individuals assisted in other 2026 petition campaigns with the ballot sponsors.
Jessica Flanagain, a partner with the conservative political consulting firm Axiom Strategies and a consultant to Good Government Lincoln, said Friday that “circulators are only compensated for valid signatures to eliminate any incentive for fraud.”
“We eagerly await the outcome of the criminal investigation to determine the full scope of what occurred and identify all actors, at every level, who may have been involved,” Flanagain said. “We are also considering our civil options.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: For WA GOP, a tough primary delivers alarming results
description: David Stuebe gets a lot of phone calls from constituents, more than usual these days as he campaigns for reelection to the Washington Legislature.  Ahead of this month’s primary, the first-term House Republican received a particularly jarring call. The person didn’t ask about his vote against a new state income tax on higher earners or […]
text:
Washington state lawmakers in the House chamber on the first day of the 2026 legislative session. With several incumbent House Republicans trailing in the Aug. 4 primary, Democrats are positioned to add to their majority in the chamber for 2027.  (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)David Stuebe gets a lot of phone calls from constituents, more than usual these days as he campaigns for reelection to the Washington Legislature. 
Ahead of this month’s primary, the first-term House Republican received a particularly jarring call. The person didn’t ask about his vote against a new state income tax on higher earners or his opposition to a gas tax increase that Democrats pushed through a year ago. 
They wanted to know his stance on the war with Iran, which is unfolding 7,000 miles from Stuebe’s district. That’s when it hit home. For many voters, Tuesday’s primary wasn’t about what state lawmakers were doing in Olympia. They were paying attention to Washington, D.C. 
“I honestly think people are so mad with Trump that they say, if you’re an R, then you’re a Trumpster and you’re evil,” Stuebe said. “Why aren’t people in tune? Why aren’t they looking at what’s happening with the state?”
Rep. David Stuebe, R-Washougal, is trailing a Democratic challenger as he runs for reelection to a second term in southwest Washington’s 17th Legislative District. (Photo courtesy of Stuebe campaign)
Primary results suggest that for GOP candidates in Washington, there’s no escaping headwinds created by President Donald Trump. If Republicans appeared unified with the national party, they were out of sync with the state’s electorate.  
That sentiment was especially strong in southwest Washington, where Stuebe, who also serves as mayor of Washougal, trails Diana Perez, a Democrat, by more than 4,000 votes. Stuebe’s seatmate, Kevin Waters, and two other Republican lawmakers in a neighboring district, Stephanie McClintock and John Ley are also trailing. 
“It’s absolutely nationalized,” said House Majority Leader Joe Fitzgibbon, D-West Seattle. “You have a historically unpopular president and his party is not interested in differentiating themselves from him.”
House Minority Leader Drew Stokesbary, R-Auburn, said it is “no secret” that Trump’s favorability “is underwater” in Washington. Polling also shows disenchantment with Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson and some policies pushed through by the majority Democrats in the state Legislature, he asserted.
“I do think there is some dissatisfaction with everybody in charge,” he said. “People are hungry for change. Our goal is to get out the message. Based on our polling and modeling, our message is winning over voters who go into this election with an open mind.”
‘A really big wave year’
Democrats hold 59 of the 98 seats in the state House of Representatives. With 66, they’d have a supermajority, giving them the ability to bypass Republicans to try to advance goals such as constitutional amendments protecting abortion and lowering the voter approval threshold for passing school bonds. 
Following Tuesday’s primary, Democrats are abuzz about the prospect of reaching that rarified level of political dominance. They last gained seven seats in one election cycle in 2018, the midterm election of Trump’s first term.
Fitzgibbon tamped down expectations. Conditions are ripe for a “really big wave year,” he said, but it is probably “more likely than not that we are under 66.”
Democrats are confident they’ll flip all four Republican-held seats in the 17th District, where Stuebe and Waters are running, and the 18th District, represented by McClintock and Ley.
They also are eyeing the 26th District, where Republican Katy Cornell is looking to succeed Rep. Michelle Valdez, R-Gig Harbor. Cornell’s 43.4% total is less than the combined tallies of Democrats in the primary race.
Other possible pick-ups could come in the 25th district where Republican Rep. Cyndy Jacobsen is ahead with a total under 50% and her GOP seatmate, Rep. Michael Keaton, is leading with a tally just above 50%. There are Republican-held seats in the 12th and 14th districts that could be at risk if Democrat turnout surges in the fall.
Big picture
In a state like Washington where Democrats have long held power, Republicans already have a structural disadvantage, said Ben Gaskins, a political science professor at Lewis and Clark College.
That’s only part of the story. Over the past half-century, American political parties have become far more nationalized, Gaskins said, making it harder for Republicans to separate themselves from the national party, and by extension, from Trump. 
Trump “sucks the oxygen out of all the other Republican institutions,” Gaskins said. Trump’s strong media presence coupled with his demand for unrelenting loyalty in the party make it hard for even sitting Republicans to win back power, he said.
While Republicans need to focus on November’s general election, they shouldn’t lose sight of the long term, said Mark Stephan, an associate professor of political science at Washington State University Vancouver. 
“Is their party willing to be the permanent minority party in the state of Washington?” Stephan said. “If you actually want to win elections and you actually want to maybe even have some power in the state overall, then you have to change. You have to moderate.” 
The party should lean into independent voters and away from Trump, and accept candidates that do so, he said. 
“Be principled, but be willing to compromise and be willing to have a bigger tent,” Stephan said. 
Joe Fain, Bellevue Chamber president and a former state senator, said that both Republicans and Democrats will face challenges due to the direction the national parties are heading. 
At a time when two-thirds of Washingtonians disapprove of Trump, “voters are steering clear of the Republican brand,” Fain wrote in an email. “Even the most talented local Republican candidates, of which there are several, are finding it difficult to swim against that tide.”
As for Democrats, some may conclude from the primary that the electorate is veering to the left, Fain said. 
But “the rejection of high-profile Democratic-Socialist aligned candidates, including three prominent races in downtown Seattle, show Democratic voters are right alongside Independents and many Republicans in tiring of the political side-show,” Fain said. 
‘We can save these seats’
Rep. Jim Walsh, chair of the Washington State Republican Party, called the nationalization of the election a “Democrat talking point.”
Walsh attributed the low GOP turnout to the timing of the Aug. 4 primary, stating many folks are on vacation, but he’s hopeful for the general election. 
“There are more persuadable voters in November,” Walsh said. “There are more moderate and conservative voters in November.”
GOP leaders cautioned against drawing conclusions from the primary because, they said, there was no concerted effort to turn out the base. Rather, they focused on zeroing in on voters who hadn’t made up their minds, and messaging about the records of Republicans and Democrats.
Attention will broaden to energizing the base to show up in the general election. Without Trump on the ballot, it will be tough. Republican lawmakers are counting on the presence of three ballot measures, including one to ditch the new income tax, to motivate GOP and independent voters.
Rep. Travis Couture, R-Allyn, in the House Appropriations Committee on Dec. 4, 2025. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)
“There is a lot of work to do,” said Rep. Travis Couture, R-Allyn, assistant floor leader for the caucus. “We can save these seats. These are Republican districts.”
In southwest Washington specifically, where Stuebe and the three other Republican incumbents trail, Couture expressed confidence that they will turn things around in November because “they know how to win down there.”
“There is absolutely a pathway to come back,” he said. “We just have to make sure our voters turn out.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Bankhead staying in Senate race, setting up a four-way battle
description: Alani Bankhead is running for the U.S. Senate as a Democrat to represent the Montanans with “five dollars in their pocket and a whole lot of heart,” not billionaires or corporate interests.  That’s why she’s committed to staying in the race to replace outgoing Republican Sen. Steve Daines, Bankhead said during a press conference in […]
text:
Alani Bankhead is running for the U.S. Senate as a Democrat to represent the Montanans with “five dollars in their pocket and a whole lot of heart,” not billionaires or corporate interests. 
That’s why she’s committed to staying in the race to replace outgoing Republican Sen. Steve Daines, Bankhead said during a press conference in Helena on Monday. 
Monday is the deadline for candidates to take themselves off the November ballot in Montana, and voters are set to have four candidates on the ballot. 
Bankhead won the state’s Democratic primary by 12,000 votes, but has faced stiffer competition from an independent candidate, Seth Bodnar, whose campaign has consolidated left-of-center support in the state. 
Having multiple candidates has split Democrats within Montana and nationally, many of whom see Bodnar as having a likelier path to victory. A similar trend has played out in other reliably Republican states, with the Democratic candidates in Nebraska, South Dakota and Idaho dropping out in races with independents. 
In polling, a four-way race — with Libertarian Kyle Austin — is easily won by the Republican candidate, Kurt Alme. The race becomes more competitive in a two-way race, but only Bodnar ever tops Alme, according to polls affiliated with his campaign. 
But Bankhead cited her experience as an Air Force veteran who ran special operations against child sex traffickers and as a body guard as reasons she will not back down from the challenge. 
“I already signed a blank check for my life to America 25 years ago, and that’s why I cannot be intimidated and I can’t be pushed out of this race,” Bankhead said. “That’s what makes me dangerous to the establishment — they know that I’m never going to kowtow to money or power.”
Several organizations and political action committees, as well as Democratic lawmakers, have put out explicit calls for Bankhead to drop out of the Senate race to coalesce support against Alme. 
On Monday, Bankhead said her family — including extended family members and her underage daughter— has been included on a “target list of harassment” and that her family has received death threats. 
“I find this completely unacceptable, disgusting, and unethical,” Bankhead said. “And across the board, whether you’re Republican, Democrat, independent, vegetarian, libertarian, I don’t care, this behavior is unacceptable.”
Bodnar’s campaign put out statements on Monday denouncing any efforts to contact candidates’ family members, saying that if any organization that supports him was involved, they must “stop this immediately.”
“This is completely f-ed up and we’re seeing in this senate race the exact reason people hate politics today,” Bodnar said in a video posted to social media. “I’ve never asked Alani Bankhead to drop out of this race, I’m not asking her to do that right now.”
Bodnar said his personal cell number was released recently by “Republican dark money groups,” and that those same groups have sent out fundraising emails in support of Bankhead. 
“This is what Steve Daines and Kurt Alme do,” he said. “We see it, and we reject it.”
The Montana Freedom PAC, an organization that has spent heavily supporting Bodnar’s campaign, and the Wild Montana Action Fund, also put out statements condemning the harassment of any candidate or their families. 
Bodnar addressed questions about whether he might bow out of the campaign on Friday, also vowing to stay in the race against Alme. 
Bodnar leads all candidates in fundraising and has endorsements from the state’s top organizations that often endorse Democrats, as well as from current and former elected officials. 
Bankhead has raised just under $60,000 in her campaign so far, behind the millions raised by her opponents, but she reiterated on Monday that money doesn’t always win elections, and polls don’t determine the outcomes. 
“Montanans are very clear they don’t want politicians who are bought and paid for,” Bankhead said, saying her opponents are both accepting political action committee money. “Do not disrespect grassroots Montana efforts, because I sure as hell would rather partner with Bill, who gave me five bucks, than the D.C. corporate interest that pays six and seven figures to manipulate the vote here in Montana.”
Two Bankhead supporters spoke at the press conference about their reasons for supporting her. Bankhead also listed off some of her policy plans, including protecting data from corporations and AI companies, using the military’s healthcare as a model for universal healthcare, working to address the state’s affordability crisis, and supporting the Montana Plan, an initiative to get dark money out of politics. 
“You should always know exactly who your senator answers to, and for the record, I answer to you,” Bankhead said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico health officials warn of smoke impacts as Frijoles Fire grows to more than 3,000 acres
description: New Mexico officials on Monday warned that smoke from the Frijoles Fire and other wildfires burning in the state poses health risks, particularly to the elderly and those with respiratory illnesses.
text:
The Frijoles Fire, pictured Aug. 8, 2026, has grown to more than 3,000 acres as of Aug. 10, 2026. (Photo courtesy Santa Fe National Forest)New Mexico officials on Monday warned that smoke from the Frijoles Fire and other wildfires burning in the state poses health risks, particularly to the elderly and those with respiratory illnesses.
Smoke from the Frijoles Fire, which is burning in the Pecos Wilderness and has grown to more than 3,000 acres, is currently visible from Santa Fe, Cundiyó, Nambe, Chimayó, Pojoaque and Española, according to Santa Fe National Forest officials. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Frijoles Fire was among eight, presumably lightning-caused wildfires that ignited last week in the Santa Fe National Forest, along with several others burning across the state as a heat wave collides with the expected onset of the monsoon season. 
State health and environment department officials said in a news release that people should use the “5-3-1” visibility rule in assessing their smoke risk. 
Those who are experiencing visibility limited to five miles due to smoke should limit their time outdoors if they are over age 65, pregnant or have a heart issue or respiratory illness. 
People otherwise “more likely to be affected by smoke” should stay inside if visibility is less than three miles. 
And everyone should stay inside if visibility is less than one mile due to smoke, the health department notice says, unless an evacuation notice is issued. 
“As smoke from any fire impacts the state, we encourage residents to stay informed and take steps to protect their health,” said Cindy Hollenberg, air quality bureau chief for the New Mexico Environment Department, in a statement.
The Frijoles Fire grew to roughly 3,300 acres Monday, marking a huge increase in acreage from the 500-acre footprint it reached Saturday. The fire remained 0% contained as of Monday morning, though crews were at work throughout the day building containment lines and dropping retardant and water on the blaze.
No evacuation orders are currently in place, though Santa Fe County officials have alerted residents of Cundiyo and Cerro Piñon to be on “ready” status, which means they should work on creating a wildfire buffer around their home and also keep an eye on official announcements.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Democrats, Working Families Party sue ‘Working People Party’
description: Two efforts to establish new parties in Nebraska have been sued by the Democratic and Republican parties.
text:
A Nebraska Democratic Party office in Omaha on April 3, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Democratic Party and the national Working Families Party have sued Nebraska’s Working People Party to block it from the fall ballot. 
The two objecting parties are asking Lancaster District Court Judge Darla Ideus to stop Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen from officially recognizing the party, and to declare that the party’s name is breaking state law because it is meant to confuse voters. 
“The name of the ‘Working People Party’ is clearly designed to draw a false association with independent U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn, who is supported by the Nebraska Democratic Party’s leadership and likely to receive overwhelming support from the party’s members in his challenge to the Republican incumbent U.S. Senator Pete Ricketts. Osborn has framed his campaign around giving ‘working people a seat at the table,’” the lawsuit reads. 
The lawsuit filed Monday cites state law that says the secretary of state can reject a candidate’s filing if the state’s top election official determines that someone is not a “good-faith candidate” or is trying to cause confusion for voters. The law also says objections to party names can be considered. 
A lawsuit filed last week by the Nebraska Republican Party suing the America First Party also cites that law. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb has accused U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts of being behind the effort to establish the Nebraska Working People Party. 
Republicans objected to efforts to establish the America First Party, pointing to Omaha Tribe Attorney General John Cartier’s connection to Legal Marijuana Now Senate candidate Mike Marvin.
The sponsor of the Nebraska Working People Party effort is registered Democrat Robin Richards, according to paperwork submitted to the Secretary of State’s Office. She lost as a write-in candidate in Legislative District 12 earlier this year. That district is in south-central Douglas County and includes Ralston and parts of Omaha. Following her loss, Richards endorsed incumbent Republican state Sen. Merv Riepe for the general election. 
Working Families Party is a progressive party based in New York that focuses on working-class issues. 
The lawsuit says, “The Working Families Party has worked for decades to build a reputation and brand based around its name. Although it does not currently maintain a chapter in Nebraska, the Working Families Party supports candidates aligned with its values and deliberately avoids diverting votes from those candidates in States like Nebraska.”
A Working Families Party representative told Nebraska Public Media earlier this year that it was considering legal action against the Nebraska Working People Party. 
The lawsuit from the Democratic Party adds to litigation in this Nebraska midterm cycle. Another lawsuit seeks to force Nebraska Democrats to find a replacement for their Senate nominee, Cindy Burbank, who dropped out. Burbank had previously sued to get back on the primary ballot after Evnen removed her for not being a “good faith” candidate.
The state Secretary of State’s Office announced last week that both new political parties had met the petition signature threshold. If the parties meet the deadline to submit organization documents, they must name candidates for the Nov. 3 general election by Sept. 1.
It’s unclear which races will see candidates from these two new parties, but most of the political drama has centered on the Senate race between Osborn and incumbent Republican Ricketts. The attorneys for the Democrats and the Working Families Party plan to request that their case be heard at the same time as the Republican lawsuit. 
A hearing in the Republican suit has been rescheduled for 1 p.m. Wednesday. Judge Ideus granted a new emergency injunction stopping certification of the America First Party through Aug. 20.

name: VTDigger
title: New England, Canadian leaders tout cross-border ties in face of Trump’s latest tariff threat
description:
“What we're living through right now with the tariffs, with the threat of tariffs, with some of the insults and the talking points, they're difficult. There's no way around that,” said Tim Houston, the premier of Nova Scotia.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New England, Canadian leaders tout cross-border ties in face of Trump’s latest tariff threat.
text:
Gov. Phil Scott speaks during a press conference at the end of a summit of New England governors and premiers from eastern Canada in Shelburne on Monday, August 10, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
SHELBURNE — Some of Canada’s top regional leaders on Monday touted the value of a close relationship with the U.S. and the need for both countries’ federal governments to reach a comprehensive trade deal in the face of President Donald Trump’s latest tariff threat.
Their comments to reporters at the end of this year’s New England Governors and Eastern Canadian Premiers conference came amid tense U.S.-Canada negotiations in recent days to potentially avert Trump’s proposed 50% levies on a new slate of Canadian goods, which are set to take effect next week.
The president’s on-again, off-again approach to trade policy over the past year and a half only continues to hurt the entire region, the leaders said.
“What we’re living through right now with the tariffs, with the threat of tariffs, with some of the insults and the talking points, they’re difficult. There’s no way around that,” said Tim Houston, the premier of Nova Scotia. “They’re very difficult.”
Instead, said Rob Lantz, the premier of Prince Edward Island, “We would all benefit from more free, fair, tariff-free trade.”
At the conference, regional officials and business leaders discussed ways to bolster supply chains supporting business in New England and eastern Canada that are insulated from the whims of U.S. trade policy, Lantz added. The conference included a visit to the South Burlington electric aviation company Beta Technologies, which was one of the event’s largest financial supporters, according to meeting materials.
“We want to continue that strong economic relationship that we’ve benefited from for generations,” Lantz saidHouston and Lantz addressed reporters alongside the international minister of Quebec’s provincial government, Gov. Phil Scott and officials from the five other New England states. The press conference was held at Shelburne Farms.
Gov. Phil Scott looks on as Rob Lantz, premier of Prince Edward Island, left, gives way to Tim Houston, premier of Nova Scotia, at a press conference at the end of a summit of New England governors and prime ministers from eastern Canada in Shelburne on Monday, August 10, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Trump announced last month that he would apply 50% tariffs to a wide range of Canadian products including motor vehicles, dairy products and alcohol, to take effect Aug. 19. The tariffs are a response to “Canada’s discriminatory treatment of American products” through uneven trade policies, the White House has said.
Most Canadian provinces, for example, have halted the sales of U.S.-made alcoholic beverages though haven’t restricted similar products from other countries. Some Vermont distilleries, like their counterparts around the country, have felt the pinch of those bans.
Canadian provincial leaders have told their federal government that ending those alcohol bans should be on the table in negotiations with Washington, D.C., Lantz told reporters, acknowledging that it was “an irritant” for the president.
“This seems to be an opportunity to come to a comprehensive deal and try to put most of this behind us, if not all of it, and move forward,” he said. “So those alcohol bans are simply on the table — but we would like to know what we get in return.”
Vermont officials have criticized the latest round of proposed tariffs.
Scott, a Republican, sent a letter last month to Howard Lutnick, Trump’s commerce secretary, urging the administration to reverse course for the sake of Vermont’s economic dependence on its northern neighbor. 
“We can support American workers, strengthen domestic manufacturing, and insist on fair trade without unnecessarily increasing the cost of living for working-class Americans or weakening our economic partnership with Canada,” Scott wrote.
The governor said that, as of Monday, he had yet to receive a response.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi State basketball icon Kermit Davis Sr. has died at 91
description: Kermit Davis Sr.
text:
Mississippi Sports Hall of Famer Kermit Davis Sr., a Magnolia State basketball icon, was surrounded by family when died Monday in Tupelo. He was 91.
Davis, who played basketball at Mississippi State and later coached the Bulldogs, was the father of former Ole Miss coach Kermit Davis Jr. 
Father and son share an amazing distinction: Kermit Sr. was Southeastern Conference Coach of the Year in 1971, his first year as State’s head coach. Forty-eight years later, in 2019, Kermit Jr. was SEC Coach of the Year in his first year at Ole Miss.
“Dad had 91 great years,” Kermit Davis Jr. said Monday. “I think the highest compliment a man can have is when his children all say he was their best friend. I can say that for sure, and my younger brother, Bill, says it and my sister, Jennifer, says it, too. Dad was special.”
Kermit Davis Sr. was preceded in death by his seven siblings. He was born and raised in Walnut, a small community in Tippah County in northeast Mississippi.
Basketball is king in that part of the state known as Hill Country. There, small-town high school teams are historically a huge source of community pride. Walnut was no exception. In 1954, Davis led Walnut to the state championship in the smallest classification of schools. Then, he sparked Walnut to the overall state championship, defeating much, much larger Forest Hill of Jackson in what was then known as the Tournament of Championship. 
Like father, like son: This photo of two SEC Basketball Coaches of the Year was taken in 2017 before the wedding of Kermit Davis Jr.’s daughter, Claire. That’s Kermit Davis Sr. on the left. Credit: Courtesy of the Davis family
That Walnut team was similar to the Hickory, Indiana, team made famous by the 1986 movie “Hoosiers,” which starred Gene Hackman. The movie’s Hickory team was loosely based on a real-life team from Milan, Indiana, which won the 1954 Indiana state high school championship, the same year Walnut won in Mississippi.
“Dad and I watched ‘Hoosiers’ together,” Kermit, Jr. said. “He loved that movie. He loved all the similarities. In many ways, Dad was Jimmy Chitwood,” the player who scored the winning basket for Hickory, Indiana.
Kermit Davis Sr., was much more than that. He was the first player legendary coach Babe McCarthy successfully recruited to Mississippi State. McCarthy was actually officiating one of Walnut’s games in 1954, and afterward asked Davis where he was going to play college basketball. Davis answered that he was probably going to play at Ole Miss.
McCarthy told Davis he should reconsider because he knew who the new Mississippi State coach was going to be and also knew that the coach was interested in Davis.
“Oh yeah, who’s that?” Davis asked.
Answered McCarthy: “Me.”
When Davis agreed to play at State, McCarthy asked him if he knew of any taller players State should recruit. Davis told McCarthy he should recruit a tall fellow in Tennessee Davis had once played with in junior high, a young man named Bailey Howell.
McCarthy did just that and over the next few years, Howell became a superstar and State became one of the nation’s best teams, challenging Kentucky and Adolph Rupp for SEC basketball supremacy. Howell averaged 27 points and 17 rebounds a game for his State career and many of his baskets came on passes from Davis.
After his playing days Davis became an outstanding high school coach, leading Tupelo to back-to-back state championships.
Kermit Jr. grew up going to Kermit Sr.’s games at Tupelo and then State. 
“I knew exactly what I wanted to do,” Kermit Jr. has said.
Asked what he learned most from watching his father, Kermit Jr. answered that it wasn’t so much the X’s and O’s of basketball or the strategy.
“What I got from Dad – at least what I hope I got – was his ability to handle and treat people,” Kermit Jr. said. “He was the ultimate people person. He treated people right. He cared about people and people knew it. That’s what made him who he was.”
•••
Rick Cleveland column on Kermit Davis Sr., from 2022.

name: VTDigger
title: Kinney Drugs pulls back AI tool after customer complaints
description:
The tool was causing medication delays and confusion, several of the pharmacy’s customers previously told VTDigger. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Kinney Drugs pulls back AI tool after customer complaints.
text:
Kinney Drugs inEssex Junction on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
When Kathy Callaghan called her local pharmacy for a prescription refill last Wednesday, she expected to hear the usual AI voice that had attempted to assist her for the last three months. 
Instead, a pharmacist picked up. 
“We were thrilled,” she said, describing her and her partner Dave Bellini’s reaction to the voice. 
The call came as the pharmacy, Kinney Drugs, recently pulled back its AI assistant, John Marraffa, president of the Vermont and New York pharmacy chain, told WCAX on Friday. 
In May, Kinney Drugs had implemented the AI tool, named Burt after the pharmacy’s founder, to improve patient communication and refill services. Customers, however, complained that it was coinciding with a range of issues, including medication delays, inaccurate refill information and general confusion. Privacy experts raised concerns surrounding the security of protected health information, a characterization Kinney Drugs denied. 
“Burt was introduced to improve access, convenience, and responsiveness for patients. Burt is designed to supplement pharmacy teams by handling routine, non-clinical interactions so staff can focus more time on direct patient care, clinical questions, and in-pharmacy services,” a Kinney Drugs representative previously wrote in a statement to VTDigger. 
But Marraffa acknowledged in his interview with WCAX that the new technology had been creating issues for customers, saying it did not get customer experience “right,” while defending the AI tool’s security. Marraffa and a Kinney representative did not respond to requests for comment Monday from VTDigger. 
The scaling back of the AI tool means that the pharmacy has returned to its previous prompt-based, touch-tone phone system for patient calls, Marraffa told WCAX. The AI tool will still be used for prescription refill texts. Now, however, patients must opt in to receiving these texts. 
Previously, any customer who provided their telephone number to Kinney Drugs automatically consented to interacting with the AI tool, according to the pharmacy’s terms. That lack of transparent consent was one of the many issues that both customers of Kinney Drugs and experts had with the AI.
Callaghan previously told VTDigger that she would frequently receive calls from the AI tool requesting refill orders on her prescriptions. Caught off guard, she would approve the requests, believing they were accurate. Often, however, they were not, and she received refills on prescriptions she did not need more of, she said. 

READ MORE

“They got a winning team there, and they got great humans,” Bellini said. “They should have never gone to robots. Most of their customers are old, or they got an illness. They don’t want to deal with that.”
Bellini, who previously told VTDigger that the AI tool was eroding Kinney Drugs’ small-scale feel and personable customer service, said he also brought his issues to the company itself, calling their corporate office to voice his concerns.  
A Kinney Drugs representative previously told VTDigger that the company was “aware that some patients have experienced frustration with Burt, especially during rollout,” and that it was reviewing each concern and attempting to reach each patient. 
The implementation of the AI tool came as other healthcare systems nationwide are embracing the new technology. Legal experts said the implementation was outpacing regulation, leaving consumer protection thin. In Vermont, a new data privacy bill signed by Gov. Phil Scott in June does not take effect until 2028. 
“The company finally admitted that it was a mistake,” Bellini said. “It’s just a lesson learned, and let’s go back to business as usual.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Crop report: Iowa saw ‘all modes’ of severe weather last week
description: Iowa row crops are in good conditions as of the latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, though plant pathologists in the state are starting to see disease pressure creep up.  Corn, soybean and oat acres were ahead of last year’s crop across most developmental stages, according to the report […]
text:
Corn silking in central Iowa August 4, 2025. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa row crops are in good conditions as of the latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, though plant pathologists in the state are starting to see disease pressure creep up. 
Corn, soybean and oat acres were ahead of last year’s crop across most developmental stages, according to the report for the Aug. 3 through Aug. 9 reporting period.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Just 3% of corn acres in the state have yet to reach the silking stage, according to the report, and 69% of the crop reached the dough stage, which is 3 percentage points ahead of the 2025 crop. Corn in the dent stage for the reporting period was 2 percentage points behind the year prior, with 12% of corn acres reaching the stage where the ear is firm and milk has dried out from the kernels. 
Soybean acres were 1 percentage point ahead of the 2025 crop with 93% blooming in the reporting period. Slightly more than 70% of soybean acres were setting pods, according to the report, which was 2 percentage points behind last year. 
Corn rated 78% good to excellent and soybeans 77% good to excellent. 
Oat harvest was nearly finished during the reporting period with 93% of the crop harvested — 13 percentage points ahead of the year prior. 
Soil moisture conditions improved slightly from the previous reporting period with topsoil rated 67% adequate on average and subsoil moisture rated 62% adequate. 
State Climatologist Justin Glisan said Iowa had “all modes of severe weather” during the reporting period, including several tornadoes in eastern Iowa. 
Parts of southern Iowa received more than a month’s worth of rain, according to Glisan, and the “continuous rainfall” caused flash flooding in some areas. A weather station in Murray logged 5.72 inches following the Aug. 5 storms, and Glisan wrote that more than 50 stations recorded at least 2 inches of rain from the storm. 
The weekly average precipitation for the state was 1.87, about one inch more than normal. Average temperatures for the state were near equal with the climatological normal at 74.5 degrees Fahrenheit. 
While the whole state received at least some rain, Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said it was not enough to improve drought conditions in parts of western and northwestern Iowa. 
“As excitement builds for the opening day of the Iowa State Fair, cooler temperatures and additional chances for showers will stick around for the first few days, while the forecast for the next week shows better chances of significant rainfall totals,” Naig said. 
Southern rust and other diseases hitting Iowa crops
Daren Mueller, a professor at Iowa State University and a plant pathologist with ISU Extension, said disease pressure of southern rust in Iowa corn is “way lower” than what hit the state last year. 
“Last year was a disaster – I mean, it was too much disease for a plant pathologist to enjoy, and we do like our disease,” Mueller said. “But in general, it’s way lower.” 
Mueller said he has seen southern rust in about 15-25 counties and said fungicide trials have shown that in the majority of those counties, the disease is out there, but not at “oh crap levels.”
Southern rust thrives in hot, moist weather, or as Mueller said, “if you feel like you’re walking around Arkansas, then those are good conditions for this disease.”
He said southern rust, as an obligate parasite, lives on the green tissue of a plant but won’t kill the plant. Instead, he explained, it will “suck the life out of it” by reducing photosynthesis. For farmers, this means decreased yield on the crop.
Last year, southern rust in corn caused an estimated 7%-10% reduction in yield across the state, Mueller said. 
Iowa has had the sweltering, humid conditions that plant diseases need to thrive the past couple of weeks. But, Mueller said, the conditions started later in the season than when they typically foster disease pressures that cause a lot of damage to crops. 
“There’s going to be disease developing this year – we’re not naive to that, but we just know that it started two or three weeks later, so that really helps,” Mueller said. 
Mueller said many of the most prevalent plant diseases can be mitigated with fungicide application, but the tricky part is timing the application. He said research from multiple states is compiled, and used to provide information for farmers, via the Crop Protection Network.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘One person, one vote:’ House redistricting committee gets primer
description: Joseph Breen, director of the Stennis Institute of Government, addresses a House select committee on redistricting at the Capitol on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026.
text:
A select committee of House lawmakers on Monday received a 101 lesson on the basics of redistricting from a university researcher, but focused very little on the recent Supreme Court decision that has the nation and state on edge about partisan gerrymandering and minority voting rights.
“The fundamental purpose of redistricting is equal representation — one person, one vote,” said Joseph “Dallas” Breen, director of the Stennis Institute of Government at Mississippi State University, the sole presenter at Monday’s committee meeting at the state Capitol. “… Everyone should have equal say.”
Breen with a slide presentation ran through the basic principles of redistricting: population equality, contiguity of districts, compactness, keeping “communities of interest” together, respecting political boundaries such as cities when drawing districts, and complying with federal law.
READ MORE: Mississippi lawmakers launch redistricting process after Supreme Court ruling
Speaker Jason White appointed the 16-member House committee, including only five Democrats, in May. He tasked it with considering current redistricting processes and laws, fairness, transparency and compliance with constitutional requirements. This was on the heels of the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision in a Louisiana case that weakened the federal Voting Rights Act and protections for majority Black voting districts.
But White and fellow Republican Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann have also created a joint House and Senate committee on redistricting, which is expected to do the bulk of the work of redrawing Mississippi’s legislative, judicial and congressional voting lines post Callais decision. That committee held its first meeting last week, and announced plans to hold hearings across the state later this month through September before making recommendations on new voting maps to the full Legislature.
Regardless, voting rights advocates view both committees with a gimlet eye. They fear leaders in the state Republican majority will seek to undo Black voting rights gains hard won in Mississippi only after passage of the federal VRA and decades of civil rights work to stamp out Jim Crow suppression. Despite having the largest Black population in the country, the state has had relatively few Black elected leaders, including none in statewide office or the U.S. Senate since Reconstruction.
Since the Callais decision, some GOP leaders in Mississippi and Washington, D.C., have called for heavy partisan gerrymandering, including redrawing of incumbent U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson’s district to help oust him, the state’s only Black member of Congress and only Democrat.
Voting rights advocates held a press conference before the select committee meeting on Monday, and questioned why it even exists.
“Why are we really here?” said Sonya Williams-Barnes, Southern Poverty Law Center’s policy director for Mississippi. “It definitely has organizations such as mine on alert … We just redistricted (legislative seats) last year … I believe in the hearing process and hearing from the public, but that seems like an important part missing so far, hearing from average everyday citizens … Our duty is to ensure that we protect Democracy here in our state.”
Rep. Noah Sanford, co-chairman of the House select committee and vice chairman of the joint redistricting committee, said the House committee is primarily a “study committee.” And he said fear of major upheavals from redistricting are unfounded.
“I would just tell people at this point to keep an open mind,” Sanford said. “Any map passed would have to have 62 votes (in the House). So I don’t expect some major redraw that totally changes districts across the entire state, because we would never get 62 votes to do that anyway. People are generally comfortable with the communities they already represent.”
Sanford said his understanding of the Callais decision is that “maps have to be drawn race neutral.” 
“I don’t anticipate major changes (in legislative redistricting),” Sanford said. “… My intention is to try to keep counties together and cities together. There is a small town in my district that I represent half the city, and another member represents the other half of the town. That should not be. That other member lives two counties away. I live 15 minutes away. We need to get rid of that.”
Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, like many other GOP governors, after the Callais decision, faced pressure from the Trump administration and others to call a special legislative session and redraw congressional voting maps ahead of Novembers midterm federal elections. But Mississippi had already held its midterm primaries in March, and such a last-minute redrawing now appears unlikely. However, Reeves has indicated he’s likely to call lawmakers into special session by year’s end for state legislative redistricting ahead of next year’s statewide elections.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Federal judge dismisses legal challenges to South Dakota drug discount law
description: A judge has ruled in favor of a South Dakota law that helps rural healthcare providers buy discounted drugs and mark up their sale price to fill budget holes created by low Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement rates. AbbVie, maker of the arthritis drug Humira, among other medications, sued the state in April 2025. The Chicago-based […]
text:
The federal courthouse in Sioux Falls is pictured in November 2022. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of a South Dakota law that helps rural healthcare providers buy discounted drugs and mark up their sale price to fill budget holes created by low Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement rates. (John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)A judge has ruled in favor of a South Dakota law that helps rural healthcare providers buy discounted drugs and mark up their sale price to fill budget holes created by low Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement rates.
AbbVie, maker of the arthritis drug Humira, among other medications, sued the state in April 2025. The Chicago-based company argued that South Dakota lawmakers unconstitutionally regulated interstate commerce with Senate Bill 154, which they passed and Gov. Larry Rhoden signed into law earlier that year.
The drug company AstraZeneca filed a similar lawsuit last August, and the trade group Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America filed one in September.
The law, which took effect last year, blocks drug companies from restricting which pharmacies health care providers can use to access discounts through the federal 340B program. It requires drugmakers who want to participate in Medicare and Medicaid to offer steep discounts to hospitals and clinics that deliver care to underserved or vulnerable populations. Providers who qualify for 340B can then upcharge patients for the drugs, which helps them pay their bills when federal reimbursement rates are too low to cover the cost of providing service.
South Dakota among states to restrict drug company contracting
The 340B program initially required discounts for providers that serve mostly Medicaid clients. It was expanded to “sole providers” under the Affordable Care Act in 2010, which opened it up to rural healthcare providers in places like South Dakota. Federal guidance issued that same year also allowed participating providers to contract with an unlimited number of pharmacies. Until then, providers had to use one.
In response to the expanding 340B usage that followed, drug companies have moved to restrict the pharmacies through which providers can purchase discounted drugs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Supporters of Senate Bill 154 argued that such restrictions can put 340B discounts out of reach for rural hospitals that need the financial boost of participation to stay open and serve their rural clientele.
Other states have passed similar laws, and faced similar lawsuits. 
The laws amount to an unconstitutional “taking” of drug company property through forced discounts, the lawsuits have argued, as well as to state-level regulations on interstate commerce. They also argue that because 340B is a federal program, states can’t regulate it.
Judge: South Dakota law is constitutional, protects ‘legitimate interest’ 
The ruling from U.S. District Judge Roberto Lange dismissed all three lawsuits against South Dakota. Lange relied in part on appeals court rulings supporting similar laws in states including Arkansas and Missouri. 
Lange noted that 340B participation is optional. Other courts, and now Lange, have ruled that drug companies cannot opt into a voluntary program and then argue that their products have been taken without just compensation. 
Drugmaker sues SD over law preserving broad access to discounts for hospitals, pharmacies

The judge also ruled that South Dakota’s law does not unfairly burden interstate commerce, in part because the state has a “legitimate interest in regulating the delivery of 340B drugs ultimately dispensed to its citizens.”
To the argument that the state cannot change the setup of a federal program, Lange ruled that South Dakota’s law deals with the delivery of drugs. It doesn’t make any changes to the federal law, he wrote, because the federal law deals with drug pricing.
South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley praised Lange’s decision in a press release.
“This ruling guarantees that our healthcare providers will continue to access these discounted medications and use them in ways that best serve their communities,” Jackley wrote.
AbbVie appealed Lange’s decision to the Eighth Circuit on Monday morning. AstraZeneca and Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America had not appealed as of Monday afternoon. Lawyers for the latter two did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: With feds’ eyes on quantum technology, Utah pushes its own efforts
description: Following similar steps of elected officials in Washington D.C., Utah Gov. Spencer Cox is spearheading the state’s own push to bolster quantum technology development with a new executive order. The technology, often used to create tools in computing, sensing and communications by applying the principles of quantum physics, has been in the eye of leaders […]
text:
Gov. Spencer Cox speaks during a news conference broadcast by PBS Utah in Salt Lake City on Thursday, March 19, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune) Following similar steps of elected officials in Washington D.C., Utah Gov. Spencer Cox is spearheading the state’s own push to bolster quantum technology development with a new executive order.
The technology, often used to create tools in computing, sensing and communications by applying the principles of quantum physics, has been in the eye of leaders across the country, including President Donald Trump, who signed an executive order in June directing his cabinet to accelerate its deployment.
The state, Cox said in his own executive order signed Monday, will create the Utah Quantum Initiative and the Quantum Coordination Council, a governing body to oversee the effort led by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Quantum technology is going to change how we compute, communicate, manufacture, discover new medicines and defend our country, and Utah has the people and infrastructure to help lead that transformation,” Cox said in a statement. 
“We already have world-class researchers, a strong semiconductor and advanced manufacturing base, a growing technology sector and important defense assets,” he said. “This initiative is about connecting those strengths, building a workforce ready for what comes next and making sure the technologies of the future are invented, built and put to work here in Utah.”
While quantum technologies are still under development, Cox’s office said in a press release they have the potential to “create extraordinarily precise sensors and enable advances across national security, medicine, energy, manufacturing and other industries.” 
The move also follows bipartisan intentions to increase federal funding to improve the country’s odds against China in the race to develop quantum computing advances, according to a report from Bloomberg. The U.S. House is expected to debate increasing the annual military spending on the technology by 68% to $567 million sometime this year.
The state doesn’t need to build a quantum ecosystem from scratch, Jefferson Moss, commissioner of the Governor’s Office of Economic Development, said in a news release. Some pieces are already in Utah, including research teams in state universities and high-performance computing infrastructure.



Let us know what you think...


 


Utah’s semiconductor, electronics and advanced manufacturing sector may also play a role in the state’s endeavor, the release says.
“Our job is to connect our researchers, manufacturers, entrepreneurs, investors and workforce around a common strategy,” Moss said. “If we do that well, Utah can become a place where quantum discoveries move from the laboratory into companies, products and real-world applications.”
One of the priorities of the Utah initiative is to develop career pathways and education programs to increase the workforce that’s expected to work in the industry, as well as supporting the commercialization of quantum technologies. 
The order also directs those involved in the initiative to “develop a defense-sector strategy focused on quantum sensing and communications,” to pursue federal funding opportunities and to identify policy strategies to advance the technology.
By March, 2027, the Quantum Coordination Council is expected to deliver a “quantum landscape report,” identifying the state’s infrastructure, manufacturing and workforce assets, as well as gaps and opportunities to attract investment.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas professor falsely accused of espionage wants university to pay for firing, harm to reputation
description: TOPEKA — An anonymous tip accusing a Chinese-American chemist and researcher of espionage spurred the University of Kansas into action, notifying the U.S. Department of Justice and building a case against its own employee, Feng “Franklin” Tao said in a lawsuit. Tao was a tenured chemical engineering professor at KU in 2019 when he became […]
text:
From left, Gisela Perez Kusakawa, executive director of the Asian American Scholar Forum, Haipei Shue, president of United Chinese Americans, Peter Zeidenberg, Franklin Tao’s criminal defense attorney, and Tao’s wife, Hong Peng, appear in 2023 outside of the Robert J. Dole Federal Courthouse in Kansas City, Kansas. They spoke after Tao was sentenced following a criminal convictions of making a false statement, which was eventually overturned. “We will as a community fight for the equal treatment of Chinese Americans going forward,” Shue said. (Photo by Chloe Anderson for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — An anonymous tip accusing a Chinese-American chemist and researcher of espionage spurred the University of Kansas into action, notifying the U.S. Department of Justice and building a case against its own employee, Feng “Franklin” Tao said in a lawsuit.
Tao was a tenured chemical engineering professor at KU in 2019 when he became one of the first professors arrested under the first Trump administration’s “China Initiative,” a DOJ campaign purportedly created to thwart economic espionage and intellectual property theft.
After a federal indictment, a criminal conviction and an acquittal by an appeals court, Tao said in a lawsuit filed July 21 in federal court that the university violated state and federal workplace discrimination protections and caused harm to his reputation and career prospects.
The lawsuit is Tao’s second against KU. He sued in 2025 in an attempt to regain his job and claimed the university discriminated against him. The July lawsuit accused KU of retaliating because of the 2025 discrimination complaints.
Central to the newest lawsuit is KU’s choice to create a temporary faculty review board, made up of non-tenured faculty, that was tasked with wading through charges against Tao.
“By installing non-tenured faculty — whose careers and advancement remain subject to KU’s discretion — KU compromised the very independence the FRB was designed to protect by creating exactly the kind of conflict of interest that the policy was meant to prevent,” his lawsuit said.
Tao objected to the review board’s makeup, but the board dismissed his concerns in March of this year, according to the lawsuit.
It said Tao had been left again “unable to contest the charges against him, unable to secure reinstatement, and indefinitely denied the fair process to which he is entitled.”
KU had not responded to the lawsuit as of Monday. According to the complaint, Tao accepted a non-tenured position in April in Arizona.
Tao asked KU to pay him for lost wages and an unspecified amount for “reputational injury, emotional distress, pain and suffering.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Facing criminal charges, former nursing home worker surrenders his license
description: A nurse who landed a job in an Iowa care facility last fall after Nebraska officials labeled him a “significant risk” to the public has agreed to voluntarily surrender his Iowa license. The nurse, Raymond DeLeon of Glenwood, is currently facing a felony charge of neglect or abandonment of a dependent person. Prosecutors allege that […]
text:
The Garden View Care Center in Shenandoah, Iowa. (Photo via Google Earth)A nurse who landed a job in an Iowa care facility last fall after Nebraska officials labeled him a “significant risk” to the public has agreed to voluntarily surrender his Iowa license.
The nurse, Raymond DeLeon of Glenwood, is currently facing a felony charge of neglect or abandonment of a dependent person. Prosecutors allege that on Nov. 12, 2025, he left the Garden View Care Center in Shenandoah when he was the only licensed nurse on duty.
DeLeon has pleaded not guilty to the charge and a trial is scheduled for Aug. 25, 2026.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
DeLeon’s licensing issues stem from action taken by Nebraska regulators last year prior to his employment in Iowa.
Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services records indicate DeLeon, a 66-year-old licensed practical nurse, was working at Douglas County Health Center, a 254-bed nursing home in Omaha, in February 2024 when the facility received what the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services calls “photographic evidence of DeLeon using illicit controlled substances.”
After DeLeon refused the facility’s request that he submit to drug testing, he was allegedly fired for unlawful use of a controlled substance in the workplace or reporting for work while under the influence of drugs or alcohol, incompetence in performing his assigned nursing duties, and engaging in activities prejudicial to his employer’s reputation.
Declaring that DeLeon to posed a “significant risk to public safety,” the department revoked his privileges to work as a nurse in Nebraska on Aug. 2, 2025.
With his Iowa license unaffected by that decision, DeLeon continued to work as a nurse in Iowa and in September 2025, was hired at the Garden View Care Center, a state-licensed nursing home in Fremont County.
According to state inspectors, the administrator at Garden View later explained that when she hired DeLeon last year, she was aware of some sort of adverse action against his license in Nebraska and had asked DeLeon about that. Inspectors allege the administrator told them DeLeon informed her that his girlfriend had taken a photo of him smoking marijuana and sent it to his employer.
The administrator allegedly told the inspectors that since she had started work at the home in July 2025, the facility had not been checking the references of job applicants and new hires.
A registered nurse at Garden View allegedly told the inspectors DeLeon would routinely leave the building during his overnight shift, would go out to his car, and would then return “hyped up” to complete his shift. The registered nurse allegedly added that she wouldn’t give DeLeon the keys to the home’s narcotics cabinet because she didn’t trust him — a concern she said she had relayed to the home’s management.
State records indicate that around 1 a.m. on Nov. 12, 2025, while working the overnight shift at Garden View, DeLeon went out to his vehicle to smoke and then drove away, before his shift had ended, to purchase gasoline for his vehicle.
According to police, DeLeon was pulled over about 1:15 a.m. by a Fremont County deputy, allegedly after driving on Highway 59 with no lights on. The deputy reported following DeLeon into the parking lot at Garden View, and then arresting DeLeon after finding a glass methamphetamine pipe, with residue, in the vehicle’s glove compartment.
DeLeon was subsequently convicted of possession of methamphetamine and at sentencing received a deferred judgment that will result in his conviction being wiped from his record after the successful completion of a year’s probation. A charge of possession of drug paraphernalia was dismissed.
At some point, the Iowa Board of Nursing filed disciplinary charges against DeLeon, accusing him of being subject to disciplinary action in another state, being involved in the unauthorized possession or use of a controlled substance, excessive use of drugs and/or alcohol, engaging in behavior that is contradictory to professional decorum, and leaving a nursing assignment without properly ensuring the safety and welfare of patients.
Board records give conflicting information as to when those charges were filed. The board’s published Statement of Charges is dated Sept. 8, 2025, but references board action three months later in December 2025. Recently, the board agreed to accept DeLeon’s voluntary surrender of his Iowa license, and in that agreement the board indicated the disciplinary charges against DeLeon were filed in March 2026.
Garden View is currently one of two Iowa nursing homes designated a “special-focus facility” by the federal government. Such facilities are considered to be among the worst nursing homes in the nation due to serious and recurring deficiencies in resident care.
Garden View has been designated a special-focus facility for 12 months. It currently has no quality rating on the federal government’s Nursing Home Compare website due to what the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services calls a “history of serious quality issues.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach DeLeon or his attorney for comment.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC students improve in math and reading, though less than half meet math benchmarks
description: The annual SC READY test, given to third- through eighth-graders is generally seen as an indicator of how well students are performing.
text:
Second grade students work on math equations at Seven Oaks Global Magnet in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Oct. 27, 2025. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Elementary and middle school students have posted their best scores yet on end-of-year standardized tests, though more than half still can’t calculate as expected for their age, according to state standardized testing data released Monday.
Third- through eighth graders continued to improve in both math and reading, though scores were still generally stronger in reading, according to results from the annual SC READY tests.
Just over 61% of all students tested in the spring could read on grade level, an almost 2 percentage-point improvement over last year’s statewide average. Nearly 48% could do math as expected for their grade, up from 44%.
Less than half of SC’s 3rd to 8th graders can do math on grade level, as reading scores surge

In both cases, more students are meeting or exceeding expectations for their grade levels than any year since the test’s introduction in 2015.
“These results tell a powerful story about what’s possible for South Carolina’s future,” state Superintendent Ellen Weaver said in a news release. “Our students are proving they can compete with anyone, anywhere.”
The state Department of Education has pointed to changes in how students learn to read as a big reason for improvements in English scores. A similar program training teachers in different ways of teaching math, known as the Palmetto Math Project, launched this spring, and state officials hope that will help springboard math results as well.
“This is the new starting line, not the finish line,” Weaver’s statement continued. “Just like a GPS, this data helps us locate ourselves on the map, to celebrate how far we’ve come and to focus our planning for the journey still ahead.”
Students’ scores are moving closer to the department’s 2030 goal that three-quarters of all students perform at or above grade level in both subjects. Just two districts met that goal in reading this year: York 4 in Fort Mill and Anderson 4 in Pendleton. No districts have scores that high in math.
The education department highlighted the work done at Meeting Street Elementary at Burns in North Charleston, where students were among the most improved in both math and English. Scores across the board increased 22 percentage points this year compared to last, with nearly 65% of students performing at grade level in both subjects.
Nearly 90% of students at the school live in poverty, which usually leads to lower test scores because of stressors outside the classroom and fewer resources to help struggling students.
The school is one of four Meeting Street schools, which operate under a public-private partnership in an effort to give low-income students the support they need to succeed. The schools receive support from philanthropist Ben Navarro, who supports various education initiatives through Beemok Education.
“Together, we’re demonstrating that innovative approaches can deliver extraordinary results for students and help change the landscape of public education in South Carolina,” said Josh Bell, president of Beemok Education, in a news release. “We’re proud of the meaningful progress we’ve made, and we’re just getting started.”
Younger students continued to outperform their older peers in both math and reading.
About 59% of eighth graders were reading on grade level, compared with 64% of third graders and 66% of fourth graders.
Similarly, 44% of eighth graders could do math as expected, while 59% of third graders were hitting their grade’s benchmarks, according to the statewide data.

title: Trump urges shift in childhood vaccine recommendations, calls for splitting up MMR vaccine
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Monday signed a sweeping executive order that aims to reshape guidance surrounding childhood vaccines, standing alongside Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and was met with immediate pushback.The order — which calls on federal programs and funding to “support maximal parental choice over childhood vaccines” — came as Trump continued to erroneously connect vaccines with autism during the White House event and his administration has sought to de-emphasize childhood vaccinations’ importance. “This updated recommendation finally aligns the United States with other advanced and developed nations around the world,” Trump said during a signing ceremony in the Oval Office, joined by Kennedy, a longtime opponent of vaccines, as well as National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya and “Make America Healthy Again” advocate Jayme Franklin, also founder and CEO of The Conservateur lifestyle brand, and others.“More importantly, it aligns us with common sense and knowledge,” Trump added.What the order can legally accomplish was unclear as it’s up to states to decide which recommendations to follow.GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, rebutted the new order on social media. “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” Cassidy said. “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism.”Splitting up MMR vaccineThe order recognizes “gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations” and divides the childhood immunization recommendations into three categories. The order recommends all children receive immunizations for 11 diseases, including for “measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella.” Immunizations recommended for certain high-risk groups or populations include: “respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue.” The order also lists “hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza, and COVID-19” as immunizations “based on shared clinical decision-making.” Trump’s executive order also calls for splitting up the combined measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into three separate single-disease shots and recommends that “all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits.” Such single-disease shots are not currently available in the United States, White House officials acknowledged on a background call, but said they believe work will occur in the private sector to make that option eventually available. “For example, at one year, you should have five separate visits for vaccines rather than getting them all in the same day,” Trump said during the signing ceremony. Trump said the order also directs the attorney general “to advance legal challenges against states that violate children’s rights to religious or medical vaccination exemptions.” ‘Uncertainty and fear and confusion’Meanwhile, Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, told reporters Monday during a press briefing after the Trump event that “the only thing that I can see is going to happen as a result of the announcement from today is an injection of greater amounts of uncertainty and fear and confusion, when there doesn’t need to be any of that.” Many states rely on the AAP, rather than the federal government, for guidance surrounding childhood vaccines, according to the health research organization KFF, following earlier moves on vaccines during the Trump administration.Rep. Frank Pallone, ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, blasted Trump’s order, saying the effort “lets political appointees attempt to overrule decades of peer-reviewed science and dictate vaccine schedules to American families,” in a statement. The New Jersey Democrat added that “parents deserve accurate, trusted medical guidance, not a White House-curated list designed to rubberstamp Secretary Kennedy’s radical anti-vaccine agenda.” Democrats from a coalition of states filed suit earlier this year over Trump administration changes to the federal vaccine guidelines, as did medical groups, but White House officials said Trump's recommendations were not related to the litigation and were within his authority.
