title: State finalizing agreements for about $39 million in Rural Health Transformation funding, Singh says
description: The West Virginia Department of Health is finalizing agreements to award approximately $39 million in federal funding from the Rural Health Transformation program, state lawmakers were told Monday.
text:
Dr. Arvin Singh, secretary of the West Virginia Department of Health, addresses lawmakers about the Rural Health Transformation program during legislative interims on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026 in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)The West Virginia Department of Health is finalizing agreements to award approximately $39 million in federal funding from the Rural Health Transformation program, state lawmakers were told Monday. 
The program is on track to obligate its entire $199 million in Rural Health funds by Oct. 30 to meet a federal deadline, state Health Secretary Arvin Singh said. 
Singh gave an update on the program to the Legislature’s Joint Committee on Finance. The state is not releasing names of the agencies getting the funds “until grant agreements and contracts are fully executed,” Singh said.
“A lot of these awardees, we are working and negotiating statements of work, so we don’t want to get ahead of that,” Singh said.  
During legislative interim meetings in May, Singh told lawmakers the state would pay $12 million in consulting fees to the firm KGMP for helping to set up the Rural Health Transformation program this year. Singh said Monday the final contract amount is lower — about $8 million. 
“When we submitted our application. We did our best estimate of what we could project we would estimate for contractor support,” he said.
He said the state budgeted about $18.8 million in total for administrative costs — including the consulting fees — for the year, but now projects it will actually spend about $10 million. 
“With that additional administrative dollars that we will save the state of West Virginia, which we are projecting to be around $8 million, we are looking to reinvest those administrative dollars into programmatic dollars to reinvest into the state of West Virginia,” Singh said.
The five-year Rural Health Transformation Program is funded by the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The program was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed into law last summer. The bill makes historic cuts to healthcare spending in the United States. 
The program has awarded West Virginia nearly $199 million for the first year. Singh said the state anticipates the federal government will announce year 2 funding for states on Oct. 31.
Under Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s plan for the federal program, schools, libraries and other community institutions in rural West Virginia would be outfitted for use in telemedicine. The state also plans to use the funding to address the state’s healthcare worker shortage by recruiting high school students to healthcare careers, adding healthcare faculty at regional and technical colleges and using financial incentives to attract and keep providers in rural areas. 
Another of the initiatives, the Rural Health Link, would provide patients access to transportation to medical appointments using public buses, rideshare services and volunteer drivers.
The state has until October to obligate the funds and until September 2027 to actually spend the money, he said.
Of the 75 candidates that have been chosen to receive funding, 73 are West Virginia-based agencies, Singh said. The remaining two have a connection with the state — one operates a facility in West Virginia and another partners with organizations from the state, he said. 
Approximately $4.6 million of the funding has actually been spent — all on administrative costs, Singh said. 
Singh said the department has drafted all of the funding opportunities for this year of the program and have so far posted publicly more than 80% of them. More information about the Rural Health Transformation program and grant opportunities is available on the state Department of Health website.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Senate plan shifts energy costs — it doesn’t eliminate them
description: While customers may see some short-term bill relief, securitization does not eliminate costs. It shifts them, and consumers ultimately still pay the same amount, or more.
text:
THE MASSACHUSETTS SENATE recently advanced an energy affordability bill intended to lower costs, but the fine print tells a different story. 
It approved a complex proposal called “securitization” that has been promoted as a way to save customers billions of dollars on energy costs. But this financing tool deserves scrutiny to determine whether it will actually save money or simply move costs around. 
In simple terms, securitization turns certain utility costs into long-term bonds that are repaid by customers over time through their energy bills. Because these bonds are backed by a dedicated charge on customer bills, they can often be issued at lower interest rates. 
That may sound like a cost saver. While customers may see some short-term bill relief, securitization does not eliminate costs. It shifts them, and consumers ultimately still pay the same amount, or more. 
To be clear, this tool has been used responsibly in moderation to target one-time, unexpected expenses, such as in Michigan, Florida, and Louisiana. When I served as chairman of the Michigan utility regulator, we enabled seven coal plants to retire early by securitizing the remaining $378 million of costs at a lifetime savings of $135 million. Florida and Louisiana have successfully securitized the costs of storm recovery from one-time unexpected hurricanes.  
But the Senate’s proposal takes a different approach. It would expand securitization beyond limited use and allow it to be applied repeatedly to routine grid investment costs associated with the Commonwealth’s energy transition. 
This will compound over time and drive higher bills for households and businesses. 
For example, Massachusetts energy efficiency programs, Mass Save, run in three-year cycles. Under this proposal, each new cycle could be financed with new bonds before earlier bonds are fully repaid. Rather than reducing costs, this would layer additional repayment charges onto customer bills, creating multiple overlapping charges. 
For consumers and businesses already facing high energy prices and a rising cost of living, this cost layering is concerning. It does not meaningfully lower energy prices; it simply changes the timing of payment. 
There is also a broader issue that has received little attention. Massachusetts’s utility system is built on a long-standing framework. Utilities invest private capital to build and maintain infrastructure, and those investments are reviewed, scrutinized, and approved by the Department of Public Utilities. In return, customers pay rates that include a limited, regulated return. That structure helps ensure accountability while attracting the investment needed to keep the system safe and reliable over time. 
Excessive use of securitization changes that model. 
Instead of utilities financing investments and earning a regulated return, customers effectively take on that role by repaying long-term debt directly. At the same time, utilities remain responsible for operating the system and meeting strict safety and reliability standards. 
Using securitization broadly to finance ongoing investments shifts risk to customers and undermines the long-term investment framework that keeps the system safe and reliable. Rather than investors bearing the financial risk, more of that responsibility is transferred directly to customers through long-term charges on their bills. 
There are also practical financial implications. When more costs are shifted off the traditional model and into long-term bonds, it can weaken a utility’s financial profile. That, in turn, can lead to higher borrowing costs for investments that still rely on conventional financing. Over time, those higher financing costs are passed back to customers, offsetting some or all of the intended savings. 
The Senate has suggested this proposal, which is now part of negotiations with the House over a final version of the energy bill, could deliver billions in savings, but that assumption deserves scrutiny. Securitization becomes less effective when it is overused. Repeated securitization transactions will dull the savings. Savings successfully achieved from targeted, limited securitization transactions cannot be broadly extrapolated to repeated overlapping transactions involving routine grid investment costs. 
For employers and ratepayers, the relevant question is straightforward: What will this mean for bills not just next year, but five or 10 years from now? 
To maintain its competitive edge and attract investment and talent, Massachusetts needs to focus on meaningfully lowering major cost drivers, including energy. 
Energy policy should be grounded in transparency and long-term value, not short-term optics. Complexity should not be a substitute for clarity, especially when the stakes for Massachusetts families and businesses are so high. 
John Quackenbush served as the chairman of the Michigan Public Service Commission from 2011 to 2016 and is a chartered financial analyst. He is the president of JQ Resources LLC and serves as a regulatory strategy consultant for National Grid.

name: National
title: New drug-resistant fungal disease increases among vulnerable patients
description: Twenty-eight states this year have reported over 3,500 cases of patients sick with the drug-resistant yeast candida auris, which can cause severe illness and is often reported in healthcare facilities. As of Aug. 1, 3,544 clinical cases of candida auris, or C. auris, have been reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, […]
text:
More than half the states have reported cases this year of people sick with candida auris, a drug-resistant fungus. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Twenty-eight states this year have reported over 3,500 cases of patients sick with the drug-resistant yeast candida auris, which can cause severe illness and is often reported in healthcare facilities.
As of Aug. 1, 3,544 clinical cases of candida auris, or C. auris, have been reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, compared with 4,262 the same time last year, according to the latest round of numbers from the agency’s National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System. 
Cases had risen from 2022 to 2024, and seen a slight decline since then. But experts are still concerned, as Candida auris can be difficult to treat because it’s resistant to multiple antifungal drugs. 
The first U.S. case was first reported in 2016. Between 2019 and 2021, 17 states identified their first-ever candida auris case, according to federal reports, with experts calling the yeast an emerging, urgent threat for hospitalized patients. It was first described in Japan in 2009. 
People without risk factors generally don’t get infected, the CDC says. Risk factors include severe underlying medical conditions and people undergoing complex medical care. Candida auris symptoms can vary depending on the location of the infection — such as a superficial skin infection or widespread bloodstream infection — and its severity. While there isn’t a specific set of symptoms, people can experience fever or chills. 
Tuberculosis cases have been rising as public health agencies struggle to keep up

The infection spreads more easily in healthcare or long-term care facilities among people who are already very sick with complex health conditions. Patients with breathing or feeding tubes or catheters have a higher risk.
The CDC identifies detections via two separate reports: clinical detections in people who are ill with candida auris, and screenings — public health investigation tests that detect fungal colonizations in patients who haven’t developed illness. As of Aug. 1, the nation has seen 3,325 screening detections, compared with 3,724 last year, in addition to the 3,500 clinical cases. People who have screened for colonizations can spread the fungus to other people and surfaces.
California reported the most clinical cases of any state this year, at 887.
States across the South have seen over 1,400 clinical cases, with Texas reporting the highest number in that region at 437 diagnoses, followed by Tennessee (293) and Georgia (193).
In the Northeast, only New Jersey and Pennsylvania reported cases — 55 and 131, respectively. 
Mountain states have seen 200 clinical cases — with the majority in Arizona, which has reported 171 clinical cases.
Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio and Wisconsin have collectively reported 751 clinical cases, according to the CDC.

name: Maryland Matters
title: How Maryland’s partisan election system disenfranchises a quarter of voters
description: There's an election in November, but for many Maryland offices the winners were picked in the primary, writes Roberto Alejandro, disenfranchising not only voters not affiliated with a party but the unaffiliated candidates who face a steep hill just to get on the ballot.
text:
Voting at the Portland Expo in Maine’s June 9, 2026, primary election. Maryland prohibits unaffiliated voters from voting in the state's partisan primaries, essentially disenfranchising close to a quarter of registered voters, writes Roberto E. Alejandro. (Photo by Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star)The party primary season recently wrapped up in Maryland.  Unfortunately, for many Maryland offices, there will be no real general election, as the primaries have already settled the races. This means many Marylanders end up disenfranchised, playing no role in the election.
This is especially true of the roughly one-quarter of Maryland voters registered as unaffiliated. These voters are both functionally excluded from elections as well as denied the opportunity to see unaffiliated candidates on the general election ballot.
In the 2024 presidential election, 22% of Maryland voters, almost a quarter, were registered as unaffiliated according to Maryland State Board of Elections data. Yet someone who wants to run for office as a voice for this significant population faces steep hurdles.
To run as a Democrat or Republican, one simply pays a modest fee to register in that party’s primary. In contrast, someone who wishes to run as an unaffiliated candidate must obtain 10,000 signatures from registered voters in order to get on the ballot. This is a high bar and prevents unaffiliated candidates from running for office and offering a meaningful alternative to the major parties.
The General Assembly oversees our election law and is dominated by Democratic and Republican partisans. These partisans have tilted the field to effectively exclude unaffiliated candidates from running and unaffiliated voters from participating in elections.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Unaffiliated voters are disenfranchised because Maryland’s election rules often ensure that a partisan primary, not the general election, determines who will hold a given office, cutting unaffiliated voters and members of other parties out of the election process.
The Maryland Constitution states that, “The People of this State have the sole and exclusive right of regulating the internal government.” Unfortunately, depending on the district where you live, only voters registered with a particular party have any say in the regulation of our internal government.
The consequences are obvious. A broadly unaccountable Democratic legislature has made Maryland unaffordable for working families. Our taxes are higher than those of our neighboring states with less efficient government services. Utility bills routinely crush family budgets. Businesses bear unnecessary fee and compliance burdens whose costs are built into the goods and services residents purchase, thus functioning as regressive taxes that raise cost of living.
Our MVA fees have become so obscene that many residents would rather drive all the way to Virginia and falsify a government record than pay them. Increasingly, Marylanders are simply moving to lower cost states in response.
That so many Marylanders have no say in the makeup of the legislature has not only impacted cost of living, it has fostered corruption, particularly among Democrats. Sheila Dixon, Nat Oaks, Cheryl Glenn, Catherine Pugh, Marilyn Mosby. How many Democratic office holders in a predominantly blue state have to enter plea deals before space is made for meaningful alternatives?
The party system cannot be relied upon to offer such alternatives. If you live in a predominantly Democratic district, you are faced with a Republican party that has veered so far right that Larry Hogan, a two-term governor of a blue state, no longer has a place in it. If you live in a predominantly Republican district, you are faced with a Democratic party increasingly defined by self-styled socialists whose approach to policy will never make your cost of living lower and often consists of distractions. Maryland’s third parties, whether the Libertarians, Greens, or No Labels, have made no compelling case for how they would be different from the mainstream parties and often fail to recruit or nominate qualified candidates for office.
Unaffiliated voters are not seeking a third party, in any event, and there is little to recommend additional forays down the partisan path. Unaffiliated candidates have an opportunity to serve as a corrective to poor partisan choices, if only they could get ballot access.
It may be argued that the 10,000-signature requirement prevents unelectable candidates from running. There are two obvious responses. First, unelectable candidates routinely run in the partisan primaries. Second, it is the people’s prerogative to determine who is a valid or electable candidate, not the General Assembly’s, and certainly not on an a priori basis.
The Partisans in the General Assembly who set election rules have disenfranchised a quarter of Maryland voters. By removing the 10,000-signature requirement for unaffiliated candidates, space would be made for unaffiliated candidates to state their case and potentially garner enough support among a combination of unaffiliated voters and those registered with minority parties to make our general elections competitive again.

title: Todd Blanche sworn in as attorney general after contentious Senate confirmation
text: WASHINGTON — Todd Blanche took the oath of office as U.S. attorney general at a brief ceremony in the Oval Office Monday, following the Senate’s narrow vote to approve his nomination as the nation’s top law enforcement official over the weekend. Blanche, who served as acting attorney general and was President Donald Trump’s personal lawyer before joining the government, succeeds Pam Bondi — whom Trump ousted in April — as head of the Department of Justice. Trump announced Blanche as his pick to permanently lead the department in June. U.S Circuit Judge Emil Bove, another of Trump’s former personal attorneys, administered the oath of office.After the Senate voted, 50-49, to approve his nomination early Saturday morning, Blanche wrote on social media that he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation’s 88th Attorney General.” “To the dedicated public servants of the Department of Justice, thank you for your work each day to uphold the law and keep our country safe,” Blanche wrote. Blanche’s nomination had drawn widespread concern and scrutiny from congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans, over actions such as his role in establishing Trump’s “anti-weaponization fund.” The $1.8 billion Justice Department fund aimed to compensate those “who suffered weaponization and lawfare,” including many who faced prosecution related to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Lawmakers of both parties have described it as a “slush fund,” and Blanche has stated that it will not move forward under his tenure as attorney general.  Asked if the fund has a future after an executive order signing ceremony Monday afternoon, Trump said that it “will be up to Todd Blanche.” A contentious voteIn a vote early Saturday morning, every Senate Democrat voted against Blanche’s confirmation. Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine broke ranks from their party and voted against him.Blanche ultimately won over several holdout Republicans, including Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who said Blanche had acknowledged his past “mistakes” and sought to halt the Justice Department fund. He also secured support from Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both of whom are set to leave office after their terms end this January. Speaking on the floor Friday evening before Blanche was confirmed, Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, the Senate Judiciary Committee’s chair, praised Blanche as a “tough, fair prosecutor dedicated to the rule of law.”“Between his proven track record, his presentation in committee and the support he’s received from across the country, I am convinced that Mr. Blanche is the right choice to lead the Justice Department,” Grassley said. “A vote for Todd Blanche is a vote for the safety of the American people.”Congressional Democrats quickly denounced Blanche officially taking over the department. Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, blasted Blanche’s ascension as the nation’s top law enforcement official on social media earlier Monday afternoon. “Republicans in Congress voted to turn Trump's personal attorney, Todd Blanche, into Trump's personal Attorney General,” Raskin wrote. “We need a DOJ committed to the rule of law, not the corrupt rule of a kleptocrat.”

title: EPA settles with Putnam apartment manager over lead paint
description: The company that oversaw an apartment complex in Putnam will pay nearly $360,000 for failing to warn tenants about lead paint risks.
text:
The federal government has reached a settlement requiring the management company that oversaw an apartment complex in Putnam to pay a nearly $360,000 fine for failing to warn tenants about lead paint risks.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced Monday that the Konover Residential Company, a subsidiary of the Simon Konover Company, will have to pay a fine and give residents information about the dangers of lead and provide each leaseholder copies of reports about lead at the apartment. The settlement follows years of legal filings, complaints to state and federal agencies, rent strikes and protests at the Cargill Falls Mill in Putnam.
The old mill was renovated and opened as apartments in 2020. In 2023, after several children at the complex were found to have elevated lead levels in their blood, tenants formed a union and pushed for better conditions.
The project at the old mill was completed with several funding streams from the state and federal government. But lead dust remained in several apartments.
The EPA in 2024 ordered the apartment owner, Historic Cargill Falls Mill, LLC, to remediate the lead. That investigation determined that the lead posed an “imminent and substantial endangerment to tenants.”
Monday’s settlement was with the Konover management company over alleged violations of the Lead Disclosure Rule.
The agency found that for 11 units, the company didn’t provide tenants with the required lead hazard information pamphlet, didn’t put a lead warning statement in the lease, didn’t give tenants known information about lead-based paint and didn’t provide records or reports about lead in the apartments.
The Konover company did not respond to a request for comment Monday afternoon.
“EPA’s lead-based paint disclosure requirements are essential to protecting the health of New England communities, especially children who are most vulnerable to lead exposure,” EPA New England Regional Administrator Mark Sanborn said in a Monday press release. “This settlement demonstrates EPA’s commitment to enforcing federal lead disclosure laws, promoting compliance and ensuring tenants receive the information they need to protect themselves and their families from lead hazards.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: As Pa. crime rates fall to record lows, law enforcement flags ongoing challenges
description: Even as violent crimes rates fall, drug-related offenses, financial fraud and elder exploitation continue to grow.
text:
A state trooper inside a Pennsylvania State Police Mobile Command Center on Jan. 29, 2026. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Capital-Star)Violent crime rates are down across the nation and commonwealth, and 2026 numbers appear to be even lower so far. Homicides alone fell by 23% between 2023 and 2024, which is near historic lows. 
“There’s a lot of good news in the data, and some warning signs as well that we need to be vigilant about,” said state Attorney General Dave Sunday. “In many cases, (the crime rate) actually is at or below 2019 levels, getting us back to the levels that we saw prior to the pandemic-era surge in violent crime.”
Sunday, speaking at a bicameral Republican policy committee meeting in Hazelton, cautioned that drug offenses are still increasing, noting the state had seized more than 56 million million doses of fentanyl in 2025.
Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday flags ongoing concerns for his agency, even as violent crime rates drop. (Photo from livestream)
“That amount of fentanyl is staggering. It’s enough to kill four times the population of Pennsylvania, and obviously that’s unbelievably dangerous,” Sunday said. 
Monday’s wide-ranging meeting touched on some of the biggest criminal justice topics in Harrisburg, namely sentencing for felony murder and regulating skill games. But lawmakers and Hazelton leaders also wrestled with more local issues, including caring for an aging county prison population in a deteriorating facility and navigating services for homeless Pennsylvanians.
The core function of government is to keep its citizens safe,” shared Rep. David Rowe (R-Union) in his opening remarks. “Our communities deserve to feel safe, and we need to acknowledge that there is a lot of work to be done across Pennsylvania.”
Luzerne County District Attorney Sam Sanguedolce attributed falling overdose rates in his community to “the closure of our borders,” actions he said made it difficult for drug traffickers from other countries. 
“Unfortunately, we are not now drug free. We are finding that fentanyl is being replaced with methamphetamine, a more homegrown drug. Thankfully, it doesn’t kill people with the regularity that fentanyl does,” Sanguedolce said, adding that it was still a burden on local law enforcement and emergency responders.
Nearly all fentanyl smuggled into the country is brought by U.S. citizens, not immigrants. 
 Other crime trends

Sunday highlighted several trends his office was monitoring, including large-scale retail thefts “coordinated by larger criminal enterprises” with links to human and drug trafficking. He said the agency had identified more than 100 investigations across 52 counties, meaning, “This isn’t just a big city issue. This is all throughout Pennsylvania.”
A new unit dedicated to combatting elder exploitation “is actually already overwhelmed with cases,” Sunday continued. “But that’s what we’re here for and we’re proud of doing that work.”
“I’m watching this play out sort of in real time. I have aging parents that are in their early 80s, and seeing the … increase in technology, the sophistication of the scams, it’s something that’s really scary,” Sunday added.
Luzerne County District Attorney Sam Sanguedolce speaks about the prevalence of financial scams geared toward seniors. (Photo from livestream)
Sanguedolce said one example might include a call reporting that a son-in-law is in police custody and needs money immediately. 
“It goes back to the days of the 1-800 commercials, the infomercials. ‘Act now,’ right? They create a sense of urgency. Some emergency must happen. You must act now,” he continued.
With a large senior population, Sunday said Pennsylvania was “a target” for senior scams and fraud. In response, he advocated for state Senate Bill 738, described as an update to the commonwealth’s Older Adult Protective Services Act. The bipartisan measure would allow employees at financial institutions to place holds on withdrawal requests they suspect are related to fraud. 
“That pause is absolutely critical, allowing a potential victim to realize that they are being defrauded of their money, and this is so important because in most instances, once that money is gone, it is gone,” Sunday said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Schuylkill County District Attorney Michael O’Pake, who’s the vice president of the Pennsylvania District Attorneys Association, pushed for an amendment to the Senate proposal that established mandated reporting requirements for elder abuse and neglect. 
“One of the most rewarding and often most challenging responsibilities that we face as district attorneys is dealing with victims of crimes. Victims of crimes have their lives disrupted, through no fault of their own,” said O’Pake, speaking generally. 
However, the federal funding under the Victims of Crimes Act has fallen over several budget years. With that reduction in mind, O’Pake called for lawmakers “to keep victims in mind when you are doing the budget and you are setting forth priorities.” 
O’Pate also called for continued funding for child advocacy centers, concluding with an ask to outlaw swatting, which is when someone makes a fake call to 911 to trigger a police raid. 
“These hoaxes put people’s lives at risk and waste valuable public safety resources,” he said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: After Morrisey touts agency audits to purge waste, lawmakers learn saving money is likely years away
description: In May, Gov. Patrick Morrisey stood behind a sign that said, “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” while announcing that an outside company’s audit of three state agencies revealed a potential $168 million in savings.
text:
House Finance Chairman Vernon Criss, R-Wood, listens to a presentation from the Department. of Human Services about potential cost savings following an outside audit on Sunday, Aug. 9, 2026 in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)In May, Gov. Patrick Morrisey stood behind a sign that said, “Protecting Taxpayer Dollars,” while announcing that an outside company’s audit of three state agencies revealed a potential $168 million in savings. 
The governor, focused on weeding out wasteful spending, noted a lot of the proposed changes — things like replacing outdated technology, bringing foster children in-state and cancelling unused cellphone lines — would not be easy to implement. 
Lawmakers have learned from agency leaders over the last few days that the millions of dollars in potential savings won’t be seen anytime soon. Many of the savings are tied to costly technology upgrades across multiple state agencies. 
Sen. Robbie Morris, R-Randolph. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“While I was hopeful that some of the savings discussed in the audits would be felt immediately, I didn’t necessarily expect it,” said Sen. Robbie Morris, R-Randolph. “Many of these initiatives require technology upgrades, changes in processes, and so forth, which I understand doesn’t happen overnight. However, I expect the agencies to work diligently to implement the changes, not only to save taxpayer dollars, but also to provide for more efficient and effective service to our citizens.”
The Morrisey administration paid $1 million to an outside company, BDO USA, to evaluate three state agencies — Homeland Security, the Department of Transportation and the Department of Human Services. BDO recommended a list of potential cost-saving measures for the three agencies.
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, said that it wasn’t “surprising that the potential savings for audits for each of the agencies are years away or more likely not at all.”
“The focus of the current and last administration has largely been cutting taxes, not making government work,” Young said. “The audits had splashy high numbers for saving government funding but is full of ‘could’ and ‘may,’ and departments have largely said the tactics are unrealistic and cost rather than save.”  
The BDO audit said that DoHS, the behemoth agency that runs Medicaid, foster care, social services and more, could generate an annual savings of $68.6 million for the state. A list of BDO’s recommendations included reducing the use of mailers and postage costs, fixing the broken $400 million PATH database system and reducing its reliance on out-of-state residential facilities to house foster children.
“The BDO report made clear from the beginning that many of the largest savings opportunities at (DoHS) require a multi-year implementation plan, not an immediate fix within a single fiscal year,” said Lars Dalseide, communications director for Morrisey. “Fixing a disastrous department takes work. We inherited a mess after 30 years of neglect, which is exactly why Gov. Morrisey proactively and voluntarily brought in independent auditors to get to the bottom of what was happening and identify a path forward.”
There are 248 foster children living in out-of-state residential homes, and 156 children are in out-of-state psychiatric hospitals as West Virginia can’t currently serve children with certain emotional or mental health needs in state. It could take three to five years to see savings by expanding in-state care, according to DoHS.
“Out-of-state child placements expose youths to heightened safety risk, and our current approach is financially unsustainable at a cost in the report noted at $142,000 average per child,” DoHS Deputy Secretary Christina Mullins told lawmakers. “So, the department considers contracting with providers to expand in-state residential treatment capacity to be the most feasible option.”
Sen. Ben Queen, R-Harrison. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
At the state Capitol on Sunday, Sen. Ben Queen, R-Harrison, pressed Mullins on potential sayings for the fiscal year 2028. Lawmakers will work on the FY 2028 budget in January during the regular legislative session; state agencies begin putting together budget requests to lawmakers this fall. 
“You said earlier this afternoon we don’t expect to see any savings for three to five years. Obviously, January is in most of our main view here,” Queen said. “Do we expect to see any savings or any report of savings come this next fiscal year for a budget?”
Mullins responded that she didn’t have “specific savings” to share right now.
“When we’re building the 2028 budget, but those are things that we are trying to dive into to understand more so that we can make those recommendations,” she said, noting that savings on bringing foster children back in state could be seen in three to five years. 
Dalseide said that DoHS is not waiting to act to save money.
“The department is already working to maximize available federal funding, identify potential vacancy savings, improve federal reimbursement for eligible services, reduce unnecessary spending and accelerate the migration of outdated technology systems,” he said. 
West Virginia Department of Transportation Secretary Todd Rumbaugh speaks before members of the Joint Committee on Finance on Aug. 10, 2026, in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Lawmakers question potential savings in transportation, corrections 
State Transportation Secretary Todd Rumbaugh told lawmakers on Monday that some cost-saving processes will take a couple of years to go through. The BDO audit said the department could save $50.6 million through reducing Human Resources staff, simplifying the bid process for projects, addressing technology issues and more.
“Like we have the IT strategic plan that’s being looked at as part of this, and it’s a two-year plan as they go through and review it (and) the programs that we’re using and try to consolidate and eliminate,” Rumbaugh said. “It will take a while.”

“Other things like the economic development change we made, it was already done before the audit was really completed because we’ve seen that as a problem and started moving,” he continued. 
BDO estimated in their audit that the West Virginia Department of Homeland Security could save $39.4 million by addressing workforce issues in correctional facilities, minimizing high litigation costs of $3.5 million annually and more.
“One solution which DCR proposed is using body-worn cameras to provide impartial video evidence and, thereby, reduce conflict. However, procurement and implementation of a BWC system at the scale needed for each corrections officer is expensive,” the audit said. 
David Kelly, Commissioner of the West Virginia Dept. of Corrections and Rehabilitation. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Corrections Commissioner David Kelly has said body cameras are a top priority for the department in an effort to reduce litigation risks.
“If you’ll recall, when we met in June at Canaan, I said that a lot of the savings would not be recognized directly from DCR,” Kelly told lawmakers. “We believe that savings will be recognized from lawsuits, less lawsuits, which will be a savings to the state of West Virginia.” 
Young explained that the lagging timeline for financial savings was “a direct result of years and years of a flat budget, which makes major technology upgrades impossible.” 
“Systems across multiple cabinet departments are decades old, yet we continue to pour money into them at bandaids. Without investment into making our state agencies function at a baseline, of course we are behind,” she said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: El-Sayed has a coalition to rebuild after a bruising Democratic primary
description: Abdul El-Sayed has a lot of work on his hands as he marches his U.S. Senate campaign toward the general election, and much of that will center on bridging deep divides held over from his battle against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed last week in the Aug. 4 Democratic primary. Michigan Democrats […]
text:
Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed at an election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. The Democratic primary for U.S. Senate was too close to call at the time he spoke. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Abdul El-Sayed has a lot of work on his hands as he marches his U.S. Senate campaign toward the general election, and much of that will center on bridging deep divides held over from his battle against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed last week in the Aug. 4 Democratic primary.
Michigan Democrats in some ways find themselves in 2026 where many Republicans were just a decade ago — locked in a battle of intraparty ideologies with a charismatic yet controversial figure leading their ticket in a bellwether election that could decide the party’s path forward for the next decade and beyond.
Mirroring the GOP’s 2016 struggles with an ascendant “Make America Great Again” movement, Democrats this year have to balance the rise of its progressive flank and the sensitivities of its older, center-left voters, all in a bid for unity ahead of November’s general election.
A united front against Republicans in the fall could be a tall order, and a lot of that work now falls on El-Sayed and his campaign. But his success also requires an all-hands-on-deck approach to campaigning — which would include bringing former rivals together under the common cause of winning against Republicans in the fall.
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks to Democratic supporters at a unity rally held at Renaissance High School in Detroit. Aug. 7, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
“The easy part is that most Democrats are just going to fall in line for the same reason that the overall national political environment is like D+5: President Donald Trump ran the economy into a ditch with tariffs and a war of choice in another part of the world,” Adrian Hemond, CEO of the Grassroots Midwest consulting firm, said in an interview with Michigan Advance. “That’s going to be good enough for most Democrats.”
The bruising nature of the party’s U.S. Senate primary race between El-Sayed, the nominee, and Stevens, of Birmingham, has left some bitter. It has also driven a wedge between the state’s Democrats over the Israel-Palestine conflict. 
El-Sayed’s insistence on exposing Stevens’ connection to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which was one of several groups that spent more than $60 million against El-Sayed in the primary, has also left some Jewish Democrats feeling like they no longer have a home in the party, most prominently Attorney General Dana Nessel, who has said she will not attend the party’s August convention. She has also recently called on El-Sayed to tone down his rhetoric on Israel.
U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (center) speaks at meet and greet event in Detroit with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (right) and U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina (left). July 24, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
Stevens counted Jewish Democrats as some of her strongest supporters, while some have said they won’t support El-Sayed because of his stance on Israel’s actions in Gaza, which a United Nations independent body and Amnesty International have determined to be a genocide.
El-Sayed also didn’t do very well with one of the party’s key voting blocs, Black voters in urban centers like Detroit and the surrounding Wayne, Oakland and Macomb suburbs, which swung heavily toward Stevens instead of the eventual nominee. Those dynamics have created a potentially risky situation for the party in what should be an advantageous year, and earning votes from those disaffected voter blocks will require a united consensus. 



Quotation







I have every bit of confidence that the folks who are leading this party right now in Michigan are going to be able to knit together the kind of coalition that it will take to defeat Mike Rogers, because we all know what is at stake there.


– Former Democratic state Rep. Mari Manoogian, now executive director of The Next 50


In many ways, El-Sayed survived his primary fight by activating young voters, those who do not vote often or haven’t voted in a long time. But Hemond said the issue is that there will probably need to be some heavy reshaping of the electorate this year because “the Democratic Party is losing its hold on Black and Jewish voters.” 
Some of that has to do with El-Sayed’s steadfast stance on Israel, which Hemond believes has taken some of the air out of his other main policy planks, like abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and advancing Medicare for All.
High turnout shaped Michigan primary, boosting El-Sayed and Lawrence to victory

“I think the events of the last nine months in the Michigan Democratic Party’s tent have only accelerated that process,” Hemond added, referencing the primary race. “A big part of the progressive electoral theory is that you can get people under 40 to vote. And we’re going to find out.”
What worries Hemond is that he doesn’t believe there are enough of those voters in El-Sayed’s progressive coalition to win a competitive purple state like Michigan.
That’s why full unity across the board, and a rebuilding of a winning coalition that includes some recently disaffected voters, will be necessary if El-Sayed wants to win against Republican Mike Rogers in November.
A key piece of that effort will be getting Stevens and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow of Royal Oak, who was in the U.S. Senate race but dropped out a month before the election, to actively participate in the campaign’s ground game.
McMorrow swiftly endorsed El-Sayed once he was declared the winner on the morning of Aug. 5. Stevens also last week indicated that she would stump with El-Sayed and work to corral her primary voters to support the nominee.

How do we beat Mike Rogers? By making sure everyone knows who he ACTUALLY fights for.
It’s not Michiganders. It’s Donald Trump. pic.twitter.com/bFFtKfaNDs
— Mallory McMorrow (@MalloryMcMorrow) June 28, 2026

Air support swoops in from national Democrats
The Democrats are also putting up a united front across its full slate, with El-Sayed appearing at a rally late last week featuring gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, secretary of state nominee Garlin Gilchrist and attorney general nominee Eli Savit.
Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg headlined the event at Renaissance High School in Detroit, a key site for Michigan Democratic Party rallies in the past for former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris.
Buttigieg during the Aug. 7 rally took turns excoriating each member of the Michigan Republican Party ticket, specifically naming Rogers and gubernatorial nominee John James as being rubber stamps for Trump’s agenda both in Congress and the executive office of one Trump’s favorite states.

.@PeteButtigieg amping up Michigan’s Democratic slate in November. @MichiganDems https://t.co/0m0QEKNWpL pic.twitter.com/fmTqtO38kF
— Ben Solis (@bensolis1) August 8, 2026

Over the weekend, POLITICO reported that former President Barack Obama, who did not endorse a candidate in the U.S. Senate primary race, reached out to both El-Sayed and Stevens to say that he was pleased with how both sides appeared to be coming together to unify the ticket.
POLITICO also noted that Obama does not have a formal endorsement process, and that his team does not often give readouts of his calls with Democratic candidates to the press, making this an exception and a show of force. An Obama endorsement is likely to hold sway with Black voters across the state.
A necessary heart-to-heart with disaffected voters
Mari Manoogian, executive director of The Next 50, which focuses on recruiting younger center-left candidates to shore up the future of the Democratic Party, said that if she were sitting down to have coffee with El-Sayed, she would advise him to conduct a deep listening tour in areas where he didn’t do well in the primary.
“Go have some very honest, heart-to-heart conversations with people, because ultimately … part of being a good leader is being a good listener,” Manoogian said. “If you can demonstrate that, even if you aren’t aligned exactly on policy, but you have the temperament to be a good leader, someone who is open to not always being the smartest person in the room and surrounding yourself with people who are excited to hear what you have to say, then take that feedback and improve your leadership.”
For Manoogian, Michigan is a harbinger for things to come throughout America, with Democrats nationally recognizing that its diverse demography, mix of ideologies and regional interests is “a proving grounds for how to engage voters.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That includes both the operation of getting out there and doing face-to-face voter work, but also testing the kinds of messaging and policy that would resonate with people.
In that regard, Manoogian said she’s seen El-Sayed capitalize on some of that, as well as the kind of fence mending that needs to happen if Democrats plan to win the Senate seat in November.
“One of the big flashpoints of this primary has been discussion of who he was willing to campaign with and stand beside,” Manoogian said. “I have been really encouraged to see how he has taken an approach that opens his sort of a campaign up to be a bigger tent.”
The party’s role in bridging the divide
There is some disagreement over the party’s role in the fight to rebuild the Democratic coalition in Michigan.
Hemond said it was not the role of political parties in 2026 to engage in persuasion of voters, and that they were simply pass-throughs for money to candidates and mechanisms for turning out its tried and true base.
“That’s not fair to ask them to do that,” Hemond said. “They have no mechanism to do so. That’s the way our politics works now, that the candidates and elected officials have to do that work because of how money moves through politics now.”
Manoogian, however, said that Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel has a long history of working with a diverse group of people including those “who can really wade through some thorny issues and mend fences.”
“I have every bit of confidence that the folks who are leading this party right now in Michigan are going to be able to knit together the kind of coalition that it will take to defeat Mike Rogers, because we all know what is at stake there,” Manoogian said.
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel speaks to Democratic supporters at a unity rally held at Renaissance High School in Detroit. Aug. 7, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
For Joe Spaulding, a Democratic strategist and a leading activist in Ottawa County, Hertel is the right man for the job ahead.
“Curtis Hertel is the type of leader that does not believe there is a job that’s too small, too difficult, or not his,” Spaulding  said, just hours before the party gathered in Detroit last week to hold its unity kickoff rally. “I do not think that even if it wasn’t his job, in theory, that he wouldn’t try to do it.”
El-Sayed’s role in healing wounds
Manoogian, Hemond and Spaulding agree that the ball is now in El-Sayed’s court.
“From an activist standpoint, absolutely, it is the campaign’s responsibility to make sure that the constituencies in the coalition are pulled together,” Spaulding said. “The good news is that Abdul is not doing this alone, and the better news is that over the last month, he has demonstrated a level of humility that will allow him to take full advantage of the team that he has built, and they know the mission is rebuilding this coalition.”
El-Sayed is known for his steadfastness on the issues he cares about, and some have seen that as stubbornness. That has been one of the centrist concerns about El-Sayed as he was gaining steam in the primary — that he could be uncompromising as a U.S. senator, and that may not signal success in a governing body built on compromise.
Spaulding says in his mind there is no question whether El-Sayed has the capacity to humble himself and make that coalition work, both as a nominee and as a senator.
“He’s already doing that. He’s passed the test,” Spaulding said. “I can tell you that my experience growing up, and I did get called every racial slur in the book on the playground, Abdul and I did grow up in Michigan at the exact same time. We were both in high school when the War on Terror started, and that was an atmosphere that wasn’t friendly for anybody with not white skin. When you become an activist going through that, you do get some really, really thick skin, and sometimes thick skin leads to stubbornness.”
Still, Spaulding said El-Sayed has qualities in a candidate that are impossible to fake, and that he is confident in El-Sayed’s ability to pull off what appears to be a monumental task.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Rep. Ilhan Omar raises questions about undercover ICE agent at town hall
description: An undercover Homeland Security Investigations agent parked outside a community center while Rep. Ilhan Omar held a town hall on Aug. 6, the Democratic Congresswoman wrote in a letter to Department of Homeland Security leadership in St. Paul.  According to the letter, a Richfield police officer noticed a woman sitting in a Ford Explorer outside […]
text:
WASHINGTON, DC - FEBRUARY 02: U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-MN, leaves her office at the Longworth House Office Building on February 02, 2023 in Washington, DC. Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images.An undercover Homeland Security Investigations agent parked outside a community center while Rep. Ilhan Omar held a town hall on Aug. 6, the Democratic Congresswoman wrote in a letter to Department of Homeland Security leadership in St. Paul. 
According to the letter, a Richfield police officer noticed a woman sitting in a Ford Explorer outside the building and became suspicious of the way she was monitoring the building. He ran the Explorer’s plates, but they didn’t correspond to the vehicle. The officer approached the woman, who initially identified herself as event security. 
Richfield Police confirmed with Omar’s security detail that the woman was not part of their team. The woman called her supervisor, then told the police officer that she was an undercover HSI officer stationed outside the community center as part of a nearby undercover drug operation. She then left the property. 
HSI is the criminal investigative division of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
The presence of the agent was a waste of police resources, and at best, a poor choice of location for an undercover drug raid, Omar wrote in the letter. 
“At worst, it emphasizes many Americans’ growing concern that the Trump administration uses ICE to surveil political opponents and may interfere with our democracy,” the letter reads. 
Omar has been a frequent target of President Donald Trump since his first term. Trump has said she should be jailed or “sent back to Somalia.”
During a January town hall, a man rushed at Omar as she spoke and squirted her with a liquid — later identified as apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a federal officer in federal court in May. 
The Richfield Police Department and ICE did not immediately respond to emailed questions.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Former WNMU president asks judge to reinstate state auditor, lawmakers as lawsuit defendants
description: An attorney for former Western New Mexico University President Joseph Shepard on Monday asked a judge to undo a prior ruling that shielded the state auditor and several state lawmakers from his lawsuit that alleges they colluded to force him out of the job.
text:
The campus of Western New Mexico University in Silver City, N.M., pictured March 9, 2026. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)An attorney for former Western New Mexico University President Joseph Shepard on Monday asked a judge to undo a prior ruling that shielded the state auditor and several state lawmakers from his lawsuit that alleges they colluded to force him out of the job.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Shepard resigned as university president in late 2024 after news reports and State Auditor Joseph Maestas revealed how he and other university leaders used taxpayer and university foundation money to pay for international trips and exotic home furnishings. His resignation came with a $1.9 million severance payout and a tenured teaching job in the university’s business school.
A newly appointed Board of Regents last summer voted to undo the payout and teaching contract. Shepard sued the university over the decision last October and named Maestas and several state lawmakers as defendants, alleging that they colluded to force him out of the job after he previously raised questions about some of the Legislature’s education spending.
Sixth Judicial District Court Judge Jarod Hofacket previously ruled that Maestas and the lawmakers are protected by legislative immunity — meaning they were acting within the normal course of their jobs as public officials — and granted their requests to be removed as defendants.
Attorneys representing the government officials argued during the Monday morning hearing that Shepard’s motion to reconsider was more a “motion to reargue issues that the court has already considered and decided.”
“The motion to reconsider points to no intervening change in law, no newly discovered evidence and no issue that the court overlooked,” Taylor Lueras, an attorney representing the lawmakers, said.
Hofacket did not rule from the bench and told attorneys on both sides of the dispute that he would issue a written ruling, but did not specify when. 
Shepard’s time as university president is the subject of several other ongoing lawsuits.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez sued him in early 2025 in a bid to claw back his severance payment and the State Ethics Commission sued him last summer over allegations that he built a patio near his on-campus house to host events related to his daughter’s wedding with money intended for Americans with Disabilities Act-compliance projects.
Both cases are set to go to trial in 2027.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin DOJ identifies officer involved in Madison shooting
description: The Madison police officer who killed Corey Ruiz, 38, in July has been identified by the Wisconsin Department of Justice (DOJ) as Keil Baitinger-Peterson.  In a DOJ statement released Monday, Baitinger-Peterson is described as an officer with nearly 11 years of experience. The statement describes the events of July 22, when officers from the Madison […]
text:
Hundreds of people crowded the intersection of Baldwin and Williamson streets on Madison's East Side on July 23 for a vigil in honor of Corey Ruiz, who was killed by a Madison Police officer July 22. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
The Madison police officer who killed Corey Ruiz, 38, in July has been identified by the Wisconsin Department of Justice (DOJ) as Keil Baitinger-Peterson. 
In a DOJ statement released Monday, Baitinger-Peterson is described as an officer with nearly 11 years of experience. The statement describes the events of July 22, when officers from the Madison Police Department responded to a call from the Marquette neighborhood where someone reported that a man was checking parked vehicles. 
The responding officers chased Ruiz, who fled from them on  a bicycle.  They caught up with him at the corner of Williamson and Baldwin streets, where they wrestled Ruiz to the ground in the middle of the street as bystanders captured video on their phones. 
Baitinger-Peterson can be seen on videos that were posted to social media firing several shots at Ruiz at close range.  Madison police officers do not wear  body cameras. The DOJ update reiterates statements made by Madison Police Chief John Patterson that Ruiz was carrying a knife — which was recovered from the scene — and injured Baitinger-Peterson before the officer fired. The DOJ statement also mentions that one other officer was injured, but it does not describe the nature of the injury. 
Both Baitinger-Peterson and the other unnamed officer were treated at a local hospital and released, the update states, adding that Ruiz was transported to a hospital and pronounced  dead. Bystander video shows an officer on the scene attempting medical aid immediately after the shooting, then ceasing. All four involved officers, including Baitinger-Peterson, have been placed on administrative leave.
The DOJ is leading the investigation into Ruiz’s killing, with support from the Dane County Sheriff’s Office, Wisconsin State Patrol and the Sun Prairie Police Department. After the investigation is concluded, it will be turned over to Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne, who  will decide whether or not to charge Baitinger-Peterson. Chief Patterson said that the incident is being handled as a criminal homicide investigation.
Just hours after the shooting, community members began to gather at the intersection where Ruiz was killed, where they constructed  a memorial and blocked off the streets. 
Last week the city and police agencies forcibly cleared the memorial site as  residents and city officials continue to grapple  with the fallout of Ruiz’s death.
