name: Michigan Advance
title: New partnership brings college and career resources to Detroit neighborhoods
description: A new partnership in Detroit will provide middle schoolers through adult learners with access to resources designed to help residents enter and complete college, with hubs expected to open on the city’s east and west sides this fall. Graduate 313, a partnership between the Jamie and Denise Jacob Family Foundation and Detroit College Access Network, […]
text:
Kendra Agee, program Director, and LaTonia Gee, program manager for Graduate 313, assist students with college access support during Detroit Onsite Admissions Day. Photo by Lance Knight.A new partnership in Detroit will provide middle schoolers through adult learners with access to resources designed to help residents enter and complete college, with hubs expected to open on the city’s east and west sides this fall.
Graduate 313, a partnership between the Jamie and Denise Jacob Family Foundation and Detroit College Access Network, aims to expand educational opportunities for Detroiters in what organizers describe as a first-of-its-kind, neighborhood-based college and career success initiative backed by a $3.5 million investment.
After exhausting the model of supporting what most organizations refer to as a “college coach” that walks program participants through the college experience, the Jacob Family Foundation is supporting DCAN, which has worked to ensure equitable access to postsecondary education for Detroiters since 2012, as it launches Graduate 313.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The new model will deliver college and career resources directly within Detroit neighborhoods, Jacob Family Foundation Executive Director Megan Fenkell said, funding an initial three-year investment with additional help from partners including the General Motors Foundation and Rocket Community Fund.
“We wondered what would happen if there was a place in Detroit that students all the way from middle school to adult learners could go where they could get the support to get to and through college (or) return to college,” Fenkell said. “DCAN is the intermediary, and quite frankly, the leader in Detroit when it comes to all things college-going. So, it just seemed like the natural fit for us.”
Graduate 313 will launch this fall with a flagship office for Graduate 313 and DCAN programming on the city’s west side in a building located near the intersection of Plymouth and Evergreen roads. 
Graduate 313 will launch its programming in two physical locations this fall with a flagship office for Graduate 313 and DCANprogramming on the city’s west side in a building located near the intersection of Plymouth and Evergreen roads. (Submitted photo)
On the east side of the city, Graduate 313 will occupy space in the former Winans Academy of Performing Arts building as an “impact partner” within Anchor Detroit, a community hub developed by Life Remodeled.
After a year of advising, the initiative is now fully-staffed and will begin offering services inside physical buildings. Services will include one-on-one-advising, emergency grants, wraparound services and college field trips that will either allow Graduate 313 to connect with a school, nonprofit or out-of-school time partner to take students to college campuses in the area or bring colleges to their physical locations.
Along with resources, DCAN Senior Director of Community Hubs Jasmine Brooks said Graduate 313 is modeled to provide locations that are accessible by walking, car or city bus routes based on “asset mapping” that determined locations that would be most beneficial to Detroiters.
“As a native Detroiter, you don’t necessarily operate in silos, but residents that live on the west side, that’s where they kind of stay put,” she said. “Those that live on the east side or southwest Detroit usually stick to the neighborhood in the area where you’re most comfortable in.
“We want to change that trajectory by having these neighborhood hubs across the city, so that no matter where you live, you have somewhere in your neighborhood — in your backyard — where you’re able to go and access college access resources and an opportunity to then also persist and actually complete those credentials.”
Graduate 313 was launched with the intention of improving the City of Detroit’s access to and completion of college degrees. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 18% of Detroit residents age 25 and older hold a bachelor’s degree. The initiative is aligned with helping boost that number toward Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s “Sixty by 30” goal of having 60% of working-age adults earn a postsecondary college degree or skill certificate by 2030.
MiSean Washington, program manager for Graduate 313, advises a student on next steps after applying to college during Detroit College Onsite Day. Photo by Lance Knight.
Graduate 313 will help address the challenges city residents young and old face by bringing resources closer to the communities that need them most, creating clearer pathways to college, career training and economic mobility, Brooks said.
Graduate 313 plans to measure success by tracking who’s coming through its doors, setting a goal of reaching 5,000 Detroit residents in its first year, Brooks said, with the intention of increasing that number year-over-year. This will be done by collecting data on who takes advantage of its services while assigning participants in the program to one of six advisors for high school, college and adult learners.
“We’re not only trying to connect them to credentialing and postsecondary planning, but we’re also trying to connect them to the resources that are preventing the barriers that they have right now,” Brooks said. “We want to help eliminate that. 
“So I think it’s a unique position to be in, where we’re not just concerned necessarily just with our numbers — like we’ve got to hit a certain amount of people — but we really want to make sure that we’re touching people so that they spread the word that, ‘Here’s genuinely a staff of people that are going to connect me across the city of Detroit to people in places that I may not have had access to if I had not been connected through Graduate 313 and the Detroit College Access Network.’”
While the Jacob Family Foundation is on board for a three-year funding commitment, Fenkell said the foundation and DCAN also are actively fundraising to continue the effort past the three-year grant.
The foundation believes giving residents access to support that will help them get to “day one” of college in a setting that isn’t intimidating with help from people who are embedded in the community will help remove the barriers that could be the deciding factor in whether they decide to continue toward the completion of a degree, she said.
“We know that the student counselor ratio at the high schools is extremely off balance,” she said. “It’s just challenging to get the support easily. (Graduate 313 provides) a wide range of support that you’re not necessarily able to easily seek out on all college campuses.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio’s 9th Congressional district race: The candidates’ records on data centers
description: The race for Ohio’s 9th U.S. Congressional district is one of the state’s most closely contested, and the candidates have contrasting records and positions when it comes to data center development. Derek Merrin, the Republican nominee and former state representative who is facing long-time Ohio Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur in the November election, vote[...]
text:
COLUMBUS, OH — JANUARY 03: Rep. Derek Merrin (R-Moclova Township) (center) during the Pledge of Allegiance at the opening day ceremonies of the 135th General Assembly of the State of Ohio, January 3, 2023, in the House Chamber at the Ohio Statehouse in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal)The race for Ohio’s 9th U.S. Congressional district is one of the state’s most closely contested, and the candidates have contrasting records and positions when it comes to data center development.
Derek Merrin, the Republican nominee and former state representative who is facing long-time Ohio Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur in the November election, voted for Ohio’s data center tax breaks when he was an Ohio state representative in 2017. Kaptur has spoken out against data centers for draining power and water from local communities, saying the companies should pay for that, not the citizens.

Ohio’s data centers have received $2.5 billion in state and local tax incentives between 2017 and 2024, according to a 2025 report by SRC EvalMetrics on behalf of the Ohio Chamber of Commerce. 
Merrin, who served four terms as an Ohio state representative for the Toledo district from 2016 to 2024, did not respond to the Ohio Capital Journal’s questions for this story.
Merrin received a $1,000 political donation from the American Electric Power Ohio Committee for Responsible Government in 2021. AEP had received more than $6 million in data center tax breaks in Ohio as of September 2024, according to Policy Matters Ohio. 
Merrin received a $500 political donation from Windstream Holdings’ PAC in 2022. That same year, Windstream Holdings listed eight “key data center locations” in Ohio. 
One of the data center locations was operated by Cologix, which received more than $6 million in data center tax breaks as of September 2024, according to Policy Matters Ohio. 
Another one of Windstream’s Ohio data centers location was operated by CyrusOne, which received more than $5 million in data center break breaks as of September 2024, according to Policy Matters Ohio. 
Ohio has more than 200 data centers, the sixth-highest state in the country, according to Pew Research Center. Most of the data centers are in central Ohio. Cincinnati has 26 and Cleveland has 22, according to the Data Center Map. 
Ohioans are seeing increased electric bills. The average Ohio residential utility bills are projected to be about $800 for the summer — a 17% increase compared to last summer, according to a report by Third Way. 
Merrin lost a close race to Kaptur during the 2024 election and the Cook Political Report says Ohio’s 9th Congressional District race is a toss-up.
Kaptur raised concerns over data centers at the end of last year.
“How much more will our citizens be forced to pay for power and water?” Kaptur asked, speaking on the U.S. House floor. 
“They have a right to know. Will our building trades be true partners in economic growth or just temporary labor while facing higher utility bills at home? And how many permanent jobs will these largely opaque facilities actually provide? … The American people deserve to know how AI data centers will affect their communities.”
When the Ohio Capital Journal asked if Kaptur supports bringing more data centers to Ohio’s 9th Congressional District, Kaptur’s campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer responded.
U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-OH) (2nd L) speaks as Rep.-elect Andy Levin (D-MI) (L) and Rep. Tim Ryan (D-OH) (R) listen during a news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)
“Economic development should strengthen our communities, not drain their resources, and put added burdens on our people.
“If data center companies want to do business here, they should pay their fair share — not force hardworking people and local municipalities to subsidize billions in tax breaks for wealthy CEOs and shareholders who can easily afford to pay their own way,” Blitzer said in an email. 
Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton recently announced she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers “if requirements on costs, union labor, transparency, environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and development are not met,” she said in a statement.
Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy’s data center plan is three-fold.
“If a data center is built in your community, then (1) you will no longer have to pay for your home’s electricity, (2) you will pay lower property taxes, and (3) the data center will be required to abide by all air and water quality standards without exception, and we will take the necessary steps to protect Ohio’s fertile farmland,” he said in a statement.
Neither candidate has laid out exactly how they intend to accomplish their promises, whether that be using the limited powers of the governor’s office or some combination of working with the legislature, data center operators, utilities, or utility regulators.
Lawmakers at the Ohio Statehouse have yet to pass any data center legislation. 
Conserve Ohio, the grassroots organization behind a proposed constitutional amendment to ban new data centers, are collecting signatures to make the 2027 ballot.
Follow Ohio Capital Journal Reporter Megan Henry on X or on Bluesky.

title: Launching the Somaliland Ohio Association: Building a stronger, more engaged community in Ohio
description: On July 18, 2026, Somaliland community members across Ohio gathered in Columbus to officially launch the Somaliland Ohio Association, marking a new chapter for a community that has spent years building connections, supporting families, and contributing to the state they call home. While the Association is newly established, the community behind it is not. Fo[...]
text:
Members of the Somaliland Ohio Association. (Photo provided.)On July 18, 2026, Somaliland community members across Ohio gathered in Columbus to officially launch the Somaliland Ohio Association, marking a new chapter for a community that has spent years building connections, supporting families, and contributing to the state they call home.
While the Association is newly established, the community behind it is not. For years, Somalilanders in Ohio have organized cultural events, supported families, celebrated heritage, encouraged youth, and created networks to help community members succeed. 
The launch creates a formal platform to expand that work and address the opportunities and challenges facing a growing community in Ohio.
As Ohio continues to grow and become more diverse, community-led organizations play an important role in helping families navigate the systems that impact their daily lives. 
The Somaliland Ohio Association aims to support community members in areas such as education, workforce development, entrepreneurship, civic participation, and access to resources.
Education remains one of the community’s most important priorities. Many immigrant families face challenges understanding school systems, accessing educational opportunities, and finding resources that help children succeed. 
By creating stronger networks between families, educators, and community leaders, the Association can help ensure that young people have the support they need to reach their full potential.
Small businesses are another important part of the Somaliland community’s contribution to Ohio. Like many immigrant communities, Somalilanders have built businesses, created jobs, and contributed to local economies. 
The Association can help aspiring entrepreneurs by connecting them with information about business resources, financial literacy, licensing requirements, and opportunities available throughout Ohio.
Workforce integration is also an important part of building stronger communities. Many Somalilanders in Ohio work in essential industries, pursue professional careers, and contribute to the state’s economy. 
Community organizations can help newcomers and established residents alike by providing connections, mentorship, and guidance that allow people to fully participate in Ohio’s workforce.
The launch of the Somaliland Ohio Association also represents an opportunity for greater civic engagement. A strong democracy depends on communities understanding how local and state government works and having a voice in decisions that affect their families. 
The Association aims to encourage community members to become more engaged with schools, local government, and civic institutions throughout Ohio.
The Somaliland community’s story is part of the larger American story of immigrants building stronger communities while preserving their heritage. 
Somalilanders have established communities in the United States for decades, contributing as professionals, entrepreneurs, workers, and citizens. In Ohio, they have become part of the state’s diverse fabric.
The official launch event brought together Somaliland elders, women, youth, community leaders, and guests from different backgrounds. 
The presence of community partners, including Columbus City Council Member Mark Sigrist, reflected the importance of collaboration between local institutions and the diverse communities that make Ohio stronger.
The Association’s leadership team — President Faysal M. Suubane, Vice President Mohamed Fu.ad, Chief External Relations Officer Ibraahim Mohammad, and Treasurer Abdisalam Burale — represents a commitment to service and creating opportunities for future generations.
The Somaliland Ohio Association is not only about preserving culture. It is about building pathways to opportunity, strengthening civic participation, and ensuring that every member of Ohio’s growing communities has the resources and support needed to succeed.
Ohio’s future depends on communities working together. When immigrant communities are empowered to participate fully in education, business, civic life, and public conversations, the entire state benefits.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The abandoned — CT’s talented and gifted students
description: Nearly three quarters of CT's 202 districts served no gifted and talented students in the 2025-26 school year.
text:
It’s not every day that you meet a student who can name all the countries in the world based on their flags. Have you ever met someone called “Brain” whose real name is Brian? What about the 5-year-old who can play advanced piano compositions and complete complex mathematical equations two grades above peers?
 What happens to Talented and Gifted Students (TAG)? They are the forgotten, underserved population. Some students come cloaked as twice exceptional or may be so bored in class that they have behavioral challenges.  
Connecticut is not protecting our geniuses; they are abandoned.
Why this matters
As a parent of a talented and gifted student, I’ve seen the devastating effects of districts failing to identify and serve these students. Likewise, I’ve witnessed bright, misunderstood individuals throw away their talents because systems didn’t support them. Personally, I’ve never been formally identified as talented and gifted, but I’ve been recognized for my creative talents, and I have one gift that is immeasurable: my intuition. Gifts aren’t always measurable, and don’t fit neatly into test scores. Also, I’ve empathized with Asian parents who experienced hate for their talented and gifted students.
There’s no oversight.
Let’s start with the Connecticut State Department of Education (CSDE). Districts are required to submit talented and gifted data to EdSight. In reality, the state doesn’t check the statistics. It’s up to the district to provide accurate data, with final sign-off from the Superintendent.
In EdSight , there are 202 districts; 31% identified zero talented and gifted students, and 73% served zero students in the 2025-2026 school year. Such is the case in Enfield which has a gifted and talented program and serves no students. Sadly, Connecticut identified 3% talented and gifted students and served 1.8%, which is 70% behind the national average. The U.S. Department of Education’s Office of Civil Rights estimates that 6% of public school students are enrolled in gifted and talented programs. 

Credit: CSDE

As a program manager in the Connecticut State Department of Education Performance Office, managing EdSight statistics, I would see this as a red flag if districts are legally required to identify talented and gifted students. Is it possible that all these districts have no such students, or is it more likely that they aren’t providing the correct data?
There’s no accountability and funding.
There’s no federal funding for gifted and talented programs; they are excluded from the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) . Therefore, districts aren’t required to serve students even if they have a program.
 Federal policies like   No Child Left Behind   often focus more on bringing struggling students up to grade level, rather than investing in students who are excelling. As a result, districts are pooling financial resources into children with disabilities because they are required to serve them, leaving the forgotten. 
The term “equity” fits its context.
Equity is meeting students where they are. Critics argue that talented and gifted programs under-identify minority students.
Recently, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani proposed phasing out gifted and talented programs to reduce racial disparities. There Black and Hispanic students make up 66% of the population and represent 21% of talented and gifted participants, but this is hardly a reason to kill the pathway entirely.
Asian Americans are classified as a racial minority group too. Nationally, Asian students are twice as likely to be identified. Caucasian and Asian kids represent two thirds of the gifted and talented population.
So, if you want to talk about equity, let’s look at our high-needs Connecticut students. The majority of districts served zero high-needs talented and gifted students. This includes twice-exceptional learners with a disability.
 Also, the   Washington Post   warned, “Politicians tread on dangerous ground when their pursuit of equity comes at the cost of children’s opportunities.” 
If gifted and talented students need a more advanced curriculum, they deserve to receive that at their level. Likewise, if a student with high needs requires a little extra support, then they should receive it. That’s what equity actually means. Similarly, Psychology Today argued that “Equity shouldn’t mean holding bright minds back. Equity means giving every child the support they need to reach as high as they can.” 
Identifying and serving the talented and gifted: the path forward.
Districts need to move away from the “identify, not-serve” model. They must have a highly visible and accessible process for identifying and serving gifted students, using multiple measures to determine who should receive services.
Del Siegle, Director of the National Center for Research on Gifted Education at the University of Connecticut, stated:  “We need to do a better job of identifying kids for these services, and then we need to do a better job providing these services.” 
More importantly, we should build systems that help kids nurture their gifts and talents, even those that are not measurable.  Connecticut is not protecting our geniuses; they are abandoned.
Danielle Brown lives in Enfield.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Ned Lamont finds places to speak Sunday; less so for Josh Elliott
description: Gov. Ned Lamont and his challenger Rep. Josh Elliott spent the last Sunday before the Democratic primary making appeals to urban voters.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont spent the last Sunday before the Democratic primary making  appeals to Black and urban voters from two church pulpits and get-out-the-vote rallies in Hartford, Meriden, New Britain and New Haven — all providing speaking opportunities reflecting the advantages of incumbency.
His challenger, Rep. Josh Elliott, campaigned in Bridgeport and at Ecuadorian flag-raising events in Stamford and Danbury. It was not to be a day for Elliott to deliver any speeches. His last event did put him amid 16,000 people, but it was a Nate Bargatze comedy show in Hartford.  
Elliott was in the audience, not on stage.
Sunday was the last day of early voting, and Elliott’s challenge of Lamont for the Democratic nomination is the only statewide contest in either party. More than 50,000 Democrats already have cast their votes through absentee ballots and early voting in advance of Tuesday’s primary.

Gov. Ned Lamont listens to a speaker during a Get Out The Vote Rally in New Britain on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Lamont is the beneficiary of the contacts amassed over nearly eight years as governor, as well the political infrastructure that comes with being endorsed at the state party convention. He and his wife, Annie, began the day at First Cathedral, a Black megachurch in the Hartford suburb of Bloomfield.
It was not the governor’s first visit, nor the first time he used the church as an important conduit to the Black community. Lamont chose a clinic there in February 2021 to get vaccinated against COVID-19, sharing the stage then with the church’s trusted pastor, Archbishop Leroy Bailey Jr., who vouched for the vaccine.
Bailey, now semi-retired at age 80 as pastor emeritus, welcomed the Lamonts into the office suite he shares with his son, the current senior pastor, the Rev. Michael David Bailey. The archbishop would escort the governor and first lady to their seats with him in the front row of the sanctuary.

Gov. Ned Lamont greeting congregants at Rehobeth Church of God in Bloomfield on Sunday. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror

His message at First Cathedral and then at the nearby Rehobeth Church of God, where the congregation is dominated with immigrants and descendants of immigrants from the West Indies, focused less on the primary than on what Lamont called the unsettled state politics created by the Trump administration.
At Rehobeth, where he witnessed two christenings before Bishop Jonathan Ramsey invited him to speak, Lamont congratulated the two families.
“Two things in life that get you through: God and family,” Lamont said.
The congregation applauded.
“Really proud to have my wife Annie here, the first lady. Wouldn’t be anywhere without her,” he said, pausing for more applause. “I’ll just say that there’s some storm clouds out there. I know everybody’s anxiety, but we’re here in this amazing Rehobeth Church, because we know that with God, all things are possible. With God, all things are possible.”
“Now I want to say one last thing. There’s one thing that really particularly hurts me coming out of the White House. There’s a certain sense that we’re not all God’s children. We seem to be saying we don’t all belong. I want you to know here in Connecticut, in my heart, we all belong.”

Gov. Ned Lamont speaks with New Britain resident Adrienne Benjamin about the Profound Autism Alliance during a Get Out The Vote Rally in New Britain on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal and Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam delivered testimonials on behalf of Lamont at the rally in Hartford’s North End. U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes of the 5th District did the same in New Britain. 
Last weekend, Lamont emphasized expressions of support from 10 members of the General Assembly’s Black and Puerto Rican Caucus. One of them, Rep. Toni Walker of New Haven, was featured in an attack ad.
Elliott said there was no special strategy in attending two Ecuadorian events on Sunday.
“That’s what was happening today,” he said.
He skipped a plan to work the crowd at a street festival in New Haven outside City Hall, the early voting polling place. He said he had campaigned at a Puerto Rican festival in the city earlier in the weekend. He was running late, and he and his girlfriend, Jenn Lepore, had tickets for Bargatze at PeoplesBank Arena in Hartford.

Josh Elliott arrives with his girlfriend, Jenn Lepore, for a comedy show in Hartford on Sunday. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror.org

He agreed to meet a reporter on his way to the venue to talk about his day and the decision to take in a comedy show. 
“The work’s important, being seen, talking to people,” Elliott said. But he added, “I’m not changing the result by how much I do on a Sunday before the election.”
Once he qualified for his $3.75 million public financing grant, his ads went on the air, and he could increase staffing.
“We have a full team. We hit about 4,000 doors yesterday,” he said. “I think we probably hit about 5,000 today.”
The Bargatze tickets were purchased months ago. Is he a fan of the comedian who generally stays away from politics?
“I’m a fan of comedy.”

title: Iowa Libertarians to nominate new candidates Wednesday
description: The Libertarian Party of Iowa will nominate new candidates to run for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District and as lieutenant governor at a meeting Wednesday, party leaders said Sunday. Originally, the replacement candidates were meant to be nominated at the Sunday LPIA State Central Committee meeting, but party officials moved the nominating date to comply with[...]
text:
Jules Cutler, the lieutenant governor candidate for the Iowa Libertarian Party, spoke at a State Objection Panel meeting June 15, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Libertarian Party of Iowa will nominate new candidates to run for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District and as lieutenant governor at a meeting Wednesday, party leaders said Sunday.
Originally, the replacement candidates were meant to be nominated at the Sunday LPIA State Central Committee meeting, but party officials moved the nominating date to comply with state law. The state Libertarian Party plans to name new candidates who can appear on the ballot in the contests for governor and for the 3rd Congressional District.
The original Libertarian candidates in these races were removed from the ballot by the State Objections Panel in June. In the 3rd District, Marco Battaglia was removed by the panel because they said the name he used as a candidate was too different from his legal name, Mark T. Anderson, which could cause voter confusion.
The panel also ruled the Libertarian ticket of Nicholas Gluba for governor and Jules Cutler for lieutenant governor did not qualify for the general election ballot. The state panel found Cutler had not submitted an affidavit of candidacy for lieutenant governor by the June 2 deadline, though Cutler and her attorney argued she was told by an employee at the secretary of state’s office that she did not need to submit this paperwork.
Both decisions were challenged by the Libertarian candidates in court. In late July, a Polk County District Court judge released a ruling upholding the decision to keep these candidates off the ballot. Both Gluba and Battaglia told reporters they planned to appeal the ruling. But on Tuesday, the Iowa Libertarian Party announced Battaglia had ended his campaign because of a medical emergency. Speakers at the Sunday meeting said Cutler similarly moved to end her campaign, allowing for the nomination of a new gubernatorial running mate for Gluba.
Iowa Libertarian Party Chair Stephanie Berlin said Sunday these two updates mean the party must choose new candidates to appear on the ballot.
“Unfortunately, Marco had a medical emergency, so he is completely withdrawn,” Berlin said. “So we will not be moving forward with the appeals in his case at this time, hence, the need for the nomination and voting for replacement Libertarian candidates. Jules is not able to continue either after the court cases.”
The party meeting was originally scheduled to include nominating votes for new Libertarian candidates to enter these races — a process that must be completed by Aug. 14 under Iowa law. Berlin said the schedule for nominating candidates changed because the committee had to first change its non-party political organization (NPPO) “vacancy protocol” — new language specifying how substitute candidates are chosen — before it could officially nominate new candidates.
The LPIA committee approved the new language, but Berlin said Libertarians need to file the new revised protocol with the secretary of state before nominations can happen — paperwork she said she plans to submit at 8 a.m. Monday.
After the planned nominating votes Wednesday at 8 p.m., Cutler said the chosen replacement candidates will go with her and the LPIA secretary to file affidavits of candidacy, minutes of the vote and signatures with the Iowa secretary of state.
“It’s fairly straightforward, so there’s no more, I guess, need to have a lawsuit — at least at this point,” Berlin said. “… Now, obviously, if there is an objection to this process, we will have to go through that process. But there are no more lawsuits specifically related to Battaglia or Cutler.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: In final days, Dems seeking 1st District seat take message to voters
description: John Larson, Luke Bronin, Jillian Gilchrest and Ruth Fortune focused on union rallies and door-knocking in their pitches to Democratic voters.
text:
In a campaign that’s been waged aggressively on the airwaves and through mail in recent weeks, the four Democratic candidates running for the 1st Congressional District nomination spent the final days of their primary campaigns knocking on doors and meeting voters face-to-face in blistering heat.
U.S. Rep. John Larson, who has been in office since 1999, faces three Democratic challengers who are calling for generational change. It’s the first time in 28 years that Democratic voters in the district will vote in a contested primary that features a sitting lawmaker.
Tuesday’s primary will test whether voters in the Hartford-based district want experience and seniority in Congress or a fresh face that’ll bring a new approach as incumbent lawmakers stare down challenges in primaries across the country.
In the waning days of the campaign, Larson and former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin leaned into messaging around labor, holding dueling rallies with their union supporters on Sunday. Support from unions and debate over labor records has been a recurring theme of the campaign and primarily an attack line from the congressman.
All four candidates, including West Hartford state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune, fanned out across the 1st Congressional District Sunday to make their final pitches to voters on the last day of in-person early voting before Tuesday’s high-stakes primary.
Gilchrest and Fortune spent the majority of their weekends door-knocking throughout the district. The union allies of Larson and Bronin lent a hand to the campaigns in broader canvassing efforts on Sunday.

Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, Democratic candidate for the 1st Congressional District, speaks during a rally with members of Carpenters Local 326 and the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association in Manchester on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Larson, 78, started Sunday with several dozen labor allies at a union rally before supporters embarked on a large canvass of the congressman’s native East Hartford. He’s had support from dozens of unions and the Working Families Party.
He also got backup from the president of Social Security Works PAC, which has endorsed his campaign. Social Security has been Larson’s signature issue for years, and he says there’s even more urgency with estimates showing the trust fund’s insolvency  in the early 2030s.
Larson proposes his legislation “Social Security 2100 Act”  every session to boost benefits across the board and have high earners contribute more through payroll taxes, but it has stalled in Congress regardless of the party in control — something his opponents have noted.
If Larson wins a 15th term and Democrats take back the House in the fall, he’ll regain the gavel of the House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security.

Jon “Bowzer” Bauman  speaks during a labor rally for U.S. Rep. John B. Larson with local members of the building trades in East Hartford on Sunday, August 9, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Jon “Bowzer” Bauman, the president of Social Security Works PAC and the lead singer of the rock band Sha Na Na, leaned into his musical career as he propped up Larson, at one point saying the congressman will hopefully be flexing his muscles Tuesday night — a nod to his signature pose from his days in the band.
“You know I love the music in the ’50s and the ’60s. That does not mean that I actually want to return to the ’50s or the early ’60s before Medicare and Social Security, when most American seniors lived below the poverty line,” Bauman said. “And I know that labor knows how important it is to send John Larson back to Congress.”
Larson spent most of his rally speech focused on President Donald Trump.
“This isn’t only about this race. This is about the future for the country. But for the three opponents that I’m running against, I can put them to the side,” Larson said. “Because my focus is Donald Trump. It remains Donald Trump because Donald Trump is no friend of labor.”

U.S. Rep. John B. Larson speaks during a labor rally with local members of the building trades in East Hartford on Sunday, August 9, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Instead, allies like Joe Toner, the former director of the Hartford Building Trades Council and current director of the State Building Trades Council, did the bulk of criticizing Bronin and his tenure as mayor. Toner has argued that Bronin at the time prioritized developers over project-labor agreements in Hartford.
“We understand that folks in America are being attacked,” Toner said. “But there’s a couple of ways to fight back. You could fight back with a 30-second sound bite on social media, or you could actually do what you’ve been doing for the last 28 years in Congress.”
As Larson’s opponents take aim at his decades-long career in Congress, Toner sought to flip the script on questions around age and seniority that have been percolating in other Democratic congressional races. Toner argued that Bronin’s freshman status wouldn’t position him to take on Trump: “He’s going to be in the broom closet for the first two years, trying to get his name tag spelled correctly.”
Voters “know me, they respect me, they respect the job we’ve done. I’ve always run, not only on my record, in the past, going back to the time when I was a board of education member now to the United States Congress,” Larson said. “Ironically, my three opponents and Trump have the same thing in mind — they want to get rid of me.”
A few hours later, Bronin, 47, held his own rally in Manchester that included a slate of speakers from Carpenters Local 326, which has endorsed his campaign. He’s also been endorsed by the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association of Connecticut.

Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, candidate for the 1st Congressional District, speaks during a rally with members of Carpenters Local 326 and the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association in Manchester on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The speakers commended his two terms as Hartford mayor, saying he left the city in “good hands” with the current mayor and made sure Dunkin’ ballpark was “done correctly” and that schools were built under project-labor agreements.
Referencing the flurry of mailers arriving at voters’ homes from the campaigns and super PACs supporting Larson’s and Bronin’s campaigns, Marc Okun, regional manager for Carpenters Local 326, sought to paint a different picture. He spoke about Bronin wanting to write letters to express his gratitude to workers building a school during the pandemic. Okun said Bronin had just won his second term as mayor.
“What people do when nobody is watching and they’re not running for an office, they’re not running for a position, they’re doing it because they’re a good person and they actually care,” said Okun, who said he hears from Larson every two years for a check but hasn’t met with him much in the past 15 years.
Bronin, who won the party’s endorsement at the May nominating convention, made his own reference to the ads in the race that have come from both campaigns as well as the super PACs supporting them. But he largely kept the focus on his vision for “rebuilding a party that needs to be rebuilt.”
“The carpenters are used to heat, and after about a month of b-s attacks against me, I’m used to heat too,” Bronin said with a smile, to laughter and applause, but quickly pivoted.

Miguel Fuentes, a council representative with the Carpenters Union Local 326 speaks during a rally for former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, Democratic candidate for the 1st Congressional District, with members of Carpenters Local 326 and the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association in Manchester on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“I believe in my core that you don’t have to be against somebody to be for something new. We don’t need to tear a fellow Democrat down to say that we as a party can do better,” he continued. “We don’t need to tell lies about each other. We can just lay out a different kind of vision for what we are going to be as a country.”
Miguel Fuentes, council representative with the Carpenters Local 326, said he spoke with all of the candidates but said Bronin’s campaign was the one that “had the right idea about how we move forward.”
Fuentes said his union has supported Larson for decades, but he’s “fallen short.” Similar to Bronin and some of the other Democratic candidates, they’ve been critical of Larson’s laser-like focus on Social Security.
“We’re not a monolith. We’re not a single-issue constituency,” Fuentes said. “You can’t just be a single-issue representative. You’ve got to be able to command the information on all of those issues and address those concerns one at a time to get things done.”
Before the union rally, Bronin crossed paths with Gov. Ned Lamont — who faces his own primary on Tuesday from a progressive challenger — at worship services at the First Cathedral, a Black megachurch in Bloomfield that was built under the leadership of Archbishop Leroy Bailey Jr., who is 80 and has taken emeritus status.
“I respect the person I’m running against. I do,” Bronin said in an address to the congregation, his only overt reference to his primary challenge to Larson. “But to everything, there is a season.”
He paused, waiting for the applause that quickly came. He suggested that the archbishop set an example to be admired.
Gilchrest and Fortune didn’t have big or splashy events but continued to fill their days with canvassing and smaller stops throughout the 1st District.

Democratic candidate Jillian Gilchrest knocks on doors in Wethersfield in the final weekend before Tuesday’s Democratic primary for Congress. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

Gilchrest, 44, made her way to Wethersfield in the late morning for a solo canvass of the neighborhood. Even with a week of early voting winding down on Sunday, a few Democratic voters who came to the door said they haven’t voted yet but plan to.
Canvassing has been a major piece of her campaign strategy, like it was when she unseated a 12-term incumbent in 2018 for her West Hartford seat. She goes door to door to make the same pitch: Get billionaires out of politics, restore the Democratic Party and send a social worker to Congress.
In the final months of the congressional campaign, she said the debates and forum have given her more visibility, and voters are more aware of the fact that four candidates are running, not just Larson and Bronin.
As she knocked on one door in Wethersfield, Gilchrest realized it had a no-solicitation sign and quickly left a campaign flyer on the door before moving on. While walking away, a woman walked to the door and recognized who she was. She wished her good luck and said through the screen, “I know people voting for you.”

Democratic candidate Jillian Gilchrest leaves a campaign flyer on the door of a voter’s home in Wethersfield. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

Others say they recognize her from TV. A household with split political affiliations was critical of the Democratic Party. They said Larson had been in office too long and seemed lukewarm on Bronin. He appeared open to voting for Gilchrest.
Gilchrest believes Tuesday night’s results will be a true test of whether money or grassroots wins out. And regardless of the outcome, she thinks it sends a message about the current state of the Democratic Party.
“I think it says that there’s an overall frustration with how our federal government is not working right now. And voters are sick and tired of politicians saying one thing and then not taking action,” Gilchrest said while walking between homes in Wethersfield. “So I think that this primary really illustrated that voters want people who have new ideas, and who want to push for actual change, because this country is not functioning right now. People cannot afford to live their basic lives, and it shouldn’t be this hard.”
After canvassing and visiting churches on Sunday, Fortune, 38, stopped by Blue Back Square in West Hartford to watch her husband’s band play. Interrupting the music for a few minutes, Fortune took the stage to address a smattering of listeners, some who came to see her and others who were in the town’s center with their families.

Democratic candidate Ruth Fortune addresses a small crowd at Blue Back Square in West Hartford. She took the stage in the middle of her husband’s band’s set. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

She spoke about her family’s journey moving from Haiti when she was 12 and the logistical feat of getting through the state’s restrictive ballot access laws, getting her name on the primary ballot after she collected thousands of signatures via a petition to qualify. She said her work as an estate attorney also informed her views, saying she watched some people struggle to reach financial stability while others “amass insane amounts of wealth.” 
“I think it shows you we are at a bit of a breaking point in our democracy where things are so broken that we feel like we need to do things differently,” Fortune said after addressing the crowd. “And even for Congressman Larson, I would hope to goodness that he sees that he could have served differently and effectively based on the way we have pushed him as the challengers to his campaign.”
“I think if nothing else, I hope he saw that, that there’s things he could have done differently,” she said, not just on votes but on a different legislative approach.
Sunday’s concert had small foot traffic, but it was one of many things she had on her docket for the day before she resumed more door knocking. Two people came up to her to compliment her campaign but weren’t Connecticut voters. But she approached a group of 1st District residents who hadn’t voted yet and others who were new to the area. She informed them how they still have time to register as Democrats by Monday.
One of the people in the crowd was Lisa Sanchez Gonzalez, a 59-year-old Democratic voter from Berlin. She met Fortune at a Democratic Town Committee meeting months ago and has stayed connected with her since.
But she’s deeply torn between voting for her or Gilchrest. As someone who voted for Larson in the past, she said both the congressman and Bronin “are just not for me,” both on policy and style. She’s tired of the “bickering” and the campaign ads and mutes them every time she’s watching TV.
She said going to make a “booth decision” on Tuesday between the two women, whom she said she resonates with for different reasons. She cited Gilchrest’s experience in the state legislature and someone she knows very well. (She noted the Gilchrest campaign sign that’s on her front lawn.)

Ruth Fortune, 1st Congressional District Democratic candidate, greets her husband David Reynolds after they cast their ballots during the first day of early voting for the state primary election at Hartford City Hall on Monday, August 3, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

On Fortune, Sanchez Gonzalez, whose family are Cuban immigrants, said she feels a kinship with Fortune, who came to the U.S. from Haiti as a young immigrant and was undocumented for a decade.
“[Gilchrest] represents me as a woman, as a woman of a certain age,” Sanchez Gonzalez said. “And then there’s Ruth, who represents me as a woman, as an immigrant family woman. And I know that they will both fight really hard, and I know this about the both of them.”
Sanchez Gonzalez sung Fortune’s praises as they parted ways Sunday afternoon, explaining to the candidate herself how torn she remains on her choice. Fortune said to vote her conscience.
CT Mirror reporter Mark Pazniokas contributed to this report.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Newsom says national support ‘crucial’ for Democrats to win Michigan’s U.S. Senate race
description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom came to Oakland County to support a pair of Democratic candidates hoping to flip swing seats in the Michigan House, and also said he plans to meet with progressive U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Monday in an effort to boost the support El-Sayed is receiving from outside of Michigan.  “House […]
text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (at left) campaigns Sunday in Oakland County with Michigan House candidates Sarah Pounds and Alex Hawkins. Aug. 9, 2026 | Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan AdvanceCalifornia Gov. Gavin Newsom came to Oakland County to support a pair of Democratic candidates hoping to flip swing seats in the Michigan House, and also said he plans to meet with progressive U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Monday in an effort to boost the support El-Sayed is receiving from outside of Michigan. 
“House races are important, but the Senate is in play and it’s going to go through this state,” Newsom said. “Getting behind him is important in that respect and I think that’s going to require not just the party here, but support outside of Michigan to bolster his campaign.”
Newsom thanked 54th House District candidate Sarah Pounds and 55th District candidate Alex Hawkins for stepping up to oppose the Trump administration and propose solutions to problems facing Michigan households. Neither Hawkins nor Pounds have previously held elected office. Newsom also thanked campaign volunteers for “not giving in to cynicism” and working to organize in their communities. 
“I’m here in that spirit as well,” Newsom said. “All across this country people are waking up, we’re stepping up, we’re meeting the moment. … We recognize we have agency. We’re not bystanders of the world. We can shape the future. The future is not in front of us, it is inside of us. It’s decisions, not conditions.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom campaigns Sunday in Oakland County with Michigan House candidates Sarah Pounds and Alex Hawkins. Aug. 9, 2026 | Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance
Newsom celebrated the Democratic Party’s recent success in state legislative races across the country and urged volunteers to keep working hard through the general election. 
Newsom is widely considered a potential front-runner for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, but he said his focus on visiting Michigan was to support Democrats up and down the ballot. In addition to planning to meet with El-Sayed Monday, Newsom said he campaigned earlier in the weekend with Michigan Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson.
In reaction to the visit, Republican gubernatorial nominee John James posted on X a graphic with a headshot of Newsom next to Benson and El-Sayed with the caption “don’t California my Michigan”.
James said it “makes sense” Newsom came to support Michigan Democrats, writing that “while Jocelyn Benson has been in Lansing, Michigan has been competing with California for last place on education, affordability and economic opportunity.” 
James didn’t cite his sources or link to reports to corroborate those claims. A recent ranking of “Best States” by U.S. News & World Report ranked California as the 35th best state. Michigan was ranked 46th. 
In the 54th House District, Pounds is endorsed by EMILY’s list and the UAW, and the district was listed by Gongwer News Service as one of the top 10 House seats most likely to change parties this cycle. The incumbent, state Rep. Donni Steele (R-Orion Township), is pursuing a seat in the Michigan Senate while Republicans nominated Roman Gaskey, a strategy and product analyst, to succeed her.
Pounds says people she talks to are excited for change and are excited to vote for candidates up and down the ballot. She has made housing a key issue of her campaign and says she has drafted a bill that would allow for the development of housing on land currently owned by churches, universities or nonprofits.
The 54th District spans part of Oakland County, where Pounds says many churches that no longer have active congregations still own a lot of vacant land in areas that also have access to utility infrastructure that could support housing developments. 
“They are in really great areas. The utilities are already there. It makes so much sense that we used that land and build multifamily housing there,” Pounds said. “That’s something I’m super passionate about and can’t wait to work for in Lansing.”
Hawkins served as a bomb disposal specialist in the U.S. Army and is now an officer in the Michigan National Guard with endorsements from Planned Parenthood of Michigan and VoteVets, according to his campaign website. 
Hawkins says politicians like 55th District Republican incumbent Mark Tisdel (R-Rochester Hills) haven’t been accountable for promises made while campaigning. Hawkins’ campaign focuses on strong funding for public schools and finding ways to lower costs for Michigan families. 
Michigan House Democratic Leader Ranjiv Puri (D-Canton) speaking in Oakland County Sunday while campaigning with California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Michigan House candidates Sarah Pounds and Alex Hawkins. Aug. 9, 2026 | Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance
GOP-led House “Achilles heel of Michigan politics”
Speaking at the event, House Democratic Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) said the current Republican majority in the House has obstructed Democrats from passing legislation to address Michiganders’ concerns about affording increasing costs of goods and services ranging from gasoline to healthcare, childcare and groceries. 
“Right now we need fighters because there is so much going wrong,” Puri said, referencing the increased costs facing Michigan households. He connected the legislative opposition Democrats face in Lansing with the “corruption and chaos” he says defines the Trump administration. 
Puri said Democrats can succeed by focusing on the economic issues that are having an immediate impact on Michigan families. 
“Costs have gone up, we’re in wars that no one wanted, and this is all going against the ‘mandate’ that was delivered in 2024 about bringing down costs and focusing on America First,” Puri said. “I think Democrats, Republicans and independents alike have seen enough and they want change. It’s Democrats right now that refuse to rubber-stamp the chaos coming out of D.C. and actually want to fight for Michigan’s working families.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey: WV public school funding formula needs work, spending may not be the answer
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s team laid out his office’s ideas for revamping West Virginia’s school funding formula, a decades-old equation that has been linked to public schools’ dire financial situation.
text:
Sen. Eric Tarr, R-Putnam, and Del. Joe Parsons, R-Jackson, look over a presentation in the Joint Committee on Education on Aug. 9, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s team laid out his office’s ideas for revamping West Virginia’s school funding formula, a decades-old equation that has been linked to public schools’ dire financial situation.
Debate over the funding formula is expected to be a leading topic in the 2027 legislative session.
Morrisey’s office wants to see the formula simplified and more money directed to classrooms, but that doesn’t necessarily mean a hefty financial investment into public schools. 
“The governor has a deep desire to strengthen public education. Everyone should share that desire,” said Curtis Capehart, who represented the governor’s office during a presentation to lawmakers on Sunday at the state Capitol. 
West Virginia uses a seven-step formula to determine how much state funding goes to county school systems based on factors including the number of students enrolled.
State population decline coupled with students leaving public schools for the Hope Scholarship have put many counties in urgent money trouble. The growing number of special education students, which can require costly services, has also impacted schools’ budgets.
Since lawmakers adjourned in March, school officials have sounded alarm bells on worsening school finances, warning multiple counties are headed to insolvency. An additional 5,000 students have left the school system since October, and more school closures are expected.
“The current funding formula is, in a word, complex, relying on multiple steps of intricate calculations that very few people can understand at all,” Capehart told lawmakers. “This inadvertently obscures accountability, prevents everyone, including laborers and taxpayers alike, from readily understanding how funding is out. Any future reform should need to remove complexity in order to increase transparency. 
Morrisey wants to simplify the formula and keep money tied to the student, Capehart said, and the governor’s team believes that the funding formula’s focus on enrollment is one of its better features.
Any reform to the funding formula should be carried out in “a fiscally disciplined manner,” Capehart said. 
“West Virginia ranks near the national average in terms of per pupil spending, but our education results do not. Many states spend substantially less per pupil than West Virginia does, but nonetheless, have significantly better outcomes,” Capehart said. “This demonstrates that injecting more money into the system, simply spending more, is not the answer. “
Financial resources should be focused directly into the classroom, according to Capehart. 
The legislative session concluded in March without lawmakers making any changes to the school funding formula after debate on multiple bills to deal with the issue. Roadblocks often centered on funding concerns; a House bill updating the funding formula would have cost $214 million.
Senate Education Chair Amy Grady, R-Mason. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Capehart’s presentation was the first time lawmakers had heard this list of Morrisey’s education priorities, according to Senate Education Chair Amy Grady, R-Mason.
“Whenever we’re looking at education reform, and we’re looking at how we’re going to change that funding formula, the governor’s office is also a part of that,” Grady said. “We want to make sure that we are all connecting, that we’re all working towards the same goal, instead of you know the two of us working one direction and another one fighting against us.”
Del. Mike Pushkin, D-Kanawha. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Mike Pushkin, D-Kanawha, raised concerns about the Hope Scholarship, the state’s education voucher program, and its effect on public school finances. 
More than 26,000 students have applied for full funding of the Hope Scholarship for the upcoming school year — the first year the program opens up to all West Virginia students. The program has cost the state of West Virginia an estimated $155 million so far after lawmakers allocated $277 million for the Hope Scholarship to account for any student who uses the program in the 2026-27 school year.  
A $114,000 study paid for by the House recommended that the state put some guardrails on the Hope Scholarship spending — it has a broad list of allowable expenses, including out-of-state schools — in an effort to improve overall school finances.  
“There’s no guardrails there, there’s no regulation there … that, by definition, would take money out of public education,” Pushkin said.
Capehart responded that he “was not here to speak about Hope Scholarship today.” Morrisey has been a staunch supporter of the education voucher program.
Capehart floated other ideas from Morrisey’s office to boost education outcomes in the state, including addressing teacher and staff pay. The National Education Association ranks West Virginia as 47th in the nation for average teacher salary.
“It would be in the long-term interests of the state to create a broad, competitive salary structure that draws more people to these educational professions and rewards,” Capehart said.

title: State rolls out tools for new Medicaid work requirements
description: From texts to town halls, the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration is rolling out a variety of tools to prepare Hoosies on the Healthy Indiana Plan for new work requirements. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Indiana will implement work requirements for new applicants and existing Medicaid members eligible under HIP, which provides healthcare coverage for[...]
text:
State officials are reaching out in various ways to educate Hoosiers about upcoming work requirements for able-bodied adults. (Illustration by FSSA)From texts to town halls, the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration is rolling out a variety of tools to prepare Hoosies on the Healthy Indiana Plan for new work requirements.
Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Indiana will implement work requirements for new applicants and existing Medicaid members eligible under HIP, which provides healthcare coverage for the state’s Medicaid expansion population.
Those adults generally will have to complete and report at least 80 hours per month of work, job training, education, community service or another qualifying activity to remain covered. The state will review compliance at least every six months.
The state will look back at the previous three months of activity to determine eligibility. That means anyone applying starting Jan. 1 will have to meet the requirements going back to October. Current members will have to prove compliance on a rolling basis when their renewal date comes up.
The changes will not apply to everyone on Medicaid. Children, pregnant women, older adults, people enrolled in Medicare and many people with disabilities or caregiving responsibilities are among those expected to be exempt. A parent caring for a child age 13 or younger, for example, would not have to meet the requirement, while a child enrolled in Medicaid would never be expected to report work.
To help raise awareness of the new work requirements, starting July 21, the state will periodically text HIP members general information about the new requirements. The text message will be sent from the phone number 43816and will not contain or ask about case information or have an impact on an individual’s HIP benefits or application.
The agency has also created a screening tool for HIP members check to see if they would but subject to or exempt from the work requirements. To use the tool, individuals will be asked to provide information on:

If an exemption applies to them
Health-related questions
Work activities
Income

Once the information is entered, they will be able to review and submit their answers to see if they would be required to meet HIP Work Requirements. The information is entered anonymously and is not stored or shared. Responses are used only to generate an individual’s screening results and are not accessible after the session ends.
FSSA, in partnership with Covering Kids & Families, will also host a series of public town halls across the state to help HIP members, providers and community partners learn more about the upcoming requirements.
The first two town halls are scheduled for August and September at the following dates and locations listed below. Additional town halls will be announced throughout the year.

name: Delaware
title: Copeland: Delaware Needs New Direction to Strengthen Economy
description: Former state senator tells A Better Discussion that controlling spending, reducing regulation and rebuilding Delaware’s private-sector economy should be priorities WILMINGTON, Del. (Aug. 9, 2026) — Delaware can strengthen its economy, but doing so will require policymakers to control government spending, reduce barriers to private investment and pay closer a[...]
text:
Former state senator tells A Better Discussion that controlling spending, reducing regulation and rebuilding Delaware’s private-sector economy should be priorities
WILMINGTON, Del. (Aug. 9, 2026) — Delaware can strengthen its economy, but doing so will require policymakers to control government spending, reduce barriers to private investment and pay closer attention to how state policies affect businesses, workers and taxpayers, former state Sen. Charlie Copeland said during an Aug. 3 live webcast.
Copeland joined Jane Brady, former Delaware attorney general, chair of A Better Delaware and host of A Better Discussion with Jane Brady, for a wide-ranging examination of Delaware’s economy, government spending, taxation, regulation, housing and education.
Both argued that decisions made in Dover have consequences that extend well beyond the state budget.
“Policies that the state adopts do matter,” Brady said. “They matter for every one of us.”
Copeland, a businessman and former Republican state chairman, argued that Delaware’s economic problems are significant but reversible.
“You could fix Delaware in a year,” Copeland said. “But what it takes is leadership.”
Government spending outpaces economic growth
Copeland traced what he described as a long-term acceleration in Delaware government spending.
He said state spending historically grew at roughly 2% annually before increasing to more than 4% as Delaware benefited from the growth of credit card banking, abandoned property revenue and legalized gambling.
Federal assistance during the COVID-19 pandemic helped push spending growth even higher, he said.
Copeland argued that while much of the federal money was temporary, higher levels of state spending became embedded in the budget.
“The general fund is now built on an annual 5% increase,” Copeland said.
Brady agreed that Delaware used large surpluses and federal assistance without developing enough of a long-term strategy for what would happen when the extraordinary revenue disappeared.
“We literally had $3 and $4 billion surpluses that we expended,” Brady said. “We spent it all. A lot of it we cooked into the base budget.”
She said some money went toward capital improvements, including schools, but questioned whether policymakers adequately planned for the long-term consequences of expanding recurring programs while temporary revenues were available.
Where is Delaware’s next growth industry?
Copeland said the spending issue becomes more concerning when compared with what he characterized as a stagnant private-sector economy.
He pointed to the closing of Delaware’s automobile plants, DuPont’s contraction and restructuring and Bank of America’s acquisition of MBNA as important turning points.
Copeland recalled telling then-Delaware State Chamber of Commerce President Rich Heffron while serving in the state Senate that Delaware faced a fundamental economic problem.
“Delaware’s in trouble,” Copeland recalled saying. “We have no growing industry in the state of Delaware right now.”
He said the question Delaware still needs to answer is straightforward.
“What’s your vision for how you grow this economy?” Copeland said. “Well, there hasn’t been one.”
Brady echoed that concern, saying Delaware has experienced what she described as a “slow but steady process of deterioration” in the state’s interest in developing new businesses.
She distinguished between companies legally forming or incorporating in Delaware and companies actually putting employees, facilities and investment in the state.
“There are a lot of new business formations, but they’re not for businesses that are operating in Delaware, necessarily,” Brady said.
Incorporation is different from economic development
That distinction became one of the central themes of the discussion.
Delaware traditionally points to its dominance in corporate incorporations as one of the state’s major economic strengths. Copeland acknowledged the importance of that industry but said incorporation should not be confused with companies choosing Delaware as a place to employ people.
“How many of them are headquartered in Delaware?” Copeland asked. “In other words, this is where their headquarter staff is, this is where their offices are, this is where they hire people, this is where they operate out of. And the answer is, very few.”
Brady said increasing competition from other states makes that distinction even more important.
She pointed particularly to Texas, which has been aggressively positioning itself to attract financial and corporate activity.
“Texas has really declared war on anybody who wants to go into business,” Brady said. “They’re going to bring them in.”
She said competition can benefit the economy by forcing states and institutions to innovate but warned that Delaware cannot take its historic advantages for granted.
Copeland agreed.
“Texas has made a very aggressive move,” he said, arguing Delaware is simultaneously making it more difficult for businesses to operate.
Making Delaware ‘open for business’
Asked what Delaware could do differently, Copeland said the state should begin with a clear message to employers and entrepreneurs.
“Delaware’s open for business,” Copeland said. “Get the regulatory guys off their backs.”
Copeland said a governor should personally contact businesses considering expansions and make the case for locating jobs in Delaware.
He also called for more government services to be moved online, greater use of technology and greater scrutiny of state positions and regulatory requirements.
His broader argument was that government does not need to create economic growth itself.
“There are these people that have agency and are going to make good decisions, and they’re going to grow it on their own because incentives matter,” Copeland said. “And if you get out of their way, it’s going to happen.”
Brady said the experience of businesses should receive more consideration when lawmakers make decisions affecting employers.
She said many decisions involving business finances and operations increasingly are being reviewed or influenced by people in government who may have limited experience operating businesses themselves.
That disconnect, she argued, can produce policies with unintended economic consequences.
A different view of government’s role
Not everyone agrees with Brady and Copeland’s prescription. Karl Stromberg, a leader of Delaware’s Working Families Party, has argued that higher taxes on wealthier residents and corporations can generate additional revenue for public priorities rather than necessarily driving investment away. Stromberg also supports changes to Delaware’s judicial and Court of Chancery system that he believes would make corporate governance more accountable to citizens and shareholders, and he favors a larger government role in housing policy to expand affordable options for lower-income families. Those positions reflect a different view of the same challenges: that stronger public investment, greater corporate accountability and more direct government involvement can improve economic opportunity rather than impede it.
Housing shortage highlights regulatory debate
Housing offered a practical example of the broader debate over regulation.
Copeland pointed to large parking lots and single-story retail developments near New Castle County Airport and suggested changes in land-use rules could allow residential units to be constructed above existing commercial properties.
“We’ve got plenty of place to put” housing, Copeland said, arguing that relatively modest changes to development codes could encourage private investment.
“If you get government out of the way, the incentives are there for private sector developers to put in affordable housing all over the place,” he said.
Brady questioned whether policymakers have sufficiently defined what they mean when discussing “affordable housing” and said the cost of regulation ultimately reaches consumers.
She returned to that point at the conclusion of the webcast.
“How much it costs the regulators, costs builders to build new homes affects anybody who wants to buy a new home,” Brady said.
Taxes and the competition for residents
Taxes also emerged as a major concern.
Copeland said continued government spending growth will eventually increase pressure to find additional revenue.
He warned that substantially higher income tax rates could change the calculations made by business owners and higher-income residents about where they live and invest.
“Once you start adding numbers on top, you start competing with New York and California,” Copeland said.
Because Delaware is geographically small, he said residents can relatively easily establish themselves elsewhere while businesses can direct future investments to other states.
He cited Delaware’s former estate tax as an example, arguing that some wealthy residents shifted their primary residences to states such as Florida.
“People don’t grow stupid overnight, and incentives matter, and they’re gonna make rational decisions,” Copeland said.
Brady said she personally knew several people who changed their residency during the period Delaware imposed the estate tax.
The two argued that policymakers should consider not simply how much revenue a new tax might theoretically generate, but whether it changes the behavior of the people being taxed.
Work, incentives and the safety net
Brady and Copeland also discussed labor-force participation and the relationship between public benefits and employment.
Copeland argued that government assistance should function as a safety net while preserving incentives for able-bodied people to enter the workforce.
Brady said the issue goes beyond government finances.
She argued that work provides people with a sense of productivity and personal accomplishment that government programs cannot replace.
“There’s benefits to working,” Brady said, adding that government policy can overlook “that human component.”
Copeland agreed, saying work can provide “a certain sense of self-esteem, self-worth” and personal value.
The two also acknowledged that reducing benefits after they have become embedded in household finances would be difficult.
Copeland said abruptly withdrawing assistance could create serious consequences for housing, food security and nonprofit organizations serving families.
“You have a serious transition cost that’s staring the state in the eye,” he said.
Education is economic policy, too
The discussion eventually turned to Delaware schools, with both Brady and Copeland arguing that education should be viewed as part of the state’s economic strategy.
Copeland said businesses consider workforce quality when determining where to invest and said Delaware’s education system requires significantly stronger action.
“I would declare a state of education emergency,” Copeland said.
He argued that years of incremental changes have not produced sufficient results and called for greater leadership and accountability.
Brady pointed to Mississippi’s improvement in student reading performance and said Delaware should be willing to consider policies that have produced measurable improvement elsewhere.
She argued that new education spending should be accompanied by specific accountability measures and measurable expectations for student improvement.
Brady: Policy choices matter at the ballot box
Brady ended the program by connecting the economic discussion to the elections Delaware voters will face this year.
She urged voters to look beyond political mailers and advertising and examine what candidates actually propose to do about spending, regulation, education, housing and economic development.
“It’s critical that we make good decisions about who we choose to govern us, because those policies matter,” Brady said.
The broader message from Brady and Copeland was that Delaware’s economic future is not predetermined.
Their argument throughout the webcast was that decisions made by governors, legislators and regulators influence whether businesses invest, whether people work, how much housing costs and ultimately how much government can afford.

DELAWARE LIVE TO GO

Charlie CopelandWhy watch: Brady brings Delaware policymakers, business leaders and subject-matter experts into a weekly conversation about the decisions being made in the state and how those decisions affect Delaware residents.

text:
Former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam, left, climate organizer William Lawrence, center, and former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, right, attend a rally in Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 8, 2026, meant to unite supporters of the three candidates who ran in the Democratic primary for Michigan's Seventh Congressional District behind Lawrence's general election campaign. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Following a hard-fought primary, former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam came together to support Democratic nominee for U.S. House in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District William Lawrence.
Brink and Maasdam split the moderate vote in the Aug. 4 primary nearly evenly, with 28.8% and 27.6% respectively, allowing Lawrence to win with a plurality of 43.7%, according to unofficial results.
Lawrence said both candidates called him Tuesday night and offered their full support.
He thanked Maasdam for “the fury I hear in his voice when he talks about the unconstitutional abuses committed by ICE” and Brink for “her principled resignation of the Trump administration and her focus on good healthcare.”
Lawrence said he will “unite and mobilize every single potential ally and resource to flip this district,” because “if we do not, the president’s attempts to establish an AI-powered surveillance state with permanently rigged elections may very well succeed.”
Democratic nominee for U.S. House in Michigan’s Seventh Congressional District William Lawrence speaks during a rally in Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 8, 2026. The rally was meant to unite supporters of the three candidates who ran in the primary and was also attended by former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam and former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink.
