name: Alabama Reflector
title: ‘I hear you, I see you:’ Alabama Democrats elect Bobby Singleton as chair
description: Alabama Democrats on Saturday elected Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton party chair amid calls for the organization to take advantage of the most promising electoral landscape for state Democrats in years. Singleton got 165 votes (72.7%) over current Chair Randy Kelley, who got 62 votes (27.3%) in a vote in which the 200-plus members of […]
text:
Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, watches as votes are counted during an election for Alabama Democratic Party chair at the Alabama State Democratic Executive Committee's on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026 in Montgomery, Ala. Singleton won with 73% of the votes from about 220 SDEC members. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)Alabama Democrats on Saturday elected Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton party chair amid calls for the organization to take advantage of the most promising electoral landscape for state Democrats in years.
Singleton got 165 votes (72.7%) over current Chair Randy Kelley, who got 62 votes (27.3%) in a vote in which the 200-plus members of the State Democratic Executive (SDEC) voted by holding up pieces of paper with “vote” printed on them while other members walked around to count. 
“I want you to know that I hear you, I see you,” Singleton said in a two-minute speech prior to the vote. “We need to make sure that we realize and listen to people. I’m gonna hold listening tours across all 67 counties because I want you to know: Women, I see you and I hear you. I want the LGBTQ to know that I hear you and I see you. We can no longer sit back and do things in an archaic way.”
The vote, coming amid a potentially promising year for the party, ended a tumultuous tenure for Alabama Democratic Party Chair Randy Kelley, an ally of Joe Reed, the vice chair for minority affairs for the party and a major force among state Democrats. In 2023, the SDEC passed bylaws that eliminated youth, LGBTQ+ and disabled caucuses and reduced the powers of affirmative action; Asian and Pacific Islander; Hispanic; and Native American caucuses “to monitor the affairs of the groups listed.” Most of the minority caucuses were restored in 2024 by order of the Democratic National Committee (DNC). 
The change in leadership also followed weeks of online discourse that ranged from complaints of a lack of election education to accusations of illegal campaign finance practices from former candidates. House Minority Leader Anthony Daniels, D-Huntsville, who nominated Singleton, said the party needed a chair that could raise money.
“This is no indictment on anyone, anywhere, because as we leave here today we have to be united no matter what and put our differences to the side as we move forward,” Daniels said. “We cannot let any election go unchallenged on the other side.”
Alabama Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, hugs former Alabama Democratic Party Chair Randy Kelley after winning election as party chair at the Alabama State Democratic Executive Committee’s meeting on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026 in Montgomery, Ala. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)
Singleton said in an interview after the election that the change within the party demonstrates frustrations members, candidates and legislators have felt with party leadership.
“I know I was getting frustrated as a member of the legislature when I looked around, and we’re in the middle of battles. There was never the Democratic Party that supported us. I saw the Republican Party support their people,” he said. “I want to bring that same kind of energy and say that we’re at the table.”
Kelley touted the party’s progress during his first term in his opening statement, but said the party needs to expand its reach to churches. 
“If we realized how we had the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act, the Bus Boycott victory of Montgomery, Fair Housing Act, much of that came by social-conscious pastors, Black people and white folks of goodwill, and we’re all beneficiaries of it,” Kelley said. “We’re going to have to activate the churches if we even expect to win.”
He also mentioned the flipping of a Huntsville-area House seat by Rep. Marilyn Lands in a 2024 special election, and the election of U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, in 2024, during the chairman’s report. 
As soon as SDEC members raised their vote cards for Singleton, his voters and other non-voting Democrats in attendance cheered for the lawmaker. 
In Kelley’s chairman’s report he said the party should be united and shift away from toxicity.
“Together, we can make a better future for our children. Together, we can transform Alabama,” Kelley said. 
Singleton said he has a 90-day plan, but did not have time to go over it during his allotted time. He promised to visit Alabama’s 67 counties and bring government as close to the people as possible.
“We’re going to unite as one party, one future, and we will do it right here together. And in November, we’re going to win,” Singleton said.
Singleton said in an interview after the election that his 90-day plan includes visiting every county before the general election, which is in 87 days, fundraising events and supporting county chairs and candidates. 
“It’s robust, and there’s only 87 days until the election, and I’m talking about 90 days, but it goes beyond that,” Singleton said. “I’m really talking about the core of this party and how we’re gonna have to rebuild the core of this party, being able to be attentive and allow people to have a voice.”
He also plans to release a 90-Day Progress Report that includes three stages: listen, build and mobilize. He does not plan to step down as Minority Leader.
Singleton nominated Caroline Self, an elected member of SDEC in House District 2, who won by 139 votes (66.5%) over Tori Bailey, an elected member of the SDEC from House District 3.
“I want to work to win. We have opportunities this year that we have not seen since I was a child. I get out every day and I work countless hours because we can win in November,” Self said.
Doug Jones and Rep. Philip Ensler of Montgomery, the party’s nominees for governor and lieutenant governor, lingered at the meeting but did not speak.
The meeting had a slow start, with approval of November’s meeting minutes taking over an hour. Stan Glasscox, an elected SDEC member from House District 63, left the meeting briefly and returned with two bottles of beer for himself and Amber Buck, an SDEC representative from Tuscaloosa.
Stan Glasscox gestures to the audience as he is asked to leave for drinking alcohol during a meeting of the Alabama State Democratic Executive Committee hearing on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026 in Montgomery, Ala. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)
He was asked to leave the voting area of the meeting. He handed off one beverage to a guest, stood on the side of the guest area to finish his beverage and returned to vote. 
“Whether you’re black, white, straight, or gay, whatever your pronoun may be, whether you’re young or old, I want this party to be one Democrat,” Singleton said in an interview. “That’s all we want to do, is focus on being a Democrat so we can win in November.”
Although Democrats have the largest slate of candidates since 2018 and had increased primary turnout, they remain underdogs statewide. There are a few competitive legislative seats the party hopes to flip in November.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: UP Academy Holland’s turnaround success offers a nuanced lesson on receivership
description: If the goal is to improve outcomes for students attending chronically underperforming schools, the most important question is not whether receivership succeeded everywhere. It is whether it succeeded anywhere, and if so, why.
text:
THE MASSACHUSETTS Board of Elementary and Secondary Education recently voted to end state receivership of UP Academy Holland and return the school’s operation to Boston Public Schools. It was a significant moment for a school that, just over a decade ago, was among the lowest performing in the state. 
The vote should also prompt a broader conversation. 
For the past several years, the dominant narrative surrounding state receivership in Massachusetts has been that it did not work. There is evidence to support that view. Several state takeovers produced mixed results, and the outcomes often fell short of the ambitious promises that accompanied them. 
But if the goal is to improve outcomes for students attending chronically underperforming schools, the most important question is not whether receivership succeeded everywhere. It is whether it succeeded anywhere, and if so, why. 
UP Academy Holland, soon to return to its original name, John P. Holland Elementary School, deserves to be part of that conversation. 
When the school entered receivership, it ranked in the bottom 1 percent of public schools statewide. Today, it is one of the strongest-performing schools in Boston. It ranks second among Dorchester schools in English language arts growth and is among the top-performing Boston Public Schools in ELA and math growth overall. Third-grade students outperform district and state averages in math proficiency among comparable high-needs schools, and multilingual learners exceed district and state peers on ACCESS growth measures. 
Most importantly, the school is now positioned to return to district governance while preserving the systems, culture, and instructional practices that drove its improvement. 
That outcome matters. 
BPS still has more than 40 schools performing in the bottom decile statewide, although the district is implementing numerous strategies to improve performance. Across Massachusetts, educators and policymakers continue to wrestle with the challenge of helping chronically underperforming schools improve. Holland demonstrates that meaningful transformation is possible. The question is why. 
I have spent much of my career at Holland, first as a member of the founding leadership team, then as principal, later supporting the development of school leaders, and now as CEO of UP Education Network, the organization that partnered with BPS to manage the school during receivership. 
No single curriculum, training, or intervention transformed Holland. The theory of change was more fundamental, and frankly, isn’t glamorous nor particularly innovative: create clarity about excellence, build systems aligned to that vision, and develop the capacity of leaders to improve teacher practice through sustained coaching and feedback. We were steadfast in our belief in the power of these elements, and over time, those elements did in fact reinforce one another and produced improvement that could last beyond any one leader or organization.  
Looking back, three broader lessons stand out. 
First, school transformation takes time. 
One of the challenges in education policy is that improvement timelines are often measured in election cycles, contract terms, or leadership tenures. School transformation rarely operates on those timelines. 
Holland made significant gains early in its turnaround, but lasting improvement required years of refining and strengthening the practices behind those results. It required building the capacity of leaders and teachers, responding to new challenges, and sustaining a culture of improvement through leadership transitions, changing circumstances, and even a global pandemic. With stability, persistence, and a willingness to stay the course, these systems have thrived at Holland. 
Second, successful turnarounds require true partnership. 
Too often, conversations about receivership frame districts and external operators as competing interests. In practice, successful school improvement depends on the opposite. 
Throughout Holland’s transformation, BPS and UP maintained a shared commitment to the same outcome: ensuring students had access to an excellent school. That partnership required trust, flexibility, and an understanding that improvement efforts were being carried out on behalf of the district, not in opposition to it. 
The transition now underway reflects that same spirit. District leaders, union leaders, state officials, school leaders, and UP have spent the past year working together to identify what must be preserved for the school to continue thriving and maintain student outcomes. 
Third, and perhaps most importantly, struggling schools need the right partner. 
Not every organization is equipped to lead school transformation, which requires far more than good intentions. It requires the ability to establish a clear vision, translate that vision into coherent systems, develop strong leaders, and support educators through years of challenging work. It also requires the discipline to execute those practices consistently and the willingness to keep learning when something is not working. 
It requires humility as well. The most effective partners recognize that success is not measured by how long they remain in control. It is measured by whether the school can thrive after they leave. 
At Holland, the goal was never to create a permanent alternative to district leadership. The goal was to build a school strong enough to succeed within BPS. 
As Holland returns to district governance, that work is not ending. Through ongoing collaboration, both organizations are committed to ensuring continuity for students, families, and staff. Improvement is not sustained through abrupt transitions. It is sustained through thoughtful ones. 
The lesson of Holland is not that receivership is the answer to every struggling school. Nor is it an argument for a return to broad state takeovers. 
The lesson is that school transformation is possible. 
Massachusetts remains a national leader in education, but statewide success can obscure the reality facing students in schools that have struggled for years to deliver the outcomes they deserve. 
As the state formally closes the chapter on Holland’s receivership, we should resist the temptation to view the story solely through the lens of a broader debate about state intervention. Instead, we should study it carefully. 
Because if we are serious about improving outcomes for students in chronically underperforming schools, our responsibility is not to replicate a governance model. It is to study and replicate the practices that make lasting improvement possible. 
Holland offers one example. Students and families demand that we learn from it. 
Hillary Casson is the Chief Executive Officer of UP Education Network.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Dem lawmakers call for Bankhead to drop out of U.S. Senate race
description: Twenty-two Democratic members of the Montana Legislature are officially asking Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate race, to drop out and support the independent in the race, Seth Bodnar. In a letter dated Aug. 7, seven senators and 15 house members say they are “united in believing that Seth Bodnar is the […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Alani Bankhead speaks during a Lewis and Clark County Democratic watch party for the primary at the Rialto in Helena, Montana, on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Twenty-two Democratic members of the Montana Legislature are officially asking Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate race, to drop out and support the independent in the race, Seth Bodnar.
In a letter dated Aug. 7, seven senators and 15 house members say they are “united in believing that Seth Bodnar is the candidate who shares our Democratic values and has the experience, knowledge, resources and capacity” to take on Republican Kurt Alme.
The letter was first reported by CNN’s Patrick Svitek.
A month ago, 17 lawmakers wrote a letter to both Bankhead and Bodnar, asking them to meet and discuss a way to unite voters against Alme. That letter did not explicitly ask either candidate to drop out, but highlighted that Bodnar appeared better positioned at the time to run the strongest general election campaign.
On Friday, Bodnar held a press conference assuring his supporters he would not drop out of the race, regardless of whom else was in it.
Bankhead told the Daily Montanan she is also committed to staying the course.
In their letter, the lawmakers argue the most important consideration for the U.S. Senate election is to elect someone “who will oppose the destructive policies of the Trump Administration, while advancing an agenda that benefits all Montanan.”
“It is this concern for our constituents, the direction of our country and our American Democracy that motivates our support for Seth at this time,” they wrote. “…A prolonged three-way contest — and the resulting divisions among voters, volunteers, donors, allied organizations and candidates — will weaken Democratic and allied campaigns across the ballot.”
The signatories represent more than a third of all elected Democrats in Montana.
Four representatives — Mike Fox, Shelly Fyant, Jennifer Lynch, Luke Muszkiewicz — signed the first letter asking the two candidates to discuss options, but not the latest one.
In reliably Republican states across the country, Democratic candidates dropping out of U.S. Senate races has become a trend, giving independent candidates a clearer path to head-to-head matchups with Republicans.
In recent polling, Bodnar has shown strength in a face-off with Alme, but the Republican easily wins a crowded field.
The idea is modeled on Dan Osborn in Nebraska, who ran as an independent in 2024 against a Republican incumbent without a Democrat in the field — coming within seven points of winning even as Trump carried the state by 21 points. Osborn is running again in 2026 and the state Democratic Party has supported not fielding a candidate.
Democratic candidates in Idaho, Alaska, and South Dakota have all dropped out of their respective races this cycle.
A Montana Democratic Party spokesperson told the Daily Montanan this week that the party supports Bankhead as the winner of the primary.
Bankhead won the Democratic primary by 12,000 votes more than her closest competitor, and was buoyed by more than $2.5 million in outside spending on her behalf.
As a general election candidate, she has failed to gain endorsements from traditionally left-aligned organizations and the state’s biggest Democratic players while fundraising just $60,000.
Meanwhile Bodnar outraised all federal candidates in each reporting period and has stacked up support from unions, environmental and veterans organizations, and former elected officials from both parties, including former Democratic U.S. Senators Jon Tester and Max Baucus, and former Republican Gov. Marc Racicot.
If Bankhead did drop out of the race, it is likely to spark a legal battle over whether the Montana Democratic Party is required in state law to name a replacement.
A group of Democratic lawyers wrote a memo to the state party last month laying out the legal framework behind not choosing a new candidate.
On the other side, Republicans, including Alme’s campaign, circulated a memo written by the state’s former solicitor general, arguing why Democrats would be required to name a successor.
The deadline to withdraw from November’s ballot is Monday at 5 p.m.

title: Nebraska GOP sues to block the ‘America First Party’
description: The Nebraska Republican Party suit adds to the handful of lawsuits that this Nebraska midterm cycle has seen.
text:
The Nebraska Republican party headquarters in Lincoln on Oct. 28, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Republican Party is suing to keep the America First Party off the November ballot. 
The GOP lawsuit asks Lancaster District Court Judge Darla Ideus to overrule Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen’s decision not to intervene with the party’s creation, declare that the party’s language is meant to confuse voters and therefore breaks state law, and stop the party from being officially recognized. 
The lawsuit argues that Omaha Tribe Attorney General John Cartier, the sponsor for the America First Party, “dressed up” the party with “conservative talking points: cracking down on illegal immigration, defending the Second Amendment, opposing abortion.”
“However, the façade crumbles under the slightest scrutiny. Mr. Cartier is a well-known leftist political operative with deeply held leftist political beliefs. This is not the establishment of a legitimate political party. It is political sabotage — a calculated effort to maliciously confuse voters by hijacking a nationally recognized brand inextricably linked to President Donald J. Trump and the conservative movement he leads,” the lawsuit reads. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both Republicans and Democrats have objections to the creation of two new parties in the state. 
State Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb accused U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts of being behind the effort to establish the Nebraska Working People Party. She said, “There’s only one reason to launch a new party this late: divide the vote and create chaos. Voters see through spoiler games funded by special interests.”
Republicans objected to efforts to establish the America First Party, pointing to Cartier’s connection to Legal Marijuana Now Senate candidate Mike Marvin. Republicans have accused Marvin of helping nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn, contending that Marvin would drop out of the race. Marvin says he is staying in the race. The lawsuit also points to Cartier’s receiving $500 from Osborn’s campaign for legal fees in November 2024, according to the Federal Election Commission. 
The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office announced Friday that the two proposed parties have met the petition signature threshold. If the parties meet the Aug. 27 deadline to submit organization documents, they must name candidates for the Nov. 3 general election by Sept. 1.
The GOP suit adds to a handful of lawsuits during this Nebraska midterm cycle. Another lawsuit seeks to force Nebraska Democrats to find a replacement for their Senate nominee, Cindy Burbank, who dropped out. Burbank had sued to get back on the primary ballot after Evnen removed her for not being a “good faith” candidate. 
It’s unclear which races will see candidates from these two new parties, but most of the political drama has centered on the Senate race between Osborn and incumbent Republican Ricketts. 
The Nebraska GOP, through an attorney letter, late last month asked Evnen to object to the creation of the America First Party, contending that it would confuse voters because the name is “a designation widely and nationally understood to represent President Trump’s political movement and conservative policy priorities.” The party cited state law that says the secretary of state can reject a candidate’s filing if the state’s top election official determines that someone is not a “good-faith candidate” or is trying to cause confusion for voters. The law also says objections to party names can be considered. 
Evnen responded to the NEGOP request, writing that he agreed that the party was likely created to cause confusion, but said there is no other Nebraska party that uses the words “America” and “first” in its name.

“In the event that Nebraska courts hold that I have broader authority than I have indicated here … or otherwise, I would disqualify the name ‘America First Party,’” Evnen wrote. “Unless and until a court of competent jurisdiction timely holds otherwise, however, I will not disqualify the use of the name ‘America First Party.’” 
Lancaster County District Judge Matthew Mellor granted an emergency injunction preventing certification of the America First Party until Monday afternoon. A hearing in the case is scheduled for 2 p.m. that day.

title: Federal judge orders release of unlawfully detained Yellowstone County man
description: A federal judge has ordered  the release of Jesus Verde Hernandez, a Worden man whose attorneys said he was unlawfully detained last week by Customs and Border Patrol. Hernandez was being held in the Cascade County Detention Center after authorities arrested him the afternoon of July 30 in Lewistown and transported him to Jordan, Malta, […]
text:
A sign marking entry into Cascade County along Highway 89 taken on March 30, 2024. (Photo by Nicole Girten/Daily Montanan)A federal judge has ordered  the release of Jesus Verde Hernandez, a Worden man whose attorneys said he was unlawfully detained last week by Customs and Border Patrol.
Hernandez was being held in the Cascade County Detention Center after authorities arrested him the afternoon of July 30 in Lewistown and transported him to Jordan, Malta, Havre and Great Falls during the course of 30 hours.
A news release Friday from Upper Seven Law, the law firm representing Hernandez, said Customs and Border Patrol detained him while looking for another man they said resembled him. The court order said officials had no warrant for his arrest nor probable cause.
An earlier court filing said federal authorities tried to force Hernandez to deport himself.
The government tried to argue Hernandez should “exhaust his administrative remedies” before going to federal court, but the judge disagreed.
In the order, Chief District Judge Brian Morris said the government has been dedicated to enforcing a policy “deemed unlawful by the majority of courts.”
It said Hernandez doesn’t need to run through administration options in this case because he is not required to “exhaust a process that was deficient from the outset.”
The court order said the government should release Hernandez “on appropriate conditions based on violations of his constitutional rights.”
Upper Seven is seeking class certification in the case and said Hernandez is among 17 people being unlawfully held in the Cascade County Detention Center.
The court will hear class claims on Aug. 18 in Missoula.  The order Friday applied only to Hernandez.
The nonprofit law firm filed the petition against the Cascade County sheriff and U.S. officials including Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche.
Hernandez has lived in Montana with his partner of 14 years for the last 10 years, and they have three young children. They recently fostered a homeless teen.
The court order said no record shows criminal history for Hernandez or any previous interactions between the Yellowstone County man and immigration.
“Jesus should never have been detained,” said Molly Danahy, Upper Seven Law’s litigation director, in a statement. “Federal immigration authorities have been operating in Montana with impunity, arresting people without statutory authority to do so, and transporting them out of state before their actions can be examined by the judiciary.
“Today’s order simply requires federal officials to comply with the law.”
The order said the government can’t re-detain Hernandez during removal proceedings unless it first holds a hearing, with adequate notice, and proves detention is appropriate under the correct statute.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Historic portraits telling the story of Black South Carolinians now online through USC library
description: Nearly 6,000 historic pictures of Columbia’s Black families and community, are all available free to the public online for the first time.
text:
Portrait of young woman with bobbed hairstyle and floral print dress (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)COLUMBIA — A young boy looks directly into the camera with his arms wrapped around his pet rooster.
A boxer crouches in a fighting stance, gloves up in front of his face.
Nurses dressed head to toe in white in front of the home of Dr. Matilda Evans, the first Black woman licensed to practice medicine in South Carolina.
Richard Samuel Roberts (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)
These images, featured in a collection of nearly 6,000 historic pictures by photographer Richard Samuel Roberts of Columbia’s Black families and community, are all available free to the public online for the first time.
“What we are seeing when we look at these pictures is African Americans the way they wanted to be seen and remembered,” said Rachel Young, a historian at the Center for Civil Rights History and Research at the University of South Carolina. “We are also seeing people and places that have been erased, forgotten or ignored by a broader historical record.”
The digitization of the Roberts collection is the culmination of a decades-long effort by the Roberts family, librarians and researchers at the University of South Carolina.
In 1920, Roberts moved his family from Fernandina, Florida, to Columbia, settling at a home on Wayne Street in the heart of Ward One, a working-class Black neighborhood that has since been largely erased as the university has expanded.
From 4 a.m. until noon, Roberts worked as a custodian at the U.S. Post Office, earning a living to take care of his wife and five children. After his shift ended, he would go to the photography studio space he rented on Washington Street, where he captured images of his community through glass plate negative photography.
His studio was a single room, divided into dressing and waiting areas, a dark room, and a workspace. He designed special equipment to diffuse light, produce different-sized pictures and retouch negatives.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I tell people that Richard Samuel Roberts was not simply a photographer, he was an artist and he was also a historian,” said Bobby Donaldson, executive director of the civil rights center and a history professor at USC.
“He understood that one of his assignments was to tell a complete history of African American life in Columbia and in South Carolina, and he knew that he was telling a story that was against the prevailing narrative and stereotypes surrounding Black people,” he said.
Then, in the 1970s, former South Caroliniana Library field archivist Tom Johnson worked with the Roberts family to remove boxes of the negatives from the crawlspace of the family home, where they had been stored, to the university library, where they could be preserved.
Johnson worked with Philip Dunn, a photography instructor at the college, who took the negatives to his home dark room and developed some of them into contact sheets to see what they looked like.
This portrait of Modjeska Simkins may have been taken during the time she taught at Booker T. Washington High School. (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)
What the pair found was compelling: photographs depicting a vast cross-section of Black life in the state capital during the early 20th Century, from farmers to socialites, babies to funerals, students to magicians, and businesses to community leaders, including Civil Rights activist Modjeska Simpson and celebrated school teacher Celia Dial Saxon.
“There’s just something different about these photos,” said Abby Cole, a spokeswoman for the university’s library system “There’s some depth of humanity.”
The collection was officially purchased from the Roberts family estate in 2020, with “tens of thousands of dollars” raised by the University South Caroliniana Society, Cole said, without specifying. Then, in 2024 the civil rights center paid students to digitize the photos, turning them into a living collection viewable by all.
Some of the people pictured are named in the collection. The center and libraries hope people continue to engage with the collection now that it’s online by identifying those they know in the photos.
“We know photographs have a way of piquing interest and stirring up memories in individuals,” Donaldson said. “These photographs push people to dig in the deep recesses of their mind and their memory, and they begin to recall details that probably would not come as easily without images to facilitate them.”
Viewers of the collection can click a box to submit identifications or notes on each image.
Many of the people pictured have descendants who still live in Columbia today.
They include Family Court Judge Michelle Hurley. Hurley grew up in Columbia, a graduate of Heathwood Hall, Howard University, and USC School of Law. When she was younger, she worked at her family’s funeral home, writing obituaries.
The Manigault-Hurley Funeral Home served the Black community in Columbia for almost a century. Hurley’s grandmother, Annie Mae Manigault-Hurley, was the first female embalmer, white or Black, to be licensed in the state.
Annie Mae Manigault Hurley (1907-1976) was a mortician who graduated from the Renouard School of Embalming in New York. Her parents, William Manigault and Annie Rivers Manigault, operated Manigault Funeral Home, and after graduating, she returned to Columbia to work with them. (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)
Hurley’s great-grandparents also lived next door to Roberts and saw first-hand the impact he had.
“People wanted their stories told, so they went to Mr. Roberts,” Hurley said.
“These photos tell the stories of people’s families, and help people identify their ancestors,” she added. “They bring that history home so people can say, ‘This is who I am, these are the people I come from.’”
One of Roberts’ surviving grandchildren, Judge Richard Warren Roberts, grew up in New York hearing stories about his grandfather.
“It’s one thing to be able to get a two-dimensional paper with your ancestry on it, but it is another thing completely to be able to see your family members in photographs like these,” he said. “You can see the clothes they wore which could signal where they were employed, or what they did for a living. These kinds of revelations infuse people with a greater sense of self.”
As a student, before coming to work for the university libraries, Cole was among those who helped digitize the collection. They scanned the thousands of the negatives, at first on a flatbed scanner and then with a high-end camera scanner. While some of the glass plates were in near perfect condition others were cracked or deteriorating.
“It was a passion to kind of recapture that history,” Cole said.
“These are communities that have been kind of pushed aside or taken advantage of,” Cole added. “And there’s a lot of distrust historically between minorities and universities or archives, because archives decide what stories get told and in what way. This was an effort to rebuild those bridges and to show these communities we want to preserve your story in addition to those stories that are more predominantly told.”
Nurses outside the home of Dr. Matilda Evans. From left to right: Gretchen Evans, Sarah Green, Elizabeth Harris, and Mattie Evans. In the background, Dr. Evan's grandnephew, Edward Evans, leans on the porch railing. (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)Portrait of a man seated at a desk with an open book (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)Portrait of young man with boxing gloves (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)	
Peter Hooper, a magician, escape artist, and puppeteer from Fernandina Florida, and his wife, "Princess" Elizabeth Hooper, a mind-reader and crystal ball gazer, pose with their assistant. They traveled and performed in the 1920s-1950s, in places including Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Maryland, and New Jersey. (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)Portrait of boy wearing a cowboy outfit (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)Seated portrait of a woman in a dark dress with her legs crossed (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)	
Walter Adams, the son of William J. and Sarah Jackson Adams, graduated from Booker T. Washington High School, served in the U.S. Navy during WWII, and was a supervisor of a lumber company on Gervais. He later moved to Hartford, CT, and worked as foreman of General Cigar Tobacco Company and as a youth officer for the State of Connecticut. He and his wife had five children. (Photo courtesy of USC libraries/Richard Samuel Roberts collection)

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Cruise ship helps stranded skiff and crew in Southeast Alaska as Zuckerberg yacht stands by
description: A small cruise ship operating in Southeast Alaska made an unexpected detour on Monday night to help a 21-foot skiff that ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau. Michael Love, a software developer from New York City, was a passenger aboard the cruise ship and described the event on social media.  What got his […]
text:
The UnCruise ship Wilderness Legacy is seen in an undated file photo provided by UnCruise. (Handout photo)A small cruise ship operating in Southeast Alaska made an unexpected detour on Monday night to help a 21-foot skiff that ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau.
Michael Love, a software developer from New York City, was a passenger aboard the cruise ship and described the event on social media. 
What got his attention the most wasn’t the rescue itself — it was when the captain announced that the yacht of billionaire Facebook owner Mark Zuckerberg was closer and hadn’t answered the radio call for help.
“There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this,” he said in a post on the social media network Bluesky.
Vessel tracking services in the area back up that account — they show the $300 million, 387-foot yacht Launchpad slowing to a halt outside Farragut Bay as the UnCruise Adventures ship Wilderness Legacy steams around and past the Launchpad, stops at the apparent site of the skiff, then tows it into sheltered Farragut Bay.
Through a Bluesky message, Love said it was nice to be on a boat that was engaging with its surroundings in a positive way.
“Frankly, if I was Mark Zuckerberg I would be absolutely ecstatic at a chance to do something helpful for someone in need and maybe get some good PR out of it,” he said.
Social media accounts responding to Love’s account accused the yacht’s crew of violating international agreements that mandate aid from the nearest ship to one in distress.
According to the U.S. Coast Guard and the Marine Exchange of Alaska, which monitors ship traffic in Alaska, there was no distress call — just a general request for assistance.
Coast Guard Public Affairs Specialist Shannon Shepard said by email that the Coast Guard heard the call for help just after 9:30 p.m. Monday night.
“At approximately 9:56 p.m., the Coast Guard determined they were not in distress and issued a marine assistance request broadcast on their behalf,” she said. 
John Hollingsworth is the chief operations officer of the Marine Exchange, which is based in Juneau and repeated the broadcast. 
“We did assist the Coast Guard with callouts on our radio and (were) able to hail the Wilderness Legacy who ended up rendering assistance,” he said.
“From my experience, I know that situations like this contain myriad details for the vessels involved, so the AIS (tracking) snippet you obtained only reveals one of those details,” he said by email. “I do know that Wilderness Legacy is an UnCruise vessel and is very familiar with Alaska waters, so that may have contributed to them rendering assistance quickly.”
No information was available Friday about who may have been aboard the Launchpad on Monday evening. The Launchpad has been in Southeast Alaska for much of the summer. 
The Wilderness Legacy’s detour is the second incidence of aid rendered by a small cruise ship in Southeast Alaska within two weeks. On July 30, the National Geographic Quest assisted a family who had to swim to shore in Glacier Bay National Park after a humpback whale sank their sailboat.
Dan Blanchard, who owns UnCruise, said he wasn’t initially aware of the Wilderness Legacy’s detour because “this kind of aid is such a common thing that it does not always rise to my attention.”
Sarah Scoltock, a spokeswoman for UnCruise, said the Wilderness Legacy was able to refuel the skiff after towing it into a sheltered area.
“The next day the (Wilderness Legacy’s) captain, Sean Manske, contacted them and received word they made it safely to Petersburg,” she said by email.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Trump administration eyes coal reserves under federal lands in Alabama, western states
description: This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here. More than 356 billion tons of coal resources lie beneath federally owned land in the contiguous United States, according to a government report, whose new and comprehensive fi[...]
text:
Trucks operate at a coal mine in Lost Creek, Ky. (Diane Desobeau/AFP via Getty Images)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
More than 356 billion tons of coal resources lie beneath federally owned land in the contiguous United States, according to a government report, whose new and comprehensive findings could escalate mining in those areas, most of them in the West.
The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) issued the report, which estimated an additional 4.2 billion tons of coal reserves are already within a mining area and could be profitably extracted in the lower 48 states.
Alaska has at least 140 billion tons of available coal and could contain as much as 5.5 trillion tons, the report said. There are currently 34 active coal mines on federal lands.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“American Energy Dominance is more important than ever, and so is beautiful clean coal’s role in the production of electricity needed to fuel our future prosperity,” Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said in a press release. “Thanks to the USGS’s rigorous and independent assessment, we’re better equipped to manage America’s vast public lands responsibly while supporting energy security and economic opportunity.” The press release estimated that the coal reserves under federal lands “would be enough coal to supply all the nation’s needs for at least 600 years at the current rate of consumption.”
The environmental consequences of coal mining have been well-documented over many decades. Across the country, mining practices have polluted waterways with heavy metals and changed how water flows. Coal mining and abandoned mines have also caused subsidence, sinkholes and underground fires. A 2021 report from the nonprofit Appalachian Voices estimated the true cost to clean up and remediate the damage caused by coal mining in seven eastern states could be as much as $9.8 billion.
Worldwide, emissions from coal-fired power plants are the main driver of climate change. Global levels of carbon dioxide have dramatically increased, especially since the mid-20th century, and have warmed the planet, raised sea levels and destabilized weather patterns, causing droughts, heat waves and unprecedented flooding.
In 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring several federal agencies to report on coal resources and reserves on lands owned by the U.S. government. The Department of the Interior, which manages federally owned lands, could then use that data to fulfill the other tenets of the executive order to revitalize the declining coal industry: expediting coal leasing, eliminating or weakening environmental regulations and ramping up coal exports.
This year, the Department of Energy allocated a half billion dollars to retrofitting or restarting 10 coal-fired power plants in the U.S. and Puerto Rico. At a National Coal Council meeting this week, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin told members that “many of the items that were on your wish list are now done.” Earlier this year, coal industry leaders presented Trump with a trophy reading “Undisputed Champion of Beautiful Clean Coal.”
The USGS report focuses on the Mountain West and Alabama, the latter of which has three mines whose coal is used for making steel. However, Alaska, where the U.S. government owns 61 percent of the state’s 224 million acres, could be the next frontier for mining on federal lands. Because of Alaska’s remoteness and difficult terrain, its coal supply has been understudied. Only one mine is operating in the state, and it is on private property.
The Sierra Club Wyoming Chapter criticized the Trump administration’s plans to resurrect coal. “We’ve already seen the federal government try and fail to prop up coal mining on public lands, as we’ve seen from its failed bids across Wyoming and Montana,” said Acting Chapter Director for the Sierra Club in Wyoming Kelsey Yarzab Yates in a statement to Inside Climate News. “The reality is that demand for coal is declining, and no amount of political pressure will reverse the direction of the market. Is it really worth continuing to sacrifice our public lands and health to boost coal company profits?”
U.S. coal production has fallen by 56 percent since 2008, its peak year, according to the latest figures from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The EIA cited a number of factors in the industry’s downturn: rising mining costs, increasingly stringent environmental regulations and competition from other sources of electric power generation.
Between 2011 and 2019, utility companies nationwide replaced or converted more than 100 coal-fired power plants with natural gas, the EIA reported.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Parties repeat mistakes as Republicans set elections back and Democrats fail to find a key candidate
description: Maybe politics in South Dakota is cyclical. Or maybe the state’s political parties just keep making the same mistakes. Either way, both parties have taken actions, or inactions, that eerily resemble their past actions. At their state convention in June, Republicans once again chose to jettison their incumbent secretary of state. This time, delegates at […]
text:
Delegates, party officials and guests attend the South Dakota Republican Convention on June 27, 2026, at The Monument events center in Rapid City. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Maybe politics in South Dakota is cyclical. Or maybe the state’s political parties just keep making the same mistakes. Either way, both parties have taken actions, or inactions, that eerily resemble their past actions.
At their state convention in June, Republicans once again chose to jettison their incumbent secretary of state. This time, delegates at the convention were in favor of someone who would like us all to use polling booths as time machines so we can go back to an age when ballots were counted by hand.
At the 2022 convention, Monae Johnson, an election integrity candidate, upset incumbent Steve Barnett. She did this by claiming he was putting a dangerous emphasis on technology by pushing for online voting and online voter registration. This year, Johnson was cast aside as convention delegates selected Heather Baxter, a legislator, as their nominee.
This year Johnson told convention delegates: “I trust the county auditors and I fully support the use of secure, tested ballot tabulators.” Big mistake.
State’s top election official loses nomination to challenger who supports hand-counting

Baxter’s candidacy was based on a platform that calls for hand-counting ballots. She got 59% of the vote in the convention hall. Maybe she churns her own butter, too, and just likes to do things the old-fashioned way. Whatever the reason, she’s promising to take South Dakota elections back in time for no good reason.
When she was running for office the first time, Johnson would never give a straight answer about whether Joe Biden won the presidency in 2020. However, she’s right about the reliability of tabulating machines. They work fine and they’re more accurate than hand counting.
Republicans may be back in the same position in four years after Baxter finds out what Johnson already knows: there’s a difference between being an agitator for change and an elected official. Johnson’s original backers are upset that she didn’t do more to instill integrity in South Dakota elections. The lesson here is that our elections already have plenty of integrity and they certainly don’t need to be slowed down to the pace of hand counting.
Democrats made some news at their convention, too. Only it’s not who they nominated but who they didn’t nominate. It seems that the always candidate-starved Democratic Party won’t be running a candidate for attorney general. Again. They’re leaving a blank spot on the ballot next to the words attorney general for the second election in a row and for the fifth time in the last eight elections.
The Republican candidate will be Lance Russell, a former legislator and the state’s attorney for Fall River and Oglala Lakota counties. It took two ballots for Russell to defeat two other candidates seeking the nomination for attorney general.
Somehow Republicans could come up with three people who wanted to be attorney general. For Democrats, the cupboard was bare, even though there’s no easier way to get on the general election ballot than running as a Democrat. Maybe there are no Democratic lawyers in the state with experience in law enforcement or as prosecutors. But a lack of experience didn’t keep Republicans from nominating Jason Ravnsborg eight years ago.
Maybe there aren’t any Democratic lawyers willing to take one for the team. It would seem to be worth the effort, though, as being in the office boosted Bill Janklow to the governor’s office and will serve as a launching pad for Marty Jackley’s likely election to the U.S. House of Representatives.


Let us know what you think...


 

This is supposed to be a good year for Democrats in November. Some people are predicting a blue wave. In South Dakota, it’s more likely to be a blue trickle.
Yet, it’s hard to understand why there isn’t a Democratic candidate for attorney general. It’s true that the candidate would be running against odds that heavily favor the Republican candidate. But the payoff could be huge in the event of an upset.
A Democratic attorney general in heavily red South Dakota would stand out nationally. If the presidential pendulum swings back to Democrats in two years, a Democratic attorney general from South Dakota could be in line for a place on the federal bench or an appointment as U.S. attorney. Maybe Democratic lawyers in this state don’t dream big enough.
Russell, the Republican candidate, may have all the qualifications to serve as attorney general. Qualified or not, the fact is that he’ll slide into the attorney general’s office not because voters of the state chose him but because he was the most popular candidate at a convention of 700 delegates.
Something needs to change. An office as important as attorney general shouldn’t be left to the whims of a convention full of Luddites who prefer the prospect of hand-counting ballots. Democrats need to fulfill their obligation to find candidates up and down the ballot so that voters have a debate on the issues and a choice at the polls. If something doesn’t change, this cycle of mistakes is bound to continue.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Who was No. 1 in college football 66 years ago? The US Senate chimes in
description: In this photo from the 1960 Sugar Bowl, Jake Gibbs (12) is about to throw a touchdown pass to Cowboy Woodruff for the first touchdown of Ole Miss' 21-0 victory over LSU. Ole Miss claimed a national championship, but so did several other teams.
text:
You could not make what follows up, and I am not. 
Anyone keeping up with all that’s going on in college athletics knows the U.S. Senate is discussing and presumably debating the Protect College Sports Act. The proposed legislation attempts to bring some sanity in the form of regulations on name, image and likeness; the transfer portal; eligibility; and the ever-shifting landscape of college athletics.
Rick Cleveland
Most, if not all, major conferences support the Protect College Sports Act. It’s not perfect, but it’s a start. University presidents and athletic directors clamor for legislation because the NCAA has failed its membership miserably. Still, nothing as yet has been resolved.
Ah, but the Senate did act on something Thursday, and you won’t believe what it was – or maybe, considering all the ways our legislators have failed us, you will. The Senate adopted by unanimous consent Senate Resolution 833, recognizing Missouri as one of the teams with a claim to the 1960 college football national championship. I am laughing through tears as I type.
If you can’t fix what’s wrong today, do something about something that happened 66 years ago, I guess. 
You should know four other universities, including Ole Miss, already claim a version of the 1960 national title. Ole Miss finished 10-0-1 that year, beating Rice in the Sugar Bowl. The only blemish was a 6-6 tie with LSU. Those Rebels were voted No. 1 by the Football Writers Association of America, which was a pretty big deal back then.
Missouri finished the 1960 season with a 10-1 record, defeating Navy in the Orange Bowl. But Missouri was thrashed by Kansas 23-7 at Missouri in a late-season game. It was later determined that Kansas used an ineligible player in the game, therefore Missouri claims victory by forfeit. Never mind that the Tigers didn’t achieve a first down until late in the third quarter of the game.
Other claims to the 1960 title:

Minnesota, which finished 8-2, and still was recognized as national champion by both wire service polls, The Associated Press and United Press International.
Iowa, which finished 8-1, losing only to Minnesota, and was recognized as No. 1 by Litkenhous Ratings.
Washington, which finished 10-1 and defeated Minnesota in the Rose Bowl, was deemed the national champion by the Helms Athletic Foundation. The Huskies’ only loss was by one point to Navy.

As you can see, none of the teams have a clear claim to the national championship, but Missouri was the only one the five that suffered a one-sided defeat – at home, no less. That didn’t deter current Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt, a Republican, who introduced and championed the resolution.
“More than six decades later, the 1960 Tigers embody the character of Missouri,” Schmitt said. “We are a people who work. We are a people who endure. We are people who keep our promises. The men of that team brought home a Big Eight Championship and the Orange Bowl championship game in a perfect season.”
Spoken like a true politician. No doubt, it will earn Schmitt some brownie points in the Show-Me State. Only, it wasn’t a perfect season, not even close. Kansas, which lost twice to other teams and by two touchdowns to Iowa, crushed Missouri at Missouri.
What the Senate achieved was adding one more team to the four that already claimed a disputed national championship. Again, Ole Miss claims two more of those. The 1959 Rebels finished 10-1 and avenged their only defeat that season, trouncing LSU 21-0 in the Sugar Bowl. The Rebels, for my money the best college football team in Mississippi history, out-scored opponents 329-21. Nevertheless, Syracuse (11-0 and winner over Texas in the Cotton Bowl) was No. 1 in both wire service polls and is widely considered the 1959 national champion. Perhaps Ole Miss was better, but we will never know. Syracuse did have a player, perhaps the greatest ever, named Jim Brown.
The 1962 Rebels, who finished 10-0 and beat Arkansas in the Sugar Bowl, were ranked No. 1 by Litkenhous Ratings. But Rose Bowl champion Southern Cal finished 11-0 and was ranked No. 1 in both major (AP and UPI) polls.
College football is all screwed up these days. Teams now travel across three time zones to play conference games. Players transfer willy-nilly from school to school, based on how many hundreds of thousands of dollars (sometimes millions) the next school will pay. So now seems a good time to remind every one that college football at least does one thing right in 2026.
That is, the national championship is now decided on the field – not by wire service polls, not by various fly-by-night rating services and certainly not by the U.S. Senate.

name: VTDigger
title: Into the belly of the whale: Summer readers embark on a unique voyage
description:
The life-sized inflatable whale model allows children to see inside the anatomy and life of a humpback named Nile, and is part of a summer reading partnership between the McCullough Library and the Bennington Free Library.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Into the belly of the whale: Summer readers embark on a unique voyage.
text:
Nile the inflatable life-sized Humpback Whale is temporarily at the McCullough Library in North Bennington. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Bennington Banner

This story by Danielle M. Crosier was first published in the Bennington Banner on Aug. 6, 2026.
NORTH BENNINGTON — On Wednesday, local kids didn’t just learn about whales, they went inside one.
The Park McCullough Carriage Barn was temporarily transformed into the belly of the sea when the Whalemobile rolled into town, inflating a life-sized model of Nile, a 39‑year‑old humpback whale who spends her summers perusing the waters off of Cape Cod.
The program was part of the McCullough Library’s summer reading lineup, which for the first time has been combined with the Bennington Free Library’s summer reading program into a single, shared and collaborative effort.
“It’s been great to partner with Bennington Free Library,” said Martha Bradford, youth services librarian at McCullough Library. “We’ve had a very successful program. I think we’re up to 220 readers that have registered, and we are about to cross the 200,000 minutes of reading for our readers. So, they’re doing a great job.”
Readers from both libraries will have until Aug. 19 to record and report minutes, said Bradford, adding, “Come on down to either library and get those minutes in.”
Bradford said the combined program is already paying off in enthusiasm and numbers. Last year, she noted, McCullough’s standalone program drew around 165 readers; this summer’s joint effort has nudged that number upward while also pulling in families from beyond the immediate village.
“Well, I definitely have seen new faces,” she said, crediting the collaboration with bringing in “Bennington folks and surrounding areas.”
A whale named Nile

Children and adults inside the life-sized Humpback Whale at McCullough Library in North Bennington. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Bennington Banner

Inside the inflatable whale, educator Cinde McInnes walked kids through the anatomy and life story of Nile, a humpback whale that she has personally observed in 31 of the 33 years she’s been whale watching.
The life-like blow-up model replicates the distinctive black‑and‑white tail pattern that allows researchers to recognize individual humpbacks in much the same way that humans recognize each other by their faces. Nile, for example, was first identified by a Nile River shaped tail marking.
Youngsters who attended learned that Nile is currently 39 years old, and is considered a “young” adult for a species that can live to between 80 and 100 years — and they also learned that young Nile is now on her eighth calf.
McInnes also explained why whales bulk up in New England waters and slim down on their winter migration, how blubber works as both insulation and an energy storage and why whale poop — to the delight of the audience — matters for the planet and matters to researchers. 
By the time she was finished, children could explain baleen versus teeth, blubber versus muscle, and why a 440‑pound blue whale heart is roughly the size of a very large human being — or even two human beings.
Inside of the whale, kids studied baleen, examined sperm whale teeth and passed around some faux samples of sand eels (possibly a humpback’s favorite treat).
Sand eels — they learned — are slender, silver-bodied and pencil-thin, and form massive schools along Cape Cod. They serve as the core foundation of the local marine food web and attract striped bass, bluefish, bluefin tuna  and whales to the shallow flats, shoals and offshore banks during the spring, summer and early fall months.
Ocean health was also stressed and a gasp was heard as they learned that whales are eating plastic pollution that originates from far inland. Another gasp came when they learned that the plants of the ocean are responsible for about 50% of the oxygen that we humans breathe.
Reading, and a job whale done
While the science lesson took place inside of the massive inflatable humpback, Bradford was focused on the bigger picture: connecting that excitement to reading and stewardship.
The Whalemobile visit was the seventh of 10 events in the two library’s summer reading series this year. Bradford stressed the success of the combined programming efforts, and emphasized that families still have time to log summer reading.
Each Whalemobile session hosted roughly 20 people, with four sessions scheduled over the course of the day, and brought in a wide variety of young readers from throughout the area.
The event also reinforced a quieter message: the link between whales, ocean health and everyday choices in a landlocked Vermont village.
McInnes urged kids to think beyond recycling and focus on reducing plastic use — especially single‑use water bottles — and to adopt “whale‑safe habits” like picking up litter and using reusable containers.
Children left with stickers, coloring sheets and brochures about whale watching, along with a few very solid talking points about phytoplankton, food chains and why the ocean is responsible for roughly every other breath we take.
For Bradford, the inflatable whale was more than just a novelty experience. It was a way to make that science — and the act of reading about it — feel immediate and feel applicable.
“It’s been great to partner with Bennington Free Library,” Bradford said, noting again that the collaboration has brought new families through the doors and driven up both registration and minutes read.
With three more events on the schedule and thousands of minutes still to be logged, Bradford is hoping that local youth will continue to be curious and will keep diving into books in the same way that they dove into Nile — feet first, eyes wide and eager to learn what’s inside.
