name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri should dump the use of junk science in its courtrooms
description: Missouri patients deserve confidence that the science presented in our courtrooms is credible, reliable and grounded in evidence. When unreliable expert testimony is allowed to influence juries, the consequences extend far beyond the courtroom. Manufactured claims can scare patients away from proven treatments and make medical innovators think twice about in[...]
text:
(Photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus)Missouri patients deserve confidence that the science presented in our courtrooms is credible, reliable and grounded in evidence.
When unreliable expert testimony is allowed to influence juries, the consequences extend far beyond the courtroom. Manufactured claims can scare patients away from proven treatments and make medical innovators think twice about investing in research and development in Missouri, ultimately limiting access to tomorrow’s lifesaving therapies.
Missouri has worked hard to build a reputation as a great place to live, raise a family and do business. Protecting that reputation requires our legal system to reflect that same commitment. Updating Missouri’s expert testimony standards to align with the most up-to-date federal standard will protect patients, consumers and innovation, and it will keep manufactured science out of our courtrooms.
In 2017, Missouri aligned its expert testimony standard with Federal Rule of Evidence 702, bringing greater consistency with federal courts and helping ensure that expert witnesses rely on reliable scientific methods rather than speculation.
However, Rule 702 was amended in December 2023 to clarify a critical principle: judges — not juries — must determine whether an expert’s opinions are based on reliable methods and have been properly applied before testimony reaches the courtroom. The amendment strengthened the judge’s role as the gatekeeper against unreliable scientific evidence.
Unfortunately, Missouri has yet to update its evidence admissibility standard to reflect the 2023 amendment.
Although state Sen. Jamie Burger introduced legislation during this year’s legislative session, it did not pass before the Missouri General Assembly adjourned.
For too long, litigation-driven science has found its way into high-stakes court cases. Unlike rigorous, peer-reviewed research, these opinions are often developed for lawsuits rather than scientific discovery. Once introduced into the courtroom, unsupported claims often extend beyond the verdict. They can fuel a broader cycle of misinformation, amplified through news coverage, social media and public discussion, creating lasting reputational damage for safe and effective products and treatments.
The consequences are real. Patients may abandon proven medicines, medical devices or other products because of faulty data or misleading claims — not because science has changed but because misinformation can spread faster than facts. When junk science reaches the public, it erodes confidence in our legal system, distorts verdicts and ultimately places patients in a perpetual loop of misinformation about their everyday medicines.
Updating Missouri’s expert evidence standard is not about providing favor to plaintiffs or defendants. It’s about ensuring that courtroom decisions are informed by reliable science rather than speculation. Several states have already aligned their state evidence admissibility standards with the amended Rule 702, recognizing that stronger standards improve the integrity of the judicial process.
Patients, consumers and businesses deserve a legal system where scientific evidence is held to the highest standard and courtroom decisions are based on sound science and not junk science. It’s time to put patients first and align the state’s standard with Rule 702.

name: Maryland Matters
title: My disabled son has civil rights, just like all of us
description: Maryland has a proud history of protecting civil rights of marginalized people — except for disabled people, writes Jeneva Stone, who said state cuts to care for people with complex medical needs denies them the right to stay safe and thrive in the community.
text:
Advocates for people with developmental disabilities called on lawmakers at the special session Monday, Aug. 3, to expand the scope of the special session to include solutions to a $126 million budget cut approved this year. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)My disabled son Rob and I are often in Annapolis to advocate for health care and disability rights. If the weather’s nice, we sit on Lawyer’s Mall in front of the State House and reflect on the legacy of Thurgood Marshall, whose statue stands there. Maryland has a proud history of protecting the civil rights of marginalized people — except, it seems, for disabled people.
In 2019, when Rob began his advocacy journey at age 21, we joined Little Lobbyists, a family-led advocacy group committed to the rights of children with complex medical needs and disabilities. Through Little Lobbyists, which turns nine this year, we learned about disability civil rights: Rob and others have the right to use their Medicaid funding to allow them to live in their community, not a nursing home. But because Rob has complex medical needs, his transition from high school to adulthood was packed with roadblocks by state agencies.
This winter, the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) pressured the General Assembly to make dramatic cuts to disability services that keep people like my son in their homes and communities, using arguments Fox News Baltimore questioned in recent reporting.
Legislators were told that Medicaid home services to all disabled people were in jeopardy unless they slashed funding to self-directed services, which allow disabled people to hire their own staff (including family members) and make their own choices about where they live and how they want to be part of their community. Self-direction is Maryland’s only Medicaid home services option for people like Rob.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Despite criticism, the Department of Health is taking away critical support from disabled people with complex medical conditions. These include breaks for family caregivers, extra staff for safety considerations, and funding for classes that keep them included in their communities.
In addition, the Department of Health is demanding that family caregivers supply more and more unpaid care, beyond the second-shift levels  already required of us to stay eligible for paid nursing care — when nurses are even available. The state is ignoring legal definitions of “extraordinary care” designed to prevent the abuse of family caregivers in state Medicaid programs. This expectation to provide free labor on behalf of the state will drive families like ours into poverty. In addition to providing that routine unpaid care, my husband and I must drop everything at a moment’s notice to fill care gaps due to the home nursing shortage, which leaves us unable to hold traditional jobs outside the home.
The expert care our families provide — amounting to several full-time jobs — saves taxpayers millions in unnecessary ER visits and hospitalizations. We often know more about our child’s medical care than the best home nurse. We are the families who manage medical care for children and adults with tracheostomies, ventilators, tube-feedings, wheelchairs, and other medical interventions.
Our loved ones typically need care from someone who is awake at all times, including overnight. We often go without sleep due to the home nursing crisis. The nursing situation in facilities where the state wants to force Rob to live isn’t any better; in fact, it is far more dangerous.
Now, changes to the programs Rob and people like him count on are limiting paid family caregiving and other resources we critically need. At the same time, the Department of Health is also denying access to respite care, cruelly expecting family members to act as caregivers indefinitely with no one to help them. Existing department policy on home nursing even strips family caregivers of nurses on holiday weekends.
Rob has lived safely and successfully in his community for 29 years. But MDH staff are now questioning whether Rob “can be safe” at home when their own policies are stripping away the resources that would keep him safe.
Maryland has chosen to undermine the civil rights of disabled people with the most complex needs, defunding the programs they need to stay safe, thrive, and beloved in their communities. Caregiving is a collective responsibility and joy, and we cannot do it alone. The state’s decision to turn its back on us has our families facing horrifying choices, including institutionalizing our children because state policy keeps us exhausted and unable to pay our bills.
No parent should ever be asked to choose between themselves and their child.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Trump’s slapdash Reflecting Pool renovations stand in stark contrast to ingenuity of its creation
description: In the latest twist in one of the strangest ongoing scandals in Washington, D.C., U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro announced that the government would be dropping charges against the four people accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the 2,000-foot long water basin that connects the Lincoln Memorial to the Washin[...]
text:
Work on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., began in 1919. (Bettmann/Getty Images)In the latest twist in one of the strangest ongoing scandals in Washington, D.C., U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro announced that the government would be dropping charges against the four people accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the 2,000-foot long water basin that connects the Lincoln Memorial to the Washington Monument. Pirro said faulty construction — not vandalism, as President Donald Trump had claimed — caused the pool’s liner to peel off in June 2026.
As I’ve followed this bizarre saga, I’ve found myself reflecting on the history of the pool itself. It was built in the 1920s, when Washington was transformed by ambitious construction projects, even as the nation grappled with political division, racial conflict and clashes between religion and secularism.
To me, everything about the pool’s early history — the debates over its placement, the innovative engineering techniques used during its construction, and its proponents’ longing for something visually and metaphorically unifying — stands in stark contrast to the slapdash renovations, blame games and abuses of power playing out today.
 
Coming to a consensus
In 1901, the U.S. Senate formed the McMillan Commission, a group of architects, landscape designers and artists, to develop a parks system for the nation’s capital.
The commission’s 1902 report also recommended a location for the future Lincoln Memorial. Although proposals for a memorial had emerged shortly after Lincoln’s assassination in 1865, decades of political disagreement over its design, location and purpose had delayed construction.
The report proposed situating it at the western end of the Mall, near the Potomac River. Inspired by the waterways of Versailles and the reflecting basins of the Taj Mahal, the commission envisioned a reflecting pool linking the future memorial to the Washington Monument. In this way, these two magnificent monuments could be reflected in a huge mirror of water, framed by manicured, green grass.
Over the ensuing decade, the plans continued to elicit debate and controversy, pitting supporters of the commission’s vision against members of Congress, railroad interests and real estate developers.
The American Institute of Architects and American Federation of Arts backed the report, arguing that isolation from the city’s bustle created a dignified space for reflection. They also called attention to the qualifications of the artists on the commission, and to the economic viability of the site: The land was owned by the federal government, so the project’s funds could go toward the memorial itself rather than acquiring land.
But some House leaders insisted that the memorial be built on Capitol Hill, two miles to the east, since Lincoln had preserved the Union and worked closely with Congress during the Civil War.
Railroad interests wanted the memorial near the soon-to-be-completed Union Station, a proposal backed by some real estate developers. Even the National Highways Association joined the fray, arguing that the US$2 million Congress had authorized for the memorial in 1911 would be better spent on a memorial highway named for Lincoln linking Washington and Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.
The Union Station plan drew ridicule in the Washington press and failed to gain congressional support. When the proposal to replace the memorial with a highway came before Congress in 1912, the House of Representatives rejected the idea, too — despite some fears that moneyed interests would win out — and moved ahead with plans for a traditional monument.
Around the same period, plans were also put forward for Lee Highway. Named for Confederate General Robert E. Lee, the road reflected the era’s ongoing debates over how Americans memorialized the Civil War.
 
A pool on a swamp
With the riverside location for the monument settled, construction of the Lincoln Memorial began in 1914. The excavation of the basin for the reflecting pool started in 1920, two years before the memorial itself was completed.
Author J.W. Duffield, writing in 1922, compared the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the one in front of the Taj Mahal, that “exhalation of a dream.”
“It is in accord with the eternal fitness of things,” he continued, “that these memorials to America’s two greatest Presidents — Washington, under whom the nation came into being; Lincoln, by whose labors it was preserved and by whose blood it was hallowed — should stand in close proximity, as shrines to which posterity may pay pilgrimage and tribute.”
Yet there were several obstacles involved in the construction of the pool — namely, the area was swampland, so the settling of the ground and the drainage presented practical construction challenges.
Engineer Charles A. Peters Jr. worked on the pool. In a 1923 article for the journal The Military Engineer, he described some of the creative solutions.
To deal with the settling, Peters and his team developed flexible flooring lined with an impervious three-ply fabric. The drainage system had to empty the pool in less than 24 hours without leaving puddles. So it was designed with a sloped basin and drainage system that allowed crews to empty the pool for maintenance while preventing water from collecting in low spots.
An additional consideration was cold weather. Engineers had to account for the stresses of freeze-thaw cycles, which can gradually damage waterproofing layers, crack concrete and masonry, and create leaks.
The waterproofing worked: It held up for decades, and in its early years, members of the public could be seen ice skating on the frozen reflecting pool.
 
A convoy with U.S. President Donald Trump drives across the floor of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., on May 7, 2026. (Photo by Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images)
From Lincoln to Trump
On May 30, 1922, 50,000 people — including Robert Todd Lincoln, the late president’s only surviving son — gathered on the National Mall for the unveiling of the monument for the man whom some call “America’s secular saint.”
During the ceremony, President Warren Harding declared Lincoln’s accomplishments “so colossal that none will dispute that he was incomparably the greatest of our Presidents” due to “the greatness of his intellect, his honesty of purpose, and his kindness and gentleness.”
The same year that the Lincoln Memorial was inaugurated, the tomb of Tutankhamum was discovered in Egypt, fueling a broader fascination with ancient civilizations, monuments and the ways societies preserved memories of powerful figures. The Egyptian pharaoh Menes appears first among the lawgivers represented in the interior frieze on the South Wall of the U.S. Supreme Court building, completed in 1935. These friezes reflected the aspirations of the nation’s leaders to place America on the continuum of great civilizations.
The deliberative, thoughtful process of remaking the nation’s capital in the early 20th century bears little resemblance to Trump’s insistence on remaking the capital in his image.
After Trump announced his wish to change the color of the pool to what he calls “American flag blue,” the National Park Service awarded a no-bid contract to a politically connected firm, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, to repair leaks and paint the pool. It signed another no-bid contract to install a filtration system with Greenwater Services, a construction company whose owner had donated to Trump.
The rushed renovation that ensued — and the squabbling over whether the peeling liner was the result of vandalism — led to charges against four suspects that were eventually dropped.

The pool debacle came on the heels of other attempts to modify the nation’s capital, from a new White House ballroom to a proposed monumental arch. In October 2025, Trump dismissed all six members of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts in order to circumvent the independent design review board.
The 1920s weren’t devoid of partisanship, graft and scandal. Far from it. But unlike Trump’s top-down approach, the process for building monuments and civic spaces involved Congress, artists, architects, engineers and city planners who debated, offered their expertise and listened to public.
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
Jennifer Tucker is a professor of history at Wesleyan University and the founding director of Wesleyan’s Center for the Study of Guns and Society. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Three Democrats vie to take on Steil in Wisconsin’s 1st CD in Tuesday’s primary
description: The race among Democrats to pick a candidate to run in Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District for 2026 grew to a record crowd. The district stretches from Lake Michigan to South Central Wisconsin,  anchored by Racine, Kenosha, Beloit and Janesville. It has been in Republican hands for 32 years — 20 years represented by Paul Ryan, […]
text:
Three Democrats are running in Tuesday's primary to pick a challenger to run against Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil in Wisconsin's 1st Congressional District.  Pictured are, from left, Steil and Democrats Miguel Aranda, Mitchell Berman and  Lorenzo Santos. (Wisconsin Examiner photo illustration)The race among Democrats to pick a candidate to run in Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District for 2026 grew to a record crowd.
The district stretches from Lake Michigan to South Central Wisconsin,  anchored by Racine, Kenosha, Beloit and Janesville. It has been in Republican hands for 32 years — 20 years represented by Paul Ryan, and since 2018 by U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil, a former Ryan aide and corporate lawyer.
Democrats have gone in virtually every direction in the last three decades in their efforts to recapture the seat — once reliably blue from the 1970s until 1994. For most of the races against Ryan, Democrats only rarely received more than one-third of the vote. Since Steil took over, the margins have been narrower, but still solidly in favor of the GOP.
Forecasts from national oddsmakers have so far kept it in the GOP column in 2026. The Cook Political Report rates the seat as “Likely Republican” — but hasn’t updated that assessment since February 2025.
Steil has amassed a sizable financial advantage, with nearly $5.5 million raised since January 2025 through the middle of July, the most recent Federal Election Commission data show.
Messages tie Steil to Trump
Despite those odds, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee listed Wisconsin’s 1st CD along with the 3rd CD among the group’s first targets to pick up this year.
Even before that announcement, the current cycle drew a record number of prospective Democratic candidates, with nine people over the last year and a half announcing their intention to run.
Three dropped out before the district’s Democratic convention in April, and two more failed to file nomination papers in June. That left four who filed enough signatures to make it to the ballot for the primary on Tuesday.
Since then, one — Milwaukee alder Peter Burgelis — has dropped out, although he remains on the ballot. Burgelis lives outside the district and was the last to enter, basing his candidacy on the premise that he would be able to raise more money than any of the others in the contest.
He abandoned his campaign after his fundraising report filed July 15 showed him far behind Mitchell Berman, the top fundraiser, and he urged his other 1st CD rivals to join him in backing Berman.
The three remaining Democrats — Berman, Miguel Aranda and Lorenzo Santos — have similar messages. All have focused on President Donald Trump, whose plummeting popularity has increased hopes that Democrats can regain a majority in the U.S. House in November.
They cite affordability, rising costs for healthcare, tariffs that have driven up consumer costs and dampened farm exports, and the attacks on immigrants and immigration enforcement that have led to confrontations and civilian deaths across the country.
All three portray Steil as out of touch with district residents despite his past success at the ballot box, and as a lawmaker who has enabled Trump’s agenda rather than standing up to him. Each argues that they can motivate broad support to score an upset in November.
At the same time, each has a distinctive biography and set of emphases in their campaigns.
Working class message
Of the Democrats on the ballot, Mitchell Berman, a rural Racine County nurse, has been in the race the longest. Berman declared his candidacy a year ago, on Aug. 12, 2025, and since then has garnered a number of endorsements, including from the United Auto Workers, which has a long heritage in the district. Democrats in the state Legislature from Kenosha, Milwaukee, Beloit and Janesville have also signed on to his campaign.
Of the Democrats, he has been the most successful fundraiser, with more than $700,000 in receipts as of this week, according to the FEC. The resources have enabled his campaign to staff up, printing yard signs and flyers and producing merch.
Berman centers his campaign argument on his working class identity, growing up on a Wisconsin dairy farm and the first person in his family to gain a college degree.
“A lot of the issues that we’re facing today are not Republican issues, they’re not Democratic issues. They are working class and middle class issues,” Berman told voters at a UAW hall in Janesville this week.
“We’re up against people who have no idea what it’s like for you and me to struggle through this economy that they’ve created while they’re sitting in Washington and enriching themselves,” he said.
Berman points to having to still pull emergency room shifts that have forced him to skip some joint candidate forums, such as one held in Kenosha in July.
“I’m a working class candidate, like in the true meaning of working class candidate — I’ve still got to work to pay the bills,” Berman said in an interview.
Healthcare is one of Berman’s chief talking points. Until he entered the race, he worked for the Veterans Administration health system, leaving only because the Hatch Act bars federal employees from political involvement. He says he decided to run because of Trump administration cuts to the VA during the DOGE  operation led by Elon Musk in the first half of 2025.
His immediate healthcare priorities would be to restore enhanced subsidies for  insurance policies purchased through the ACA marketplace and to reverse cuts to Medicaid that were part of the massive 2025 tax-cut and spending law. He said he also wants to see an ACA public option — a federal insurance plan that people could purchase through the marketplace.
Emergency services and military experience
Lorenzo Santos, the former Racine County emergency services manager, is the most recent of the three to have entered the primary race. An East Coast native, Santos served in the U.S. Navy, then took a job as an industrial sales manager. His territory included Wisconsin, and he settled in the state, then moved into the emergency services role after getting a degree in Homeland Security. He gave up the Racine County job in April after entering the congressional primary.
Santos previously ran in the 1st District primary in 2024, but left the field along with other Democratic hopefuls after former state Department of Revenue Secretary Peter Barca entered the race.
Barca was the last Democrat to hold the 1st District seat, losing it to a Republican after one term in the 1994 election that flipped the U.S. House from a Democratic majority to a Republican one.
Santos bases his pitch on his experience in both private and public sector positions as well as his military service.
“I understand the national implications. I understand the international implications. I understand the economic implications of what this administration is doing right now,” Santos told the audience during the July 17 Kenosha forum, organized by the activist group Hands Off Kenosha. In his closing, he said, “I’m ready to take the fight.”
Santos has taken positions that have a slightly harder edge than some of his rivals — Medicare for All to address healthcare, vociferously condemning the U.S. war with Iran and categorically rejecting data center development projects.
“I’ve heard overwhelmingly that our communities are opposed to them and not enough of our elected officials are standing with them on this issue,” Santos said in an interview.
Santos contrasted Berman’s healthcare positions with his own support for Medicare for All — which he called “the first bill that I think we should be putting into legislation” at the Kenosha forum.
Berman responds that it will be faster to implement the policies he has focused on such as the public option and restoring ACA subsidies and reversing Medicaid cuts.
“Being an emergency room nurse, I’m very pragmatic,” Berman said in an interview. “When someone comes into the hospital emergency room and they’re hemorrhaging, the first thing that we need to do is stop the hemorrhaging. And I think that right now is ensuring that people can afford to go to the doctor.”
On data centers, Berman told a questioner at the Janesville UAW hall that he wants to see regulatory guardrails, assurances that “they’re paying their own way” rather than saddling the public with costs for the energy they use, and that they don’t contribute to air or water pollution. “And also, I think communities ought to have a say on whether they come in or not,” he said.
University administrator and school board member
Miguel Aranda, a University of Wisconsin-Whitewater administrator, the third candidate, is frank about the shoestring campaign he’s running.
“There’s no consultants involved at this point,” he said at the Kenosha forum. “It’s almost a one- or two-man team doing all of this.”
 Aranda, who entered the race a few weeks after Berman, was born in the U.S. to parents who emigrated from Mexico.
He points out that he’s the only candidate in the primary who speaks fluent Spanish. That could give him an advantage, he has said, with the district’s growing Hispanic population.
“One of many reasons I put my name in was to really start cracking into that populace that usually doesn’t vote for primaries,” Aranda said in an interview.
A Whitewater school board member, Aranda has emphasized education as well as immigration reform in his campaign.
He is circumspect on some issues. Asked during the Kenosha forum how he would propose to fix the country’s healthcare problems, Aranda replied, “I don’t want to give people the false promise that that’s in the past if I were to win.”
Aranda said he supports Medicare for All, but also sees the pathway there as a complicated one that would include addressing public education funding and immigration reform.
Like Berman, Aranda is running while also holding down another job — which has made the effort tiring, he admitted in an interview.
“I tell people I’m going to go all the way to August, and after that we’ll see what happens,” Aranda told the Kenosha audience. “But you know, if I can’t fly, I’m gonna keep running. If I can’t run, I’m gonna keep walking, and if I can’t walk, I’m gonna keep crawling, and that’s what I want all of you to do.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska state elections attorney says it’s OK for candidates to temporarily conceal finances
description: An attorney defending the Alaska Division of Elections against a lawsuit argued in state court Friday that candidates for state office are not obliged to disclose their finances when they file for office. If that argument is upheld in court, it would upend existing practices and could end voters’ ability to examine political candidates’ personal […]
text:
(Photo by Krisanapong Detraphiphat/Getty Images)An attorney defending the Alaska Division of Elections against a lawsuit argued in state court Friday that candidates for state office are not obliged to disclose their finances when they file for office.
If that argument is upheld in court, it would upend existing practices and could end voters’ ability to examine political candidates’ personal finances in the early stages of a primary election.
The lawsuit in court on Friday was filed by the Alaska Democratic Party, which is challenging the eligibility of Jose Roel Tagle to run for Alaska House District 22. Tagle, a Republican, is the only challenger to incumbent Rep. Ted Eischeid, D-Anchorage.
The Alaska Democratic Party challenged Tagle’s eligibility after he filed a completely blank Public Officer Disclosure Form alongside his candidacy application. State law requires candidates to use that form to list all income — including Permanent Fund dividends — that a candidate and their immediate family received during the previous year.
The Division of Elections frequently rejects candidates who file no form at all.     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Despite Tagle’s blank form, the Division of Elections accepted his candidacy and rejected the Democratic Party’s challenge, causing the party to file suit. 
In front of Anchorage Superior Court Judge Josie Garton, Alaska Department of Law attorney Griffin Deitz said that filing a blank form is acceptable because the relevant law gives candidates 30 days to make corrections.
“A candidate could comply — they could submit a financial disclosure, as Mr. Tagle did here, that was blank, and then if there are financial interests to be reported, could report those at a later date,” Deitz said.
This year, Alaska’s candidate filing deadline was June 1 and election day is Aug. 18. If a 30-day delay becomes common, almost half the primary campaign season could elapse before voters are informed about candidates’ personal wealth.
Garton, from the bench, asked: “Why wouldn’t every candidate file a blank form?”
Deitz appeared to briefly struggle for an answer.
“In this case — well — I couldn’t begin to guess why candidates would or wouldn’t do so,” he said. “But they have that 30 days. So the presumption that the (Division of Elections) would make in this case, Your Honor, is that the Legislature intended to provide this grace period so that people could file at the very last minute and then bring that financial disclosure into compliance before the election.”
Attorney River Sterne, representing the Alaska Democratic Party, said that position is unacceptable.
“An important thing here is that filing a totally blank POFD is the same as not filing a POFD at all,” he said, arguing that the Division of Elections should have excluded Tagle from the primary election ballot.
In written arguments before Friday, and again in court, Deitz argued that the Alaska Public Offices Commission — not the Division of Elections — is the agency that should determine whether a POFD is properly filed.
The Division of Elections does not have investigation powers, he said, and is thus unable to judge. Tagle may have no income to report, Deitz suggested.
Sterne countered that other public records clearly list Tagle as the officer of a privately held company, and there is no “de minimis” exemption for reporting shares of a privately held company if the profits are vanishingly small or nonexistent. Given that, he said, the Division of Elections could easily conclude that Tagle’s filing was incorrect.
Neither Tagle nor the Alaska Republican Party filed legal briefs in support of Tagle’s candidacy ahead of Friday’s oral argument. The party’s chair, Carmela Warfield, did not answer a phone call or email asking why not. 
Regardless of how Garton rules on the lawsuit, Tagle’s candidacy appears unlikely to proceed. As of Friday, Tagle had not amended his financial disclosure form, meaning that even under the Division of Elections’ interpretation of the law, he is beyond the 30-day grace period.

title: Idaho governor, Forest Service chief say significant wildfires are stretching resources thin
description: Idaho Gov. Brad Little and U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz said Friday that firefighting resources are stretched thin as significant wildfires burn across Washington, Oregon, Idaho and much of the Western United States.  As a result, both officials called on the public to redouble its efforts to prevent wildfires as hot, dry weather continues […]
text:
Crew 18 conducts mop-up operations on the Autumn Lane Fire, extinguishing remaining hot spots and securing the fire's edge to prevent rekindling along the south eastern flank of the fire near the Little Spokane River. Mop-up is a critical phase of wildfire suppression that helps ensure the fire remains contained and reduces the risk of additional spread. (Photo courtesy of California Interagency Incident Management Team 7 and the Washington Department of Natural Resources/InciWeb)Idaho Gov. Brad Little and U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz said Friday that firefighting resources are stretched thin as significant wildfires burn across Washington, Oregon, Idaho and much of the Western United States. 
USDA Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz meets with employees of the Kisatchie National Forest in Louisiana on April 2, 2025. (Photo by Preston Keres/USDA)
As a result, both officials called on the public to redouble its efforts to prevent wildfires as hot, dry weather continues to create conditions that add to the threat.
“We have to recognize the reality of the conditions: we have an extremely dangerous fire season across the West,” Little said during Friday’s press conference, which was streamed live by the Idaho Department of Lands. “Hot temperatures, dry fuels, low humidity and changing winds are creating conditions where wildfires can spread rapidly and unpredictably. These conditions are placing tremendous demands on the firefighters and the firefighting resources throughout the region, and for that matter, throughout the country… Every hose, every tool, every piece of protective equipment for every firefighter matters when these resources are stretched across multiple incidents.”
So far this year, Schultz said there have been more than 1,000 fires in Washington and more than 600 in Idaho. Across the country, the number of fires and number of acres burned is above the 10-year average. 
“This fire season has been significantly more challenging than some more recent fire seasons,” Schultz said. 
“(The) top priority for the department right now is keeping communities safe and firefighters safe,” Schultz said, adding that four wildland firefighters have already died in the line of duty this year. 
Across the country there were 95 large, uncontained fires burning as of Friday, Idaho Department of Lands Fire Management Bureau Chief Josh Harvey said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 State and federal officials provide update on Spokane fires in Washington

Little and Schultz conducted their press conference Friday afternoon at the Coeur d’Alene Interagency Fire Cache located a short distance from where the nearby Spokane Area Fires have destroyed hundreds of homes and displaced thousands of Washington residents. 
Wildfire veterans fear federal tactics, extreme fires could put crews at risk

The Spokane Area Fires, which include the Old Trails Fire, Autumn Lane Fire and Fairview Fire, started Aug. 1 and have damaged or destroyed an estimated 846 structures, according to the California Interagency Incident Management Team 7 and the Washington Department of Natural Resources daily fire briefing issued Friday morning. 
Officials suspect the Old Trails Fire was started by arson. 
“I want to express our incredible thoughts and sympathy for the people of the Spokane area – the families, the businesses, everyone that’s been dislocated – it’s just heartbreaking what’s taking place over there,” Little said. “Wildfires do not recognize municipal lines, state lines, and so that’s why we’re all in the same camp.”
 Idaho sends resources to help suppress Spokane-area fires

Idaho state officials said the state has sent two strike teams of engines to North Idaho, as well as a team of Idaho Department of Lands engines to support wildfire efforts in Spokane.
Little spoke about the importance of Idaho helping its neighbors in Spokane and called on the public to heighten its fire prevention efforts because worsening fire conditions are expected over the coming weeks. 
Wildfire smoke is now the primary pollutant affecting pregnancy, study shows

“Preventing the next wildfire may be the single greatest way people can help support the firefighters who are already working nonstop,” Little said. “Human-caused wildfires are preventable. If there are fire restrictions in your area, follow them. Avoid activities that create sparks. Make sure your campfires are completely extinguished. Be careful with trailers, dragging chains, outdoor equipment, fireworks – I shouldn’t need to say that, but I will – and anything else that would ignite dry grass or brush. 
“One careless moment can change lives forever,” Little added. “Protecting our communities begins with personal responsibility.”
As of Friday, most of Idaho is under fire restrictions, which prohibits campfires outside of approved U.S. Forest Service metal fire rings, including prohibiting campfires at dispersed and undeveloped campsites 
 Crews from 20 states, including Idaho, helping fight Spokane wildfires

As of Thursday, more than 1,500 personnel from 20 states and 100 different jurisdictions were helping in the effort to fight the Spokane Area Fires, officials said. 
As of Friday morning, the Spokane Area Fires had burned an estimated 10,363 acres in Spokane and Stevens counties in Washington, with containment estimated at 23% for the OId Trails Fire. 
Alexandra Duggan of The Spokesman-Review newspaper reported Thursday that local police arrested 37-year-old Aaron Farinacci on suspicion of first degree arson, and that Farinacci confessed to police detectives to having planned and set the Old Trails Fire. 
Fire officials said hot, dry and windy conditions near the Spokane Area Fires will elevate the fire danger throughout the area through Saturday.

title: Idaho lawmakers hear updates on efforts to improve children’s residential care, state 911 system
description: Idaho has taken several steps to increase oversight of facilities where foster children and other youth reside or get treatment. The actions stem from recommendations in an oversight report released last year, and the Legislature may consider additional changes next year.  Evaluators with the independent state agency the Office of Performance Evaluations, or[...]
text:
Fidget toys inside a therapy room at an Idaho youth residential facility. Idaho has taken a number of steps to improve oversight of youth residential facilities statewide. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho has taken several steps to increase oversight of facilities where foster children and other youth reside or get treatment. The actions stem from recommendations in an oversight report released last year, and the Legislature may consider additional changes next year. 
Evaluators with the independent state agency the Office of Performance Evaluations, or OPE, on Friday provided legislators with a follow-up report on progress made in response to recommendations from a 2025 report that found significant gaps in oversight of children’s residential facilities. 
The Joint Legislative Oversight Committee, which directs OPE evaluations, also heard about a new report on challenges around hiring and funding career and technical education in public K-12 schools, about progress on updating 911 systems, and an update of changes to address gaps in death investigations. 
The committee also voted to direct OPE to open a new evaluation on hospital billing of Medicaid for services and about whether facilities are engaging in “upcoding,” or charging for more expensive services that may not be needed to get higher reimbursement from Medicaid. 
Once directed to so, OPE looks into specific questions regarding the effectiveness of policies or potential gaps in state oversight or funding. The reports and information about studies underway can be found online at legislature.idaho.gov/ope/reports. 
Below are some main takeaways from OPE presentations on Friday. 
 Lawmakers say they plan to address remaining oversight gaps for children’s residential centers 

Last year, the OPE report found gaps in investigations of abuse, a lack of unannounced visits, and a lack of process for enumerating rights to children at residential facilities. These facilities could be congregate care settings for foster children or treatment facilities. 
Idaho House committee approves oversight bill for youth in residential treatment facilities 

Of the report’s 19 recommendations to improve oversight, 13 have been completed and two are in progress, according to the follow-up report. These include the passage of House Bill 723 this year, which created a youth bill of rights for children at the facilities, required an unannounced facility visit annually, created a new child and staff interview process, and required restraint and seclusion reporting. 
The remaining four recommendations, which would require legislative action, are: 

The report recommends the Legislature extend the licensing authority to include treatment oversight. Licensing requirements for these facilities do not assess whether treatment is being administered, if that treatment is appropriate for the children’ s needs, and whether children are making adequate progress. 
The new report released Friday recommends requiring that the data be reported publicly and to the Legislature. The changes made this year require facilities to only report to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare if it uses restraint methods or seclusion on children in care. 
The report underscores that there is still no process to include perpetrators of abuse at children’s residential facilities on Idaho’s Child Protection Central Registry. The recommendation is to create a process to prevent staff perpetrators from going to other facilities if it’s been substantiated that they abused children at a facility. 
The report also recommended that the Legislature assign an entity to investigate abuse in facilities. Licensing authority is regulatory and meant to be preventative, but if abuse occurs, there isn’t a standardized process to investigate and adjudicate it. 

JLOC Co-Chair Rep. Jordan Redman, R-Coeur d’Alene, said the remaining four recommendations should be a “focus” for committee members during the upcoming legislative session, slated to begin in January. 
“Because I think at the heart of it, it’s protecting kids,” Redman said. “And I think there’s some excellent recommendations. I also want to applaud all the work that’s been done.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho schools face challenges in proving career technical education, or CTE, programs 

Idaho’s schools face funding restrictions and difficulty hiring and keeping teachers as they try to provide career pathways and skills programs, said Casey Petti, a principal evaluator on a study to explore the difficulty in recruiting and retaining CTE educators in Idaho. 
Career technical education, known as CTE, includes classes and training programs to provide practical skills or to allow students to explore career options in different fields. 
There were more than 1,000 CTE programs offered in the 2026 school year, and over 151,000 public school and public charter students enrolled in them, according to the report. However, 40% schools surveyed for the report said they have paused or cancelled a CTE program since 2022, with 76% of them citing a lack of qualified instructors as a reason. 
One of the biggest needs for programs was in health professions and public safety, with 54% of schools citing the area as a need that they aren’t able to meet. Engineering and technology was also highly cited as an industry schools weren’t able to offer CTE programs in. 
Agriculture was the highest cited need for workers, but only 14% of schools said they were unable to meet this need. 
Most of the dedicated funding schools receive for CTE cannot be used toward base teacher salaries, which can be limited, the report found. Some industries, like software engineering or civil engineering, are particularly hard to hire professionals from because CTE educator salaries are far lower than industry average earnings. However, the educator salaries are more competitive in other industries and are slightly above average non-CTE teacher pay, the report found. 
The report provided options to modify funding and credentialing but clarified, “These options are not solutions; they are choices with real tradeoffs.” 
Evaluators said CTE program leaders most wanted CTE funding to be able to go toward base teacher salaries, followed by an adjusted public school funding formula to account for smaller CTE class sizes. The report also included options for loosening some credentialing requirements from industry professionals to become CTE educators. 
The report included as an option targeting pay increases to areas where there’s the largest gap between CTE teachers and the average industry wage.  
 State has made progress to modernize a statewide 911 system 

The independent research office has done two studies related to the effort to modernize emergency communications and shift to a digital network called Next Generation 911. 
With money running out in 2031, watchdog report recommends Idaho Legislature stabilize 911 funding

Idaho watchdog agency says state should consider creating statewide 911 system 

Those reports found limitations with the lack of statewide oversight of the 911 system and contracts for upgrading it. The state created the Idaho Public Safety Communications Commission in response. 
Ben Roeber, head of the Office of Emergency Management, said the office had hired Donald Lane as the program manager to oversee the tradition. It was Lane’s fifth day on the job Friday, but he said he looked forward to creating a strategic plan for the transition. 
The state created a $15 million grant created in July last year, which is funded from a surcharge on phone bills. The grant is now being managed by Lewis County, said Andy Creech, Payette County sheriff and chairman of the Idaho Public Safety Communications Commission. 
Creech said the commission doesn’t have the authority to enter contracts or agreements.
“Naturally you might come and look at the state government and look for that procurement process, but really, it’s Lewis County that did that process,” Creech said. “So it may have the appearance that it wasn’t transparent, but it’s just the way that the laws are written in the way that that grant program works is that the IPSC themselves can’t do this, and the state can’t be an applicant to the grant program. And so the only way for it to occur is for our county to be the grant applicant and to handle the entire process.” 
 Coroners’ association working to create cross-county agreements 

The Legislature in 2025 passed a bill to overhaul the state’s death investigation system in response to an OPE report that found inconsistencies in county coroner investigations statewide. 
In addition to the legislative changes, the Idaho State Association of County Coroners is working to create a memorandum of understanding, or MOU, to allow counties to assist each other with investigations, said Kelli Brassfield, co-chair of the Idaho Criminal Justice Commission’s Coroner System subcommittee. 
“This MOU will help each other in assisting during extraordinary events and/or complex cases,” Brassfield said.

name: WyoFile
title: Church at center of Wind River controversy lodges discrimination complaint against Wyoming food bank
description:
Foundations For Nations contends Food Bank of Wyoming unlawfully cut off church’s food pantry in Riverton over sermon and wants USDA to require food deliveries to resume.
The post Church at center of Wind River controversy lodges discrimination complaint against Wyoming food bank appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Following a viral sermon that has prompted weeks of protest, the Foundations For Nations Church has lodged a federal discrimination complaint. 
Food Bank of Wyoming, the complaint filed Wednesday states, unlawfully cut off a partnership that has for years helped stock the shelves of the church’s food pantry in Riverton on the basis of religious, political and racial discrimination.
Foundations For Nations’ community food pantry had partnered with Food Bank of Wyoming, the Wyoming distribution center for Food Bank of the Rockies, to fill its shelves. Food Bank of the Rockies receives resources from the federal government through multiple U.S. Department of Agriculture programs including the Emergency Food Assistance Program, the Summer Food Service Program, and the Child and Adult Care Food Program. As a government agency, the USDA has specific non-discrimination requirements for programs that work with it and a process in place for filing discrimination complaints.
“What I said at my pulpit, which is freedom of speech, freedom of religion, has nothing to do with the pantry.”Foundations For Nations Pastor Sarah Lucas
While the Foundations For Nations Church is located on the Wind River Indian Reservation, the pantry itself is located within the city of Riverton. According to Foundations For Nations Pastor Sarah Lucas, Food Bank of Wyoming ended its partnership with Foundations For Nations on July 7, two days after her controversial sermon and told her that it was in response to a call claiming her message was discriminatory.
“Food Bank of Wyoming is our partner to supply food, so we pay money monthly and they come and deliver monthly. They shut us down,” Lucas said.
On July 27, Food Bank of Wyoming confirmed to The Ranger that it had placed its partnership with the Foundations For Nations pantry “on hold.”
In a press release sent Friday afternoon, Florida-based Christian litigation and policy nonprofit Liberty Counsel announced that it had filed a discrimination complaint with the USDA “after a Christian church was unlawfully terminated from a food bank partnership over religious statements made during a worship service.”
The filing alleges that Food Bank of Wyoming terminated its agreement with Foundations For Nations on or around July 7, and that Liberty Counsel believes this termination constitutes discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, political beliefs, and religion. According to the document, Liberty Counsel has also filed a complaint with the Wyoming Department of Family Services.
“We have collaborated with the community to ensure immediate availability of food via mobile pantries and continue to engage in conversations around a long-term, community-led resource.”Food Bank of Wyoming
Lucas said that the pantry feeds about 2,000 people a month, the majority of whom are non-Native. “What I said at my pulpit, which is freedom of speech, freedom of religion, has nothing to do with the pantry,” she said. “And now we’re not getting our food supply.”
In its email response to questions posed by The Ranger and WyoToday Media, Food Bank of Wyoming stated that it was continuing to provide food to those in need in the area. “We have collaborated with the community to ensure immediate availability of food via mobile pantries and continue to engage in conversations around a long-term, community-led resource,” it wrote.
Liberty Counsel sent a letter July 29 to Food Bank of Wyoming contending that the decision to end its partnership with Foundations For Nations constituted religious discrimination and demanding that the food bank reinstate food deliveries by Tuesday, according to Liberty Counsel’s press release.
When this did not happen, Liberty Counsel filed its discrimination complaint on Wednesday.
“By taking sides in a religious dispute, Food Bank of the Rockies and Food Bank of Wyoming are withholding food supplies from the people that they purport to serve over the demand of third parties who disagree with a church’s religious beliefs and teachings. The church’s partnership with the food bank should be reinstated immediately to avoid further constitutional and statutory violations and to resume food deliveries to those who depend on Foundations For Nations’ food pantry ministry for food,” Liberty Counsel Founder and Chairman Mat Staver stated.
The sermon
Lucas’ July 5 sermon came on the last day of the Northern Arapaho Sundance ceremony. In her message, the pastor encouraged her congregation to turn away from traditional Native practices and called the tribe’s sacred pipe used for prayer “idol worship.”
“The pipe cannot hear your prayers. It’s just a piece of material, right? And this is a cycle that they’re caught up in, and this is all they’ve ever known,” she said. “And the Lord is saying ‘Tear down the idols, tear down the altars, the idol worship.”
The church has faced weeks of protests and backlash since. The Northern Arapaho Business Council told church leaders they were no longer welcome on the reservation in a meeting on July 10. But Foundations For Nations has continued to offer Sunday worship services and other programs at its Arapahoe building.
The church’s food bank was temporarily closed immediately after the sermon, but reopened the next week and has continued providing food resources to community members, despite its conflict with Food Bank of Wyoming and Food Bank of the Rockies. It is open on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 4-6 p.m.
WyoToday’s Sarah Squires contributed to this report.

title: US Senate leaves town for recess after passing stopgap spending bill, blocking photo ID for voting
text: WASHINGTON —  The U.S. Senate adjourned for its summer recess early Saturday after approving a stopgap spending bill but declining to advance legislation that would require photo ID for voting. In a rare overnight session that began on Friday, senators trudged through a slew of measures, confirmed President Donald Trump’s nomination of Todd Blanche as attorney general and then departed the nation’s capital for the coveted August recess. The chamber is not expected to return to regular session until after Labor Day.The Senate passed, 86-11, a major effort first proposed by the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina that would impose sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, along with the country’s oligarchs and military leaders. A bipartisan education bill — championed by GOP Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Democratic Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado — served as the vehicle for the Russia sanctions package. Collins’ and Bennet’s bill would ensure that “early childhood educators can claim the same federal tax credit for out-of-pocket classroom supply purchases that is currently available to K-12 teachers,” per a press release. Averting a shutdown The Senate also passed a bipartisan measure on a 90-6 vote that would keep the federal government funded through Dec. 11. The House has passed a different version so the two would have to be reconciled.Earlier in the day, senators had advanced the legislation, known as a continuing resolution, toward a final vote on another strongly bipartisan vote of 91-6. Senators did not vote on a proposed blueprint that would unlock the complex budget reconciliation process and allow Republicans to move ahead on their third party-line bill.Attorney general vote The upper chamber also confirmed Blanche, the acting attorney general, to be the next U.S. attorney general. Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana marked the determinative vote amid GOP opposition from Collins and Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska over Blanche’s bid, as well as the absence of Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, who’s recovering from a health issue. The Senate did confirm a batch of nominees earlier Friday, including Cameron Hamilton to serve as the next administrator for the Federal Emergency Management Agency, 51-47.  Voting and photo IDThe Senate failed to advance on a 52-46 vote a bill that would require a photo ID to vote in an election to federal office. Related to the separate SAVE America Act, it was sponsored by Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio. Sixty votes were required to move ahead on the measure, which was opposed by all Democrats voting.Democrats have said in the past such a requirement would make it more difficult for all Americans to vote.Republican Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, a proponent of photo ID and the SAVE America Act who at one point had said he would hold up adjournment to obtain action, vowed afterward to continue pushing for it. “This fight’s not over. We’re just getting started,” he said.Trump is an intense proponent of the SAVE America Act and urged the Senate to stay in town to pass it though Republican leaders have said repeatedly there are not 60 votes to do so. The SAVE America Act would require voters to show proof of citizenship when they register and a photo ID when they vote. Noncitizens are already barred from voting in state, federal and almost all local elections.College sportsThe Senate did not take a procedural vote before leaving town on a sweeping bipartisan bill that would set national standards for college athletes’ compensation.GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas and Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state — the top members of the Senate Commerce panel, which has jurisdiction over the matter — introduced the bill, with GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri and Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware as original co-sponsors. The bill underwent several changes after it was passed by the Commerce panel in June, and was able to ultimately garner the support of the formidable Big Ten and Southeastern conferences. But the Congressional Black Caucus opposed the legislation in a statement earlier this week, noting that “at the very moment that Black political representation is under attack across the country, we will not be complicit in efforts to further exclude the interests of Black people by advancing legislation that will determine the economic future of Black athletes, their families, and their communities without their meaningful participation and engagement.” President Donald Trump, who’s thrown his support behind the measure, urged the Senate earlier Friday evening to stay in town until the bill passes.“Stop grandstanding, and try getting this done,” he wrote in a social media post.

title: US Senate struggles to wrap up work before August recess
text: WASHINGTON —  The U.S. Senate continued work Friday night without an indication as to when senators would vote on several key legislative priorities. In a rare Friday session that stretched from morning until night, senators had yet to trudge through a slew of measures and adjourn for the coveted August recess. The chamber is not expected to return until after Labor Day.Earlier Friday, the Senate passed, 86-11, a major effort first proposed by the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina that would impose sanctions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, along with the country’s oligarchs and military leaders. A bipartisan education bill — championed by GOP Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Democratic Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado — served as the vehicle for the Russia sanctions package. Collins’ and Bennet’s bill would ensure that “early childhood educators can claim the same federal tax credit for out-of-pocket classroom supply purchases that is currently available to K-12 teachers,” per a press release. Averting a shutdown The Senate also was expected Friday to possibly vote on final passage of a bipartisan measure that would keep the federal government funded through Dec. 11. The House has passed a different version so the two would have to be reconciled.Earlier in the day, senators had advanced the legislation, known as a continuing resolution, toward a final vote on a strongly bipartisan vote of 91-6. Still on tap was a possible vote to adopt a proposed blueprint that would unlock the complex budget reconciliation process and allow Republicans to move ahead on their third party-line bill.Attorney general vote The upper chamber also was expected before recess to confirm acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to be the next U.S. attorney general. Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana marked the determinative vote amid GOP opposition from Collins and Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska over Blanche’s bid, as well as the absence of Republican Sen. name: WyoFile
title: Angi Bruce resigns suddenly as head of Wyoming Game and Fish Department
description:
The agency’s first female director took the helm in 2024, and moves on immediately to a newly created job at Gov. Mark Gordon’s office.
The post Angi Bruce resigns suddenly as head of Wyoming Game and Fish Department appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Angi Bruce, who led the Wyoming Game and Fish Department for two years, resigned from her post effective immediately Friday and is going to work for outgoing Gov. Mark Gordon, whose term ends in January. 
The governor tapped Bruce for the job in 2024. After 4 p.m. Friday, his office announced her resignation and appointment to a new job titled “director of special policy initiatives.” She begins the position Monday. 
The governor’s five-sentence statement did not offer an explanation for the sudden change. Amy Edmonds, a spokesperson for the governor, said Friday that she could not discuss the reason for the transition because it’s a personnel matter.
“Governor Gordon thanks Bruce for her work as director and looks forward to continuing to work with her,” a news release from Gordon’s office stated.   
Eric Wiltanger, currently Game and Fish’s deputy director, has been named interim director. 
Eric Wiltanger was named interim director of the Wyoming Game and Fish Department following the Aug. 7 resignation of the agency’s director, Angi Bruce. (Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Bruce did not immediately respond to a phone call requesting an interview on Friday afternoon. 
At the time of her hire, Bruce earned plaudits for becoming the first woman to rise to the director role at the Wyoming Game and Fish Department. She was also one of the rare biologists who climbed the agency ladder to the top. During Bruce’s tenure, Wyoming completed the long-delayed designation of the state’s first pronghorn migration. She helmed the agency as it recovered from global ire over a Sublette County man’s cruel treatment of an injured wolf that he brought into a Daniel bar. 
Her tenure, however, was studded by some controversies and marked by a rift between field-level staff and leadership at the agency’s Cheyenne headquarters.
Just last month, Cody Region senior wildlife biologist Tony Mong resigned from his post in protest. In an interview with the Powell Tribune, he called the location of the Wyoming State Shooting Complex the final straw in his decision. The 3-square-mile complex was built on “crucial” range for mule deer in an area where herds are especially struggling. 
Under Bruce’s leadership, Game and Fish declined to conduct a formal environmental review of the site. 
Bruce was preceded as director of Game and Fish by Brian Nesvik, who worked the role for seven years being appointed by the Trump administration to direct the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Before that Scott Talbott, who died of pancreatic cancer in 2025, directed the agency for an eight-year stint.
This is a breaking story and may be updated.

name: WyoFile
title: Forest Service’s OK to graze cattle along grizzly-filled Union Pass sparks incoming lawsuit
description:
Conservation groups say they’ll use Endangered Species Act to ask a court to halt grazing in a 30,000-acre area along the Gros Ventre Range. 
The post Forest Service’s OK to graze cattle along grizzly-filled Union Pass sparks incoming lawsuit appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Environmental watchdogs have launched a legal challenge against the U.S. Forest Service’s decision to OK cattle grazing on allotments squarely within the most conflict-prone portion of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem for grizzly bears.  
Temporary restocking of the allotments in question, known as the Elk Ridge complex, drew scrutiny earlier this summer due to the process the Bridger-Teton National Forest used — the public wasn’t notified — and because of the history of grazing in the area. In 2016, woolgrower Mary Thoman struck a deal to waive her permit to graze sheep in the complex in exchange for an undisclosed sum. Cattle grazing there would require further analysis, federal officials said at the time.





Click to enlarge: The Bridger-Teton National Forest compiled this map showing the Elk Ridge complex allotments in relation to adjacent Upper Green allotments during an Endangered Species Act compliance process because the area is a hotbed for conflicts with “threatened” grizzly bears. (U.S. Forest Service)

On Thursday, a coalition of environmental advocates led by the Bondurant-based Yellowstone to Uintas Connection filed an 18-page notice of intent to sue the Forest Service and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, arguing violations of the Endangered Species Act.  
“They’re basically expanding the footprint of cows,” Yellowstone to Uintas Connection founder John Carter told WyoFile. “Now they’re going to have cows spread over 200,000 acres [in the Upper Green], and 30,000 of that is where grizzly bears have not had conflicts, because the sheep were removed.” 
Cora resident and Sage Steppe Wild founder Jonathan Ratner also signed onto the pending lawsuit, and so did three Montana-based groups: Alliance for the Wild Rockies, Native Ecosystems Council and the Council on Wildlife and Fish. 
At this juncture, the plaintiffs are deciding their legal arguments. 
“We couldn’t get an attorney that quick, and so I did this,” said Carter, who’s an ecologist but not an attorney. “We’ll have to [hire an attorney] to go to federal court. That process is ongoing.” 
Carter’s notice was addressed to U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, U.S. Department of Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz, Bridger-Teton Supervisor Chad Hudson, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik and other federal officials. 
Congress requires a 60-day notice for Endangered Species Act lawsuits to help resolve disputes before litigation and give federal agencies time to act. Carter alleged the federal government violated the law when the Forest Service failed to demonstrate it properly consulted with the Fish and Wildlife Service on how the federal action would impact grizzly bears, which for now remain classified as “threatened.” 
John Carter enjoys an evening walk with his dogs Nov. 5, 2019, near Paris, Idaho. (Ryan Dorgan)
In July, Supervisor Chad Hudson provided WyoFile with an Endangered Species Act compliance document that concluded stocking cattle in the complex would “not be expected to have any additional impacts to grizzly bears.” The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service agreed in a May letter.
“Given the proximity, it’s essentially the same bears and the same cows” as the previous grazing arrangement, Hudson told WyoFile. 
The Elk Ridge grazing complex — consisting of the Elk Ridge, Rock Creek, Lime Creek and Tosi allotments — is located about 30 miles southeast of Jackson and mostly falls along the foothills of the Gros Ventre Range. The complex is hugged between allotments where the Upper Green River Cattlemen’s Association is permitted to graze up to 8,772 cow-calf pairs and 47 horses each summer. 
The bought-out allotments have not been authorized for any grazing since sheep were removed in 2016. The Bridger-Teton started the process for restocking the area with cows in 2021, but did not complete its analysis. 
The Cattlemen’s Association was given the OK to run up to 650 of its cow-calf pairs in the complex anyway in 2026 and 2027. The arrangement was described briefly in Bridger-Teton’s 2026 grazing plans for the Pinedale Ranger District. It’s related to the 2025 Dollar Lake Fire, Hudson said, and moving cattle to Elk Ridge is allowing adjacent fire-damaged allotments to rest and recover.   
The Dollar Lake Fire burns along the west shore of upper Green River Lake. Squaretop Mountain is in the background. (Bridger-Teton National Forest)
Upper Green River Cattlemen’s Association President Coke Landers told WyoFile in a Friday text message that he plans to take advantage of the deal and run cows in the disputed 30,000 acres. He stood behind the process the Bridger-Teton used to OK the restocking and remarked that he was “not surprised” by the potential lawsuit. 
“That’s how those organizations survive,” Landers wrote. 
Ratner, one of the expected plaintiffs, says the Bridger-Teton didn’t accurately depict its plans during the Endangered Species Act compliance process.
“Their original consultation was for moving cows from one place to another,” Ratner said. “What they did was completely different.”
Bridger-Teton’s 2026 grazing plans still allow for cattle grazing in the Gypsum allotment rotation, which was hardest hit by the Dollar Lake Fire, he said. 
“The Forest Service lied,” Ratner said. “When an agency lies, that’s arbitrary and capricious decisionmaking.” 
Bridger-Teton National Forest officials declined comment for this story, citing the potential for litigation. 
Cattle grazing in the Upper Green has spurred litigation in the past. Calves that roam the historic 267-square-mile grazing area are especially prone to chronic grizzly depredation, which leads, in turn, to many bears being killed. In 2019, federal wildlife managers OK’d up to 72 grizzly bears being killed as a result of the conflict. That decision was litigated, and in 2023 environmental groups claimed a partial victory. 
A 2025 estimate indicated Upper Green cattle grazing could cause the “incidental take,” or death, of up to 40 grizzly bears between 2025 and 2034. There have been repeated attempts to reduce conflict, but in recent years the cattle-bovine bloodshed has worsened.

description: LSU President Wade Rousse has announced members of the committee that will select the next LSU New Orleans chancellor by the end of the year.  The university was previously led by Kathy Johnson, who served as president of the University of New Orleans from 2023 until shortly before the school left the University of Louisiana […]
text:
New signage faces the Elysian Fields Avenue entrance to the LSU New Orleans campus, formerly known as the University of New Orleans. (Photo Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)LSU President Wade Rousse has announced members of the committee that will select the next LSU New Orleans chancellor by the end of the year. 
The university was previously led by Kathy Johnson, who served as president of the University of New Orleans from 2023 until shortly before the school left the University of Louisiana System for the LSU System and adopted LSU’s branding. 
“This campus is entering a defining period of institutional transformation and its top leader must strengthen public trust, expand enrollment and research activity, and position LSU New Orleans as a model for modern urban higher education,” Rousse said in a news release. 
The committee will get its first look at the applicant pool Aug. 25, with the goal of selecting a finalist in December. 
The search committee will be chaired  by Nick Mueller, a former UNO vice chancellor. Members include: 

Boysie Bollinger, a New Orleans business magnate and ally of Gov. Jeff Landry 
Bobby Savoie, Loyola University’s business dean, an LSU alumnus and prominent donor to UNO 
Dave Sherman, a New Orleans attorney and UNO business grad
Michael Hecht, CEO emeritus for Greater New Orleans 
Gary Solomon, a New Orleans businessman and major UNO donor
Larissa Littleton-Steib, chancellor of Delgado Community College
Former state Rep. Jim Tucker of Algiers 
Chris Summa, Faculty Senate president 
Coleen Maidlow, Staff Council president 
Kamille Ison 
Mike Jackson, a New Orleans construction engineer and UNO alumnus
Jeff Ehlinger, a New Orleans bank executive and UNO graduate
Randall Langston, LSU New Orleans vice president of enrollment management

title: Legislative immunity clause protects Alaska ethics investigations, state Supreme Court says
description: The Alaska Supreme Court on Friday upheld a lower court’s decision to dismiss a lawsuit by former state Sen. Lora Reinbold, R-Eagle River, against the state of Alaska and the Alaska Legislature’s committee on legislative ethics. Reinbold had sued the committee and the state’s executive branch in 2022 after the committee concluded that Reinbold had […]
text:
Sen. Lora Reinbold, R-Eagle River, speaks Tuesday, May 10, 2022, on the floor of the Alaska Senate at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau, Alaska. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Supreme Court on Friday upheld a lower court’s decision to dismiss a lawsuit by former state Sen. Lora Reinbold, R-Eagle River, against the state of Alaska and the Alaska Legislature’s committee on legislative ethics.
Reinbold had sued the committee and the state’s executive branch in 2022 after the committee concluded that Reinbold had violated the Legislative Ethics Act by blocking people from commenting on her legislative Facebook page “solely for expressing opinions in disagreement with her own.” 
Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews dismissed Reinbold’s case in 2024. She unsuccessfully asked Matthews to reconsider, then appealed to the Supreme Court. 
Writing on behalf of the court — which ruled unanimously — Justice Dario Borghesan said, “At no point did the Ethics Committee act outside the statutorily defined investigative process. Therefore, its actions are protected by legislative immunity.”
That immunity derives from Article II, Section 6 of the Alaska Constitution, which states that “Legislators may not be held to answer before any other tribunal for any statement made in exercise of their legislative duties while the legislature is in session.”
Reinbold argued that immunity should not apply because her due process rights were violated. 
“But legislative immunity applies even to claims that a legislative body has violated the right to due process,” Borghesan wrote.
Reinbold, reached by text message on Friday morning, said she was unable to immediately talk about the issue because she was at an event with U.S. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson.
Johnson is in Alaska this week as part of a trip to boost the re-election campaign of U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III, R-Alaska.
In Friday’s 19-page order, Borghesan states that a plaintiff or defendant could make an argument that immunity conflicts with the Alaska Constitution’s guarantee — under Article I, Section 7 — of “fair and just treatment in the course of executive legislative and executive investigations.”
In this case, neither plaintiffs nor defendants briefed that argument, Borghesan said. Reinbold briefly raised the argument, he said, but “offer(ed) no legal authority to help us interpret this constitutional provision.”
“Because Reinbold’s assertion that the Ethics Committee violated her right to fair and just treatment was not adequately briefed, we do not consider it,” he said.
The court’s order this week also upholds Judge Matthews’ decision to deny Reinbold the chance to amend her legal complaint. Reinbold had requested to change it after the deadline to do so.
In addition, the order upholds Matthews’ decision to dismiss claims against the executive branch as moot.
Reinbold had objected to a letter from the governor saying that neither he nor other members of the administration would work with her because she repeatedly spread misinformation about the state’s response to COVID-19.
“Reinbold is no longer a legislator, so we could not order the executive branch to work with her,” Borghesan wrote. 
Reinbold had argued that a similar case could arise in the future and that the issue is not moot. 
But Borghesan said that if a similar case arises between another legislator and another governor in the future, the court will consider those arguments at that time.
